school-c11-maths-b.title: Class 11 Mathematics — Part B (Ch 8 to Revision & Practice)
school-c11-maths-b.description: All 14 chapters of Class 11 Mathematics, chapter by chapter, with solved examples, common mistakes, quizzes, chapter tests and a revision course with two mock papers.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Sequences and Series
courses.summary: Sequences and series, a quick recap of arithmetic progressions, geometric progressions with nth term and sums, arithmetic and geometric means with AM ≥ GM, and sums of special series.
outcomes: Learners can describe a sequence by a formula or recurrence and write the related series
Learners can find terms and sums of A.P.s and G.P.s
Learners can insert arithmetic and geometric means and use AM ≥ GM
Learners can sum infinite G.P.s and the series Σk, Σk², Σk³

scenes.text: Diya saves ₹100 in January and ₹20 more each month after that.
Her monthly savings 100, 120, 140, … form an A.P.; the yearly total is a series.

steps.title: Sequence and series
steps.body:
A **sequence** is a function from N (or {1, …, n}) to numbers: a₁, a₂, a₃, … with nth term aₙ.
- **Finite** or **infinite**.
- Given by a formula (aₙ = n² + 1) or a **recurrence** (Fibonacci: a₁ = a₂ = 1, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂).

A **series** is the sum a₁ + a₂ + … written Σaₖ. A **progression** is a sequence whose terms follow a definite pattern.

steps.title: A.P. recap
steps.body:
A.P.: a, a + d, a + 2d, …
- aₙ = a + (n − 1)d
- Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n − 1)d] = (n/2)(a + l)
- Arithmetic mean of a and b: A = (a + b)/2
- Inserting n A.M.s between a and b: d = (b − a)/(n + 1).

steps.title: Solved example 1: recurrence
steps.body:
a₁ = 1, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 2 for n ≥ 2. First five terms and the series?

- 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; series 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using n instead of (n − 1) in aₙ.
- Confusing the sequence (list) with the series (sum).
- Assuming every sequence has a formula — some (like primes) do not have a simple one.

activity.prompt: Find the 20th term of the A.P. 7, 11, 15, …

quiz.q: First three terms of aₙ = n(n + 2) are
In the Fibonacci sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, … the 7th term is
quiz.why: Each Fibonacci term is the sum of the previous two: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. So the 7th term is 13.

quiz.q: Sum of first 50 natural numbers is
quiz.why: The sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n + 1)/2. For n = 50 that is 50 × 51/2 = 1275.

quiz.q: The A.M. of 8 and 20 is
quiz.why: The arithmetic mean of two numbers is half their sum: (8 + 20)/2 = 14. 28 is just the sum.

quiz.q: aₙ = 4n − 3. The sequence is
quiz.why: Consecutive terms differ by aₙ − aₙ₋₁ = 4n − 3 − (4n − 7) = 4, a constant, so it is an A.P. with common difference 4.

scenes.text: A culture of 30 bacteria doubles every hour.
30, 60, 120, … — each term is the previous times 2. That is a G.P., and it grows fast.

steps.title: G.P.
steps.body:
A sequence is a **G.P.** if each term after the first is obtained by multiplying the previous by a fixed non-zero **common ratio r**: a, ar, ar², …

- **aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹**
- **Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1)** for r ≠ 1 (or a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)); if r = 1, Sₙ = na.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Find the 10th term and the sum of 10 terms of 5, 25, 125, …

- a = 5, r = 5.
- a₁₀ = 5 × 5⁹ = 5¹⁰ = 9765625.
- S₁₀ = 5(5¹⁰ − 1)/4 = (5/4)(5¹⁰ − 1).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
The 4th term of a G.P. is the square of its 2nd term and the 1st term is −3. Find the 7th term.

- ar³ = (ar)² → r = a = −3.
- a₇ = ar⁶ = −3 × 729 = **−2187**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rⁿ instead of rⁿ⁻¹ for the nth term.
- Using the sum formula when r = 1.
- Losing the sign of a negative ratio (terms alternate in sign).

activity.prompt: Bacteria start at 30 and double every hour. How many are there at the end of the 4th hour?

quiz.q: The common ratio of 1, −3, 9, −27, … is
quiz.why: The common ratio is any term divided by the previous one: −3/1 = −3, and 9/(−3) = −3. The signs alternate because the ratio is negative.

quiz.q: The 8th term of 2, 4, 8, … is
quiz.why: The nth term of a G.P. is arⁿ⁻¹. Here a = 2 and r = 2, so the 8th term is 2 × 2⁷ = 256.

quiz.q: Sum of 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2⁹ is
quiz.why: This is a G.P. with a = 1, r = 2 and 10 terms, so the sum is (2¹⁰ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 1023.

quiz.q: If 2, x, 18 are in G.P., x (positive) is
quiz.why: In a G.P. the middle term squared equals the product of its neighbours: x² = 2 × 18 = 36. So x = 6 for positive x.

quiz.q: Which is a G.P.?
quiz.why: Only 0.3, 0.03, 0.003 has a constant ratio (0.1). The 2, 5, 8, 11 list has a constant difference, and the others have no constant ratio.

scenes.text: An investment grows 10% one year and 40% the next. The fair 'average growth factor' is not the A.M.
For growth, multiplying matters — so we use the geometric mean.

steps.title: Geometric mean
steps.body:
The **G.M.** of positive numbers a and b is **G = √(ab)**.

To insert n G.M.s between a and b: a, G₁, …, Gₙ, b is a G.P. with n + 2 terms, so b = arⁿ⁺¹ → **r = (b/a)^(1/(n+1))**.

steps.title: AM ≥ GM
steps.body:
For positive a, b: A − G = (a + b)/2 − √(ab) = (√a − √b)²/2 ≥ 0. So **A ≥ G**, with equality iff a = b.

If A and G are the A.M. and G.M. of two numbers, the numbers are A ± √(A² − G²) (roots of x² − 2Ax + G² = 0).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Insert 3 G.M.s between 1 and 256.

- 256 = 1 · r⁴ → r = 4 (taking real positive).
- Means: **4, 16, 64**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
The A.M. and G.M. of two positive numbers are 10 and 8. Find them.

- a + b = 20, ab = 64.
- x² − 20x + 64 = 0 → (x − 16)(x − 4) = 0.
- Numbers: **16 and 4**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking the G.M. of numbers with different signs (not defined as a real positive mean).
- Using n instead of n + 1 when inserting means.
- Thinking A.M. can be smaller than G.M. for positive numbers.

activity.prompt: Match each pair with its G.M.

quiz.q: G.M. of 3 and 12 is
quiz.why: The geometric mean of a and b is √(ab) = √(3 × 12) = √36 = 6.

quiz.q: For positive unequal numbers,
quiz.why: For two unequal positive numbers, A.M. > G.M., because (√a − √b)² > 0. They are equal only when the numbers are equal.

quiz.q: Inserting 2 G.M.s between 2 and 54 gives ratio
quiz.why: With 2 G.M.s between 2 and 54 there are 4 terms, so 54 = 2r³. Then r³ = 27 and r = 3.

quiz.q: If A.M. = 5 and G.M. = 4 for two numbers, their product is
quiz.why: G² = ab, so with G.M. = 4 the product is 4² = 16. The A.M. of 5 gives the sum 10, not the product.

quiz.q: The minimum value of x + 1/x for x > 0 is
quiz.why: By A.M. ≥ G.M. for positive x and 1/x: (x + 1/x)/2 ≥ √(x · 1/x) = 1. So x + 1/x ≥ 2, with equality at x = 1.

scenes.text: A ball dropped from 10 m rebounds to half its height each time.
It bounces forever in theory, yet the total distance is finite — the magic of an infinite G.P.

steps.title: Sum to infinity
steps.body:
If |r| < 1, rⁿ → 0 as n grows, so
**S∞ = a/(1 − r)**.
If |r| ≥ 1 the infinite G.P. has no finite sum.

steps.title: Special series
steps.body:
- Σk = 1 + 2 + … + n = **n(n + 1)/2**
- Σk² = **n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6**
- Σk³ = **[n(n + 1)/2]²**

To sum Σ f(k) for a polynomial f, split into these pieces.

steps.title: Solved example 1: the ball
steps.body:
Drop from 10 m, rebound ratio 1/2.

- Down: 10. Then each rebound goes up and down: 2(5 + 2.5 + …) = 2 × 5/(1 − 1/2) = 20.
- Total distance = **30 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a/(1 − r) when |r| ≥ 1.
- Squaring the wrong thing: Σk³ = (Σk)², not Σk².
- Forgetting the first drop when summing bounce distances.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: Sum to infinity and special series may be treated briefly in some rationalised editions; they are standard for JEE.

activity.prompt: Find the sum to infinity of 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + …

quiz.q: Sum to infinity of 1 − 1/3 + 1/9 − … is
quiz.why: This is a G.P. with a = 1 and r = −1/3, and |r| < 1, so S = a/(1 − r) = 1/(1 + 1/3) = 3/4.

quiz.q: 1² + 2² + … + 10² equals
quiz.why: The formula n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 gives 10 × 11 × 21/6 = 385.

quiz.q: 1³ + 2³ + … + 5³ equals
quiz.why: The sum of cubes of the first n natural numbers is [n(n + 1)/2]². For n = 5 that is 15² = 225.

quiz.q: An infinite G.P. has a finite sum when
quiz.why: An infinite G.P. has a finite sum only if its terms shrink towards zero, which requires |r| < 1.

quiz.q: Sum of first n odd numbers is
quiz.why: The first n odd numbers form an A.P. with first term 1 and last term 2n − 1. Their sum is n/2 × (1 + 2n − 1) = n².

questions.q: The 5th term of aₙ = (−1)ⁿ⁻¹ 5ⁿ⁺¹ is
questions.why: For n = 5, aₙ = (−1)⁴ × 5⁶ = 1 × 15625 = 15625. The sign is positive because the power of −1 is even.

questions.q: The common ratio of 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, … is
questions.why: Each term is half the previous term, so the common ratio is (1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2.

questions.q: The 12th term of the G.P. 2, 6, 18, … is
questions.why: The G.P. 2, 6, 18, … has a = 2 and r = 3. The 12th term is ar¹¹ = 2 · 3¹¹.

questions.q: G.M. of 4 and 16 is
questions.why: The geometric mean of 4 and 16 is √(4 × 16) = √64 = 8.

questions.q: Sum of 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … to infinity is
questions.why: The G.P. 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … has r = 1/2, so the infinite sum is 1/(1 − 1/2) = 2.

questions.q: Sum of first 20 terms of 1, 2, 3, … squared (1² + … + 20²) is
If the 5th and 8th terms of a G.P. are 48 and 384, r =
Assertion: For positive a, b, (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab). Reason: (√a − √b)² ≥ 0.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: Both are true. Expanding (√a − √b)² ≥ 0 gives a + b − 2√(ab) ≥ 0, which is exactly (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab), so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Sum of the series 0.6 + 0.66 + 0.666 + … to n terms is
Case: A town's population of 20,000 grows 5% per year (compounded). The population after 3 years is closest to
questions.why: Compound growth gives 20000 × (1.05)³ = 20000 × 1.157625 ≈ 23,152.5, which is closest to 23,153.

questions.q: If a, b, c are in G.P., then
questions.why: In a G.P. the ratio of consecutive terms is constant, so b/a = c/b. Cross-multiplying gives b² = ac. The equation 2b = a + c is for an A.P.

questions.q: The value of 1×2 + 2×3 + … + 10×11 is
Case: A ball dropped from 12 m rebounds to 3/4 of its height each time. Total distance travelled before coming to rest is
questions.why: The ball falls 12 m first. Then each rebound up and fall back down adds twice the rebound height: 2 × (9 + 6.75 + …) = 2 × 9/(1 − 3/4) = 72. Total = 12 + 72 = 84 m.

questions.q: If A.M. and G.M. of two positive numbers are 25 and 20, the numbers are
questions.why: The sum of the numbers is 2 × 25 = 50 and their product is 20² = 400. They are the roots of x² − 50x + 400 = 0, i.e. 10 and 40.

questions.q: The sum 1³ + 2³ + … + n³ equals 3025 when n is
questions.why: The sum of cubes is [n(n + 1)/2]². Setting this to 3025 gives n(n + 1)/2 = 55, so n(n + 1) = 110, and n = 10.

questions.q: If the sum of n terms of a G.P. 1, 3, 9, … is 364, n =
questions.why: The G.P. has a = 1 and r = 3, so the sum is (3ⁿ − 1)/2 = 364. This gives 3ⁿ = 729 = 3⁶, so n = 6.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Straight Lines
courses.summary: Slope and inclination, parallel and perpendicular lines, all standard forms of a line's equation, the general equation, the distance of a point from a line and between parallel lines.
outcomes: Learners can find slope, test parallel/perpendicular lines and collinearity
Learners can write a line in point-slope, two-point, slope-intercept and intercept forms
Learners can convert the general equation Ax + By + C = 0 into other forms
Learners can find distances from a point to a line and between parallel lines

lessons.title: Slope of a line and angle between lines

scenes.text: Building rules ask for a ramp that rises at most 1 m for every 12 m of run.
That is a slope of 1/12. Slope is the steepness number of a line.

steps.title: Slope
steps.body:
For a non-vertical line through P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂):
**m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = tan θ**, where θ (0° ≤ θ < 180°, θ ≠ 90°) is the **inclination** with the positive x-axis.

- Horizontal line: m = 0. Vertical line: slope undefined.
- **Parallel:** m₁ = m₂. **Perpendicular:** m₁m₂ = −1.
- **Angle between lines:** tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)| (acute angle).
- Points A, B, C are **collinear** if slope AB = slope BC.

steps.title: Solved example 2: angle
steps.body:
Angle between lines with slopes 1/√3 and √3?

- tan θ = |(√3 − 1/√3)/(1 + 1)| = |(2/√3)/2| = 1/√3.
- θ = **30°** (the obtuse angle is 150°).

steps.title: Solved example 3: collinearity
steps.body:
Are A(−2, −1), B(4, 0), C(3, 3) and D(−3, 2) the vertices of a parallelogram?

- slope AB = 1/6, slope DC = 1/6 → AB ∥ DC.
- slope BC = −3, slope AD = −3 → BC ∥ AD. Yes, a parallelogram.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing the order: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₁ − x₂) gives the wrong sign.
- Saying a vertical line has slope 0.
- Forgetting the absolute value in the angle formula.

steps.title: Use the Geometry lab
steps.body: Drag two points in the Geometry lab and watch m change as the line turns.

activity.prompt: Find the slope of the line through (1, 2) and (4, 11).

quiz.q: Inclination of a line with slope −1 is
quiz.why: The inclination θ satisfies tan θ = slope = −1, with θ between 0° and 180°. That gives θ = 135°, not −45°.

quiz.q: Lines with slopes 2 and −1/2 are
quiz.why: Two lines are perpendicular when the product of their slopes is −1. Here 2 × (−1/2) = −1.

quiz.q: The slope of the x-axis is
quiz.why: The x-axis is horizontal, so it does not rise or fall, and its slope is 0. A vertical line (like the y-axis) is the one with undefined slope.
The slope between (1, 1) and (2, 3) is 2, and between (2, 3) and (3, 5) is also 2. Equal slopes through a shared point mean the three points lie on one line.

quiz.q: If a line makes 60° with the positive x-axis, its slope is
quiz.why: The slope of a line is the tangent of its inclination, so m = tan 60° = √3.

lessons.title: Forms of the equation of a line

scenes.text: A taxi charges ₹40 to start and ₹15 per km.
Fare y = 15x + 40 is a line with slope 15 and y-intercept 40 — the slope-intercept form.

steps.title: Standard forms
steps.body:
- **Horizontal / vertical:** y = a, x = b.
- **Point-slope:** y − y₀ = m(x − x₀).
- **Two-point:** y − y₁ = [(y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)](x − x₁).
- **Slope-intercept:** y = mx + c (c = y-intercept); or y = m(x − d) with x-intercept d.
- **Intercept form:** x/a + y/b = 1 (intercepts a on x-axis, b on y-axis).

steps.title: Solved example 1: point-slope
steps.body:
Line through (−2, 3) with slope −4:

- y − 3 = −4(x + 2) → **4x + y + 5 = 0**.

steps.title: Solved example 3: intercepts
steps.body: Line with intercepts 3 and 2 on the axes: x/3 + y/2 = 1 → **2x + 3y = 6**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using point-slope for a vertical line (slope undefined) — write x = x₀.
- Sign slips in y − y₀ when y₀ is negative.
- In intercept form, the intercept is the value on the axis, not the length (it can be negative).

steps.title: Linear models
steps.body: Celsius and Fahrenheit: F = (9/5)C + 32 is a line through (0, 32) and (100, 212). Spring length vs load (Hooke's law) is another.

activity.prompt: Match the line with its equation.

quiz.q: Equation of a line through (2, 3) parallel to the x-axis is
quiz.why: A line parallel to the x-axis is horizontal, so every point on it has the same y-value. Through (2, 3), that is y = 3.

quiz.q: Slope-intercept form of 3x + 4y = 12 is
quiz.why: Solve for y: 4y = −3x + 12, so y = −(3/4)x + 3. The slope is −3/4 and the y-intercept is 3.

quiz.q: A line with slope 1/2 through (0, −1) is
quiz.why: With slope 1/2 and y-intercept −1, y = x/2 − 1. Multiplying by 2 gives 2y = x − 2, which is x − 2y − 2 = 0.

quiz.q: Intercepts of 2x − 3y + 6 = 0 on the axes are
quiz.why: Put y = 0 in 2x − 3y + 6 = 0: x = −3. Put x = 0: y = 2. So the x-intercept is −3 and the y-intercept is 2.

quiz.q: Line through (1, 2) and (1, 7) is
quiz.why: Both points have x = 1, so the line is vertical, with the equation x = 1.

scenes.text: A village at point P wants the shortest pipe to a straight highway.
The shortest pipe is the perpendicular — its length is given by one neat formula.

steps.title: General equation Ax + By + C = 0
steps.body:
Any first-degree equation (A, B not both 0) is a line.
- Slope = −A/B (B ≠ 0); y-intercept = −C/B; x-intercept = −C/A.
- Lines A₁x + B₁y + C₁ = 0 and A₂x + B₂y + C₂ = 0 are parallel if A₁/A₂ = B₁/B₂; perpendicular if A₁A₂ + B₁B₂ = 0.

steps.title: Distances
steps.body:
- Point (x₁, y₁) to line Ax + By + C = 0: **d = |Ax₁ + By₁ + C| / √(A² + B²)**.
- Between parallel lines Ax + By + C₁ = 0 and Ax + By + C₂ = 0: **d = |C₁ − C₂| / √(A² + B²)**.
- A line parallel to Ax + By + C = 0 is Ax + By + k = 0; perpendicular is Bx − Ay + k = 0.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Distance between 3x − 4y + 7 = 0 and 3x − 4y + 5 = 0:

- |7 − 5|/5 = **2/5**.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Line through (2, 3) perpendicular to x − 2y + 3 = 0:

- Perpendicular family: 2x + y + k = 0. Through (2, 3): 4 + 3 + k = 0 → k = −7.
- **2x + y − 7 = 0**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the modulus in the distance formula.
- Using the parallel-lines formula when the x, y coefficients are not identical — first make them equal (e.g. divide 6x − 8y + 4 = 0 by 2).
- Slope sign: for Ax + By + C = 0, slope is −A/B.

activity.prompt: Find the distance of the point (0, 0) from the line 3x + 4y − 10 = 0.

quiz.q: Slope of 2x − 5y + 7 = 0 is
quiz.why: For a line Ax + By + C = 0 the slope is −A/B. Here that is −2/(−5) = 2/5.

quiz.q: Lines 2x + 3y = 5 and 3x − 2y = 1 are
quiz.why: The slopes are −2/3 and 3/2, whose product is −1. (Equivalently, a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = 6 − 6 = 0), so the lines are perpendicular.

quiz.q: Distance between x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is
quiz.why: For parallel lines x + y − 1 = 0 and x + y − 3 = 0, the distance is |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²) = 2/√2 = √2.

quiz.q: Line parallel to 3x − y + 4 = 0 through (0, 0) is
quiz.why: A parallel line has the same x and y coefficients, only a different constant. The line through the origin therefore has no constant: 3x − y = 0.

quiz.q: Distance of (1, 1) from x = 4 is
quiz.why: The line x = 4 is vertical, so the distance of a point from it is the horizontal gap |4 − 1| = 3.

scenes.text: A shopkeeper sells 980 L of milk at ₹14/L and 1220 L at ₹16/L each week.
Assuming a linear relation, she predicts sales at ₹17/L using the two-point form.

steps.title: Toolbox
steps.body:
- Feet of perpendiculars, reflections, concurrency, triangle areas.
- **Area of triangle** with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃): ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|; zero ⇔ collinear.
- A point divides a segment in ratio m : n at ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)).

steps.title: Solved example 1: linear demand
steps.body:
Points (price, litres): (14, 980), (16, 1220).

- Slope = 240/2 = 120 litres per rupee.
- L − 980 = 120(P − 14). At P = 17: L = 980 + 360 = **1340 litres**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: line through intersection
steps.body:
Find the line through the intersection of x + y = 5 and x − y = 1 and perpendicular to 2x + y = 4.

- Intersection: x = 3, y = 2.
- Perpendicular slope = 1/2: y − 2 = (1/2)(x − 3) → **x − 2y + 1 = 0**.

steps.title: Solved example 3: midpoint and intercepts
steps.body:
A line segment between the axes is bisected at (2, 3). Find the line.

- Intercepts are (4, 0) and (0, 6): x/4 + y/6 = 1 → **3x + 2y = 12**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming 'the point divides the intercepted segment in ratio 1 : 2' means the same as 2 : 1 — check which end is first.
- Not checking the answer by substituting the given points.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find the foot of the perpendicular from P(x₁, y₁) to a line L.
items: Find the slope m of L
Write the line through P with that slope
The intersection point is the foot of the perpendicular

quiz.q: Area of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 3) is
quiz.why: The triangle has a right angle at the origin, with base 4 and height 3. Area = ½ × 4 × 3 = 6.

quiz.q: If (1, 2), (3, k), (5, 6) are collinear, k =
quiz.why: For collinear points the slope between consecutive points is the same. From (1, 2) to (5, 6) the slope is 1, so from (1, 2) to (3, k) we need (k − 2)/2 = 1, giving k = 4.

quiz.q: Intersection of x = 2 and y = −1 is
quiz.why: The point lies on both x = 2 and y = −1, so its coordinates are (2, −1).

quiz.q: A line through (2, 3) and (5, 9) has slope
quiz.why: Slope = (9 − 3)/(5 − 2) = 6/3 = 2. 6 is only the rise, not the slope.

quiz.q: The perpendicular from (0, 0) to x + y = 2 meets it at
quiz.why: The line x + y = 2 has slope −1, so the perpendicular from the origin has slope 1 and lies on y = x. Substituting gives 2x = 2, so the foot is (1, 1).

questions.q: Slope of the line through (2, 5) and (−4, −7) is
The line y = 3 is
questions.why: y = 3 has the same y-value everywhere, so the line is horizontal and parallel to the x-axis. Its slope is 0, not 3.

questions.q: Equation of the line with slope −1 and y-intercept 4 is
questions.why: With slope −1 and y-intercept 4, y = −x + 4, which rearranges to x + y = 4.

questions.q: Slope of a line perpendicular to 3x + 4y = 7 is
questions.why: 3x + 4y = 7 has slope −3/4. A perpendicular line has the negative reciprocal slope, which is 4/3.

questions.q: x-intercept of 5x − 2y + 10 = 0 is
questions.why: The x-intercept is where y = 0: 5x + 10 = 0, giving x = −2.

questions.q: The acute angle between y = x and y = √3 x is
questions.why: The lines y = x and y = √3x have inclinations 45° and 60°, so the angle between them is 60° − 45° = 15°.

questions.q: Distance of (4, 1) from 3x − 4y + 12 = 0 is
Assertion: Lines 2x + 3y + 4 = 0 and 4x + 6y + 5 = 0 are parallel. Reason: Their slopes are equal.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. Each line has slope −2/3, and equal slopes (with different constants) make the lines parallel, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Distance between 6x + 8y − 4 = 0 and 3x + 4y + 3 = 0 is
questions.why: Write 6x + 8y − 4 = 0 as 3x + 4y − 2 = 0. The parallel lines 3x + 4y − 2 = 0 and 3x + 4y + 3 = 0 are |−2 − 3|/√(9 + 16) = 5/5 = 1 apart.

questions.q: Line through (1, 2) making equal intercepts on the axes is
questions.why: Equal intercepts a give x/a + y/a = 1, i.e. x + y = a. Through (1, 2), a = 3, so the line is x + y = 3.

questions.q: Case: Spring length L (cm) under load W (kg) is linear: L = 124.942 at W = 2 and L = 125.134 at W = 4 (example values). The slope ΔL/ΔW is
questions.why: The slope is the change in length per unit load: (125.134 − 124.942)/(4 − 2) = 0.192/2 = 0.096 cm per kg.

questions.q: The foot of the perpendicular from (−1, 3) to 3x − 4y − 16 = 0 is
questions.why: Perpendicular 4x + 3y = 5; solving with 3x − 4y = 16 gives x = 68/25, y = −49/25.

questions.q: If the line x/a + y/b = 1 passes through (2, −3) and (4, −5), then (a, b) =
questions.why: The line through (2, −3) and (4, −5) has slope −1, so y + 3 = −(x − 2), giving x + y = −1. In intercept form that is x/(−1) + y/(−1) = 1, so a = −1 and b = −1.

questions.q: The area of the triangle formed by x + y = 4 and the coordinate axes is
questions.why: The line x + y = 4 meets the axes at (4, 0) and (0, 4). The triangle with the axes has area ½ × 4 × 4 = 8.

questions.q: Reflection of (1, 2) in the line y = x is
questions.why: Reflecting a point in the line y = x swaps its coordinates, so (1, 2) becomes (2, 1).

questions.q: For the lines 3x + 4y = 9 and 6x + ky = 5 to be parallel, k =
questions.why: Parallel lines have equal slopes: −3/4 = −6/k, which gives k = 8. Equivalently the coefficient ratios match: 3/6 = 4/k.

questions.q: Find the point on the x-axis equidistant from (7, 6) and (3, 4).
questions.why: Let the point be (x, 0). Equal distances give (x − 7)² + 36 = (x − 3)² + 16, i.e. −14x + 85 = −6x + 25, so 8x = 60 and x = 15/2.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Conic Sections
courses.summary: Circles, parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas as sections of a double cone, with standard equations, foci, vertices, axes, eccentricity, directrices and latus rectum.
outcomes: Learners can describe conics as sections of a cone
Learners can write the equation of a circle and find centre and radius from the general form
Learners can find focus, directrix and latus rectum of a parabola
Learners can find a, b, c, e and latus rectum for an ellipse and a hyperbola

lessons.title: Sections of a cone and the circle

scenes.text: A lamp shade throws a cone of light. Tilt the wall and the bright patch changes from circle to oval to an open curve.
Those patches are conic sections — and planets travel along ellipses.

steps.title: Conic sections
steps.body:
Cut a double cone (semi-vertical angle α) by a plane making angle β with the axis:
- β = 90°: **circle**
- α < β < 90°: **ellipse**
- β = α: **parabola**
- 0 ≤ β < α: **hyperbola**
Through the vertex we get *degenerate* conics: a point, a line or a pair of lines.

steps.title: The circle
steps.body:
Set of points at a fixed distance r (radius) from a fixed point (h, k) (centre):
**(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²**; centred at the origin x² + y² = r².

General form **x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0** has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c) (needs g² + f² − c > 0).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Centre and radius of x² + y² + 8x + 10y − 8 = 0.

- Complete squares: (x + 4)² + (y + 5)² = 8 + 16 + 25 = 49.
- Centre **(−4, −5)**, radius **7**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the centre of (x + 4)² + … as (4, …): the sign flips.
- Forgetting that x² and y² must have equal coefficients (and no xy term) for a circle.
- Writing r instead of r² on the right side.

activity.prompt: Match the cutting plane with the conic.

quiz.q: Centre of (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 16 is
quiz.why: The circle (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² has centre (h, k). Here (x − 3)² and (y + 2)² give the centre (3, −2), because the signs flip.

quiz.q: Radius of x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 is
Equation of a circle with centre (0, 0) and radius 4 is
quiz.why: A circle centred at the origin with radius r is x² + y² = r². With r = 4, r² = 16, so x² + y² = 16.

quiz.q: When the plane is parallel to a generator, the section is a
quiz.why: If the cutting plane is parallel to a generator (a slant line) of the cone, the section is a parabola. A plane meeting the axis at a bigger angle gives an ellipse, and a smaller angle gives a hyperbola.

quiz.q: Circle with centre (−a, −b) and radius √(a² − b²) is
quiz.why: With centre (−a, −b) and radius √(a² − b²), (x + a)² + (y + b)² = a² − b². Expanding gives x² + y² + 2ax + 2by + a² + b² − a² + b² = 0, i.e. x² + y² + 2ax + 2by + 2b² = 0.

scenes.text: A dish antenna is shaped so that every incoming signal reflects to one point — the receiver.
That point is the focus of a parabola; car headlights use the same idea in reverse.

steps.title: Definition and standard forms
steps.body:
A **parabola** is the set of points equidistant from a fixed line (**directrix**) and a fixed point (**focus**) not on it.

With a > 0:
- y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, opens right
- y² = −4ax: focus (−a, 0), directrix x = a, opens left
- x² = 4ay: focus (0, a), directrix y = −a, opens up
- x² = −4ay: focus (0, −a), directrix y = a, opens down

Vertex at origin; **latus rectum** (focal chord ⟂ axis) length = **4a**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
For y² = 8x find focus, axis, directrix, latus rectum.

- 4a = 8 → a = 2.
- Focus (2, 0), axis y = 0, directrix x = −2, latus rectum 8.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Parabola with focus (0, −3) and directrix y = 3.

- Focus below, opens down: x² = −4ay with a = 3.
- **x² = −12y**.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Parabola symmetric about the y-axis, vertex at origin, through (2, 3).

- x² = 4ay; 4 = 12a → a = 1/3.
- **3x² = 4y**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up which variable is squared: y² = … opens left/right; x² = … opens up/down.
- Writing the latus rectum as 2a instead of 4a.
- Sign of the directrix: it is on the opposite side from the focus.

activity.prompt: For the parabola x² = −16y, what is the length of the latus rectum?

quiz.q: Focus of y² = 12x is
quiz.why: For y² = 4ax, the focus is (a, 0). Here 4a = 12, so a = 3 and the focus is (3, 0).

quiz.q: Directrix of x² = 6y is
quiz.why: For x² = 4ay, 4a = 6 so a = 3/2. The directrix is y = −a = −3/2.

quiz.q: y² = −8x opens towards
quiz.why: In y² = −8x the coefficient of x is negative, so the parabola opens towards the negative x-direction, i.e. to the left.

quiz.q: Parabola with focus (6, 0) and directrix x = −6:
quiz.why: A focus at (6, 0) and directrix x = −6 give a = 6, so the parabola is y² = 4ax = 24x.

quiz.q: A parabola's points are equidistant from
quiz.why: By definition, every point of a parabola is the same distance from its focus and from its directrix.

scenes.text: In an elliptical hall, a whisper at one special spot can be heard clearly at another far away.
Those spots are the foci: sound from one reflects to the other.

steps.title: Definition and key quantities
steps.body:
An **ellipse** is the set of points whose distances from two fixed points (**foci**) add to a constant 2a.

Standard form (major axis along x): **x²/a² + y²/b² = 1**, a > b.
- c² = a² − b² (centre to focus c)
- Foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0); major axis 2a, minor axis 2b
- **Eccentricity e = c/a**, 0 < e < 1 (e → 0 is nearly a circle)
- **Latus rectum = 2b²/a**
- If y² has the larger denominator, the major axis is along y: x²/b² + y²/a² = 1, foci (0, ±c).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
x²/25 + y²/9 = 1.

- a = 5, b = 3, c = √(25 − 9) = 4.
- Foci (±4, 0), vertices (±5, 0), major axis 10, minor axis 6, e = 4/5, latus rectum 2(9)/5 = 18/5.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Ellipse with vertices (0, ±13), foci (0, ±5).

- Major axis along y: a = 13, c = 5, b² = 169 − 25 = 144.
- **x²/144 + y²/169 = 1**.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Find a, b, e for 9x² + 4y² = 36.

- Divide by 36: x²/4 + y²/9 = 1 → a = 3 (along y), b = 2, c = √5, e = √5/3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming a is always under x²: a is under the LARGER denominator.
- Using c² = a² + b² (that is the hyperbola).
- Forgetting to bring the equation to '= 1' first.

activity.prompt: For x²/36 + y²/16 = 1, find c (the distance from centre to a focus), to 2 decimal places.

quiz.q: Eccentricity of x²/16 + y²/9 = 1 is
quiz.why: Here a² = 16 and b² = 9, so c² = a² − b² = 7 and c = √7. Eccentricity e = c/a = √7/4.

quiz.q: Length of the major axis of x²/4 + y²/25 = 1 is
quiz.why: In x²/4 + y²/25 = 1, the larger denominator 25 is under y², so a = 5 and the major axis lies along the y-axis. Its length is 2a = 10.

quiz.q: For an ellipse, e satisfies
quiz.why: For an ellipse, the focal distance c is smaller than a, so e = c/a lies strictly between 0 and 1. e = 0 is a circle and e = 1 a parabola.

quiz.q: Latus rectum of x²/25 + y²/16 = 1 is
quiz.why: The latus rectum of an ellipse is 2b²/a. With a² = 25 and b² = 16, it is 2 × 16/5 = 32/5.

quiz.q: Sum of focal distances of any point on x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b) is
quiz.why: By the definition of an ellipse, the sum of the distances from any point on it to the two foci is constant and equals the major axis length, 2a.

scenes.text: Older radio navigation measured the difference in arrival time of signals from two stations.
Points with a constant distance difference from two fixed stations lie on a hyperbola.

steps.title: Definition and key quantities
steps.body:
A **hyperbola** is the set of points where the **difference** of distances from two foci is a constant 2a.

Standard form (transverse axis along x): **x²/a² − y²/b² = 1**.
- **c² = a² + b²**; foci (±c, 0); vertices (±a, 0)
- Transverse axis 2a; conjugate axis 2b
- **e = c/a > 1**; latus rectum **2b²/a**
- y²/a² − x²/b² = 1 has foci (0, ±c).
- If a = b, it is an **equilateral (rectangular)** hyperbola, e = √2.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Hyperbola with foci (0, ±12) and latus rectum 36.

- c = 12; 2b²/a = 36 → b² = 18a.
- a² + 18a = 144 → (a + 24)(a − 6) = 0 → a = 6, b² = 108.
- **y²/36 − x²/108 = 1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a is under the larger denominator (for hyperbolas a is under the POSITIVE term).
- Using c² = a² − b².
- Rejecting nothing: in quadratic steps keep only positive a.

steps.title: Compare quickly
steps.body: Ellipse: sum, c² = a² − b², e < 1. Hyperbola: difference, c² = a² + b², e > 1. Parabola: e = 1. Circle: e = 0.

activity.prompt: Classify each equation.

quiz.q: Foci of x²/16 − y²/9 = 1 are
quiz.why: For a hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, c² = a² + b² = 16 + 9 = 25, so c = 5 and the foci are (±5, 0).

quiz.q: Eccentricity of a hyperbola is always
quiz.why: For a hyperbola, c² = a² + b² makes c > a, so e = c/a is greater than 1.

quiz.q: For y²/9 − x²/27 = 1, the transverse axis lies along
quiz.why: In y²/9 − x²/27 = 1 the positive term is the y² term, so the transverse axis lies along the y-axis.

quiz.q: Eccentricity of a rectangular hyperbola is
quiz.why: A rectangular hyperbola has a = b, so c² = 2a² and c = a√2. Hence e = c/a = √2.

quiz.q: Latus rectum of x²/4 − y²/5 = 1 is
quiz.why: The latus rectum of a hyperbola is 2b²/a. With a² = 4 and b² = 5 (a = 2), it is 2 × 5/2 = 5.

questions.q: Centre of x² + y² − 4x + 6y = 0 is
questions.why: For x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 the centre is (−g, −f). Here 2g = −4 and 2f = 6, so g = −2 and f = 3, giving the centre (2, −3).

questions.q: Focus of x² = 4y is
questions.why: For x² = 4ay, the focus is (0, a). Comparing x² = 4y gives a = 1, so the focus is (0, 1).

questions.q: Eccentricity of a circle is
questions.why: In a circle the two foci coincide at the centre, so c = 0 and e = c/a = 0.

questions.q: Radius of x² + y² + 2x − 8 = 0 is
Length of the latus rectum of y² = 10x is
questions.why: The length of the latus rectum of y² = 4ax is 4a. Here 4a = 10, so it is 10.

questions.q: Vertices of x²/49 + y²/16 = 1 are
questions.why: In x²/49 + y²/16 = 1 the larger denominator is under x², so a = 7 along the x-axis. The vertices are (±7, 0).

questions.q: Assertion: x²/25 + y²/16 = 1 has e = 3/5. Reason: for an ellipse c² = a² − b².
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true: c² = a² − b² = 25 − 16 = 9, so c = 3 and e = c/a = 3/5. The reason gives the formula used to find e, so it explains the assertion.

questions.q: Ellipse with foci (±3, 0) and a = 4:
questions.why: With foci (±3, 0), c = 3, and a = 4. Then b² = a² − c² = 16 − 9 = 7, so the ellipse is x²/16 + y²/7 = 1.

questions.q: Hyperbola with vertices (±2, 0) and foci (±3, 0):
questions.why: Vertices (±2, 0) give a = 2 and foci (±3, 0) give c = 3. Then b² = c² − a² = 9 − 4 = 5, so x²/4 − y²/5 = 1. A hyperbola has a minus sign.

questions.q: Parabola with vertex (0, 0), axis along x-axis, through (2, 3):
questions.why: A parabola with vertex at the origin and axis along the x-axis is y² = 4ax. Through (2, 3): 9 = 4a × 2, so 4a = 9/2 and the equation is y² = (9/2)x.

questions.q: Case: A parabolic reflector is 20 cm wide at the mouth and 5 cm deep. Its focus is at distance ___ from the vertex.
questions.why: The reflector is a parabola y² = 4ax. Half the mouth is 10 cm at depth 5 cm, so the point (5, 10) lies on it: 100 = 20a, giving a = 5. The focus is 5 cm from the vertex.

questions.q: Case: An arch is a semi-ellipse 8 m wide and 2 m high at the centre. Height at 1.5 m from one end is about
Circle through (0, 0), (a, 0) and (0, b):
questions.why: A circle through the origin has the form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy = 0. Using (a, 0) gives 2g = −a and using (0, b) gives 2f = −b, so x² + y² − ax − by = 0.

questions.q: Eccentricity of 9y² − 4x² = 36 is
questions.why: Divide 9y² − 4x² = 36 by 36: y²/4 − x²/9 = 1, so a² = 4 and b² = 9. Then c² = a² + b² = 13, and e = c/a = √13/2.

questions.q: For the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, the distance between the foci is
questions.why: For x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, a = 5 and b = 3, so c = √(25 − 9) = 4. The foci are 2c = 8 units apart.

questions.q: Case: A rod of length 12 cm moves with ends on the axes. The point on the rod 3 cm from the end on the x-axis traces
questions.why: With the rod at angle θ to the x-axis, the point 3 cm from the x-axis end is 9 cm from the y-axis end. It has coordinates (9 cos θ, 3 sin θ), so x²/81 + y²/9 = 1, an ellipse.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry
courses.summary: Coordinate axes and planes in space, octants, coordinates of a point, the distance formula in three dimensions and simple applications.
outcomes: Learners can name the three coordinate planes and eight octants
Learners can locate a point (x, y, z) and give its octant
Learners can find distances between points in space
Learners can use distances to test collinearity and classify triangles

lessons.title: Axes, planes and octants

scenes.text: A drone hovers in a classroom. 'Two numbers' (across, along) are not enough to say where it is.
We need a third number — height. Space needs three coordinates.

steps.title: Coordinate system in space
steps.body:
Three mutually perpendicular lines through the origin O are the **x-, y- and z-axes**. They determine three **coordinate planes**:
- XY-plane (z = 0), YZ-plane (x = 0), ZX-plane (y = 0).

These planes divide space into **eight octants**, named by the signs of (x, y, z): I (+, +, +), II (−, +, +), III (−, −, +), IV (+, −, +), V (+, +, −), VI (−, +, −), VII (−, −, −), VIII (+, −, −).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Octants of (−3, 1, 2) and (−3, 1, −2)?

- Signs (−, +, +) → **Octant II**.
- Signs (−, +, −) → **Octant VI**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Where do these lie?

- (0, 0, 5): on the z-axis.
- (4, 0, −3): y = 0, so in the ZX-plane.
- (0, 0, 0): the origin.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking (2, 0, 0) is in an octant — points on axes or planes are in no octant.
- Confusing the XY-plane equation (z = 0) with 'x = 0, y = 0' (that is the z-axis).
- Drawing a left-handed system; use the right-hand rule (x → y curls towards +z).

activity.prompt: Where is each point?
buckets: On a coordinate plane (not an axis)

quiz.q: The point (2, −3, −5) lies in octant
quiz.why: Octants are decided by sign: (+, −, −) is the VIII octant. Octant IV is (+, −, +) and V is (+, +, −), which do not match.

quiz.q: Equation of the YZ-plane is
quiz.why: Every point in the YZ-plane has x-coordinate 0, so its equation is x = 0. z = 0 is the XY-plane and y = 0 is the ZX-plane.

quiz.q: Number of octants is
quiz.why: The three coordinate planes split space into 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 regions, called octants.

quiz.q: A point on the x-axis has the form
quiz.why: A point on the x-axis has no y or z displacement, so y = 0 and z = 0, giving (x, 0, 0).

quiz.q: Signs (−, −, +) correspond to octant
quiz.why: Octant III is where x < 0, y < 0, z > 0, i.e. signs (−, −, +).

sources: NCERT Class 11 Mathematics (Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry)

lessons.title: Coordinates of a point in space

scenes.text: A robot in a warehouse picks a box at aisle 4, rack 2, shelf 3.
(4, 2, 3) is all it needs — each number is a distance from a coordinate plane.

steps.title: Reading coordinates
steps.body:
From P drop perpendiculars to the three coordinate planes. If OL, OM, ON are the intercepts on the axes:
- **x = distance of P from the YZ-plane** (with sign)
- **y = distance from the ZX-plane**
- **z = distance from the XY-plane**

The foot of the perpendicular from P(x, y, z) to the XY-plane is (x, y, 0); to the x-axis is (x, 0, 0).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
For P(3, −4, 5):

- Distance from the XY-plane = |z| = 5; from YZ = 3; from ZX = 4.
- Foot on the XY-plane: (3, −4, 0).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A box with one vertex at the origin has edges 2, 3, 4 along the x, y, z axes. List the vertices.

- (0,0,0), (2,0,0), (0,3,0), (0,0,4), (2,3,0), (2,0,4), (0,3,4), (2,3,4).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The distance from the XY-plane is |z|, not √(x² + y²).
- Mixing the order (x, y, z).
- Dropping signs when naming octants.

activity.prompt: What is the distance of P(6, −2, −9) from the XY-plane?

quiz.q: Foot of perpendicular from (2, 5, 7) to the ZX-plane is
quiz.why: The foot of the perpendicular to the ZX-plane keeps x and z and sets y = 0, so it is (2, 0, 7).

quiz.q: Distance of (−4, 3, 1) from the YZ-plane is
quiz.why: The distance from a point to the YZ-plane is the absolute value of its x-coordinate: |−4| = 4.

quiz.q: Distance of (3, 4, 12) from the z-axis is
quiz.why: The distance of a point from the z-axis is √(x² + y²) = √(9 + 16) = 5. The z-coordinate does not matter.

quiz.q: A point with z = 0 lies on
quiz.why: Every point with z = 0 lies in the XY-plane, which is the plane z = 0.

quiz.q: Coordinates of the origin are
quiz.why: The origin is where all three axes meet, and all of its coordinates are zero: (0, 0, 0).

sources: NCERT Class 11 Mathematics (Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry)

lessons.title: Distance between two points

scenes.text: An electrician runs a wire from a ceiling corner to the opposite floor corner of a room.
Its length uses Pythagoras twice — the 3D distance formula.

steps.title: The distance formula
steps.body:
For P(x₁, y₁, z₁) and Q(x₂, y₂, z₂):
**PQ = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²]**.
Distance from the origin: √(x² + y² + z²).

Derivation idea: in a box with PQ as diagonal, the base diagonal is √(Δx² + Δy²); then Pythagoras with Δz.

steps.title: Solved example 3: room diagonal
steps.body: A room 5 m × 4 m × 3 m: the longest wire from corner to opposite corner is √(25 + 16 + 9) = √50 ≈ **7.07 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the z-term (using the 2D formula).
- Squaring a negative difference incorrectly: (−4)² = 16.
- Concluding collinearity without checking that two distances add up to the third.

activity.prompt: Find the distance between (1, 2, 3) and (4, 6, 15).

quiz.q: Distance of (2, 3, 6) from the origin is
quiz.why: Distance from the origin = √(2² + 3² + 6²) = √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7.

quiz.q: Distance between (0, 0, 0) and (1, 1, 1) is
quiz.why: The distance between the origin and (1, 1, 1) is √(1 + 1 + 1) = √3.

quiz.q: Points A(0, 7, −10), B(1, 6, −6), C(4, 9, −6) form a triangle that is
If the distance between (x, 0, 0) and (0, 0, 0) is 5, x =
quiz.why: The distance from (x, 0, 0) to the origin is |x|. Setting |x| = 5 gives x = 5 or x = −5.

quiz.q: The 3D distance formula reduces to the 2D one when
options: the points are on the z-axis
quiz.why: If both points have the same z-coordinate, the z difference is 0, and the 3D formula becomes √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²), the 2D formula.

sources: NCERT Class 11 Mathematics (Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry)

lessons.title: Applications: locus and section of a segment

scenes.text: Engineers want all points equally far from two towers in 3D space.
Setting two distances equal gives the equation of a plane — a 3D locus.

steps.title: Locus with distances
steps.body: Write PA = PB (or PA² + PB² = k, etc.) with P(x, y, z), square both sides and simplify. Points equidistant from A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector **plane** of AB.

steps.title: Section formula (extension)
steps.body: The point dividing PQ internally in m : n is ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n), (mz₂ + nz₁)/(m + n)); the midpoint is the average of coordinates. (Some rationalised editions omit this; it is useful in Class 12.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cancelling terms wrongly after expanding squares — expand fully, then cancel x², y², z².
- Calling a 3D locus a 'line' when the equation is a plane.

activity.prompt: Locus of P with PA = PB where A(0, 0, 0), B(2, 0, 0).
activity.text: x² + y² + z² = (x − 2)² + y² + z² gives x = ___.

quiz.q: Points equidistant from two fixed points in space lie on a
quiz.why: Points equidistant from two fixed points lie on the perpendicular bisector plane of the segment joining them. In space it is a plane, not a line or sphere.

quiz.q: Midpoint of (1, 2, 3) and (3, 4, 5) is
quiz.why: The midpoint averages each coordinate: ((1 + 3)/2, (2 + 4)/2, (3 + 5)/2) = (2, 3, 4).

quiz.q: The set of points at distance 3 from the origin is a
quiz.why: All points at distance 3 from the origin satisfy x² + y² + z² = 9, which is a sphere of radius 3. A circle would be only in a plane.

quiz.q: If A(3, 2, 0), B(5, 3, 2) and C(−9, 6, −3) form a triangle, its sides are computed with
quiz.why: The side lengths of a triangle in space are the distances between the vertices, found with the 3D distance formula √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²).

quiz.q: The point dividing (0,0,0)–(6,9,3) in 1 : 2 is
quiz.why: Dividing in the ratio 1 : 2 puts the point one-third of the way from the first point. So the coordinates are (6/3, 9/3, 3/3) = (2, 3, 1).

sources: NCERT Class 11 Mathematics (Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry)

questions.q: Octant of (−5, −3, 4) is
questions.why: The signs (−, −, +) correspond to octant III.

questions.q: The z-axis is given by
questions.why: The z-axis consists of the points where both x and y are zero, so it is given by x = 0, y = 0.

questions.q: Distance of (3, −4, 0) from the origin is
questions.why: Distance from the origin = √(3² + (−4)² + 0²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

questions.q: Distance of (4, −3, 5) from the ZX-plane is
questions.why: The distance from a point to the ZX-plane is the absolute value of its y-coordinate: |−3| = 3.

questions.q: Distance between (−1, 3, −4) and (1, −3, 4) is
Foot of the perpendicular from (−4, 3, 2) to the x-axis is
questions.why: The foot of the perpendicular on the x-axis keeps the x-coordinate and sets y and z to 0. For (−4, 3, 2) this gives (−4, 0, 0).

questions.q: Assertion: (0, 4, −3) lies in the YZ-plane. Reason: its x-coordinate is 0.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. The YZ-plane is x = 0, and the point (0, 4, −3) has x = 0, so the reason explains why it lies in that plane.

questions.q: If the distance between (a, 2, 1) and (1, −1, 1) is 5, then a =
questions.why: The distance condition gives (a − 1)² + 9 + 0 = 25, so (a − 1)² = 16 and a − 1 = ±4. That gives a = 5 or a = −3.

questions.q: The triangle with vertices (0, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0), (0, 2, 0) is
questions.why: The two legs from the origin each have length 2 and meet at a right angle at the origin. The hypotenuse is 2√2, so the triangle is right-angled isosceles.
The distance between consecutive points is √3 each, and between the end points it is √12 = 2√3. Since √3 + √3 = 2√3, the points lie on one line.

questions.q: Case: A lamp hangs at (2, 3, 4) m in a room with origin at a floor corner. Its height above the floor is
questions.why: With the origin at the floor corner, the z-coordinate is the height. So the lamp at (2, 3, 4) is 4 m above the floor.

questions.q: The locus of points equidistant from (1, 0, 0) and (−1, 0, 0) is
questions.why: Equal distances give (x − 1)² + y² + z² = (x + 1)² + y² + z². This simplifies to −2x = 2x, so x = 0, the YZ-plane.

questions.q: Find the point on the y-axis equidistant from (3, 1, 2) and (5, 5, 2).
questions.why: For (0, y, 0): 9 + (y − 1)² + 4 = 25 + (y − 5)² + 4. This simplifies to −2y + 14 = −10y + 54, so 8y = 40 and y = 5, giving (0, 5, 0).

questions.q: Locus of P with PA² + PB² = 2k² for A(3, 4, 5) and B(−1, 3, −7) is
questions.why: Expand PA² + PB² with P(x, y, z). The x², y², z² terms double, and the constant is 9 + 16 + 25 + 1 + 9 + 49 = 109. Setting it equal to 2k² gives the stated equation.
The distances are √14, 2√14 and 3√14, and √14 + 2√14 = 3√14. When two shorter distances add to the longest, the points lie on one straight line.

questions.q: A point P on the x-axis is at distance 13 from (0, 12, 5). Then P is
questions.why: A point P(x, 0, 0) on the x-axis is at distance √(x² + 12² + 5²) from (0, 12, 5). Setting this to 13 gives x² + 144 + 25 = 169, so x² = 0 and x = 0, i.e. P is the origin.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Limits and Derivatives
courses.summary: An intuitive idea of limits, left- and right-hand limits, algebra of limits, standard limits for polynomials, rational and trigonometric functions, the derivative from first principles and rules of differentiation.
outcomes: Learners can find limits by substitution, factorisation and rationalisation
Learners can use lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ and lim sin x/x = 1
Learners can find derivatives from first principles
Learners can apply sum, product and quotient rules to polynomials and trigonometric functions

scenes.text: A car's speedometer shows speed *right now* — but speed is distance over time, and 'right now' has zero time.
We look at smaller and smaller time intervals and see what value the average speed approaches. That is a limit.

steps.title: Intuitive meaning
steps.body:
**lim (x→a) f(x) = l** means f(x) gets as close as we like to l when x is close enough to a (x ≠ a).

- **Left-hand limit** (x → a⁻) and **right-hand limit** (x → a⁺).
- The limit exists iff both exist and are equal.
- The limit need not equal f(a); f(a) may not even be defined.

steps.title: Solved example 2: one-sided
steps.body:
f(x) = x + 2 for x ≤ 1, and f(x) = 3x for x > 1. Does lim (x→1) f(x) exist?

- LHL = 1 + 2 = 3; RHL = 3(1) = 3. Equal → limit is **3**.

For g(x) = |x|/x at 0: LHL = −1, RHL = 1 → **no limit**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 0/0 means the limit is 0 or does not exist — it is *indeterminate*; simplify first.
- Assuming lim f(x) = f(a) always.
- Checking only one side for piecewise functions.

statements.s: If f(a) is undefined, lim (x→a) f(x) cannot exist.
statements.why: (x² − 1)/(x − 1) is undefined at 1 but has limit 2.

statements.s: A limit exists only if LHL = RHL.
lim (x→0) |x|/x exists.
0/0 is called an indeterminate form.
For a polynomial p, lim (x→a) p(x) = p(a).

quiz.q: lim (x→3) (x + 3) is
quiz.why: The function x + 3 is continuous, so the limit is found by direct substitution: 3 + 3 = 6. There is no 0/0 problem to resolve.

quiz.q: lim (x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2) is
quiz.why: Direct substitution gives 0/0, so factorise: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2. At x = 2 this is 4.

quiz.q: For f(x) = [x], lim (x→2⁻) f(x) is
quiz.why: The greatest integer function [x] is 1 for 1 ≤ x < 2. As x approaches 2 from the left (2⁻), values are just below 2, so [x] = 1.

quiz.q: If LHL = 5 and RHL = 5 at x = a and f(a) = 7, then lim (x→a) f(x) is
quiz.why: A limit depends only on the values near x = a, not on f(a) itself. Since the left and right limits are both 5, the limit is 5 even though f(a) = 7.

quiz.q: lim (x→1) (x³ − 1)/(x − 1) is
quiz.why: Factorise x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) and cancel (x − 1). The limit is x² + x + 1 at x = 1, which is 3.

lessons.title: Algebra of limits and standard limits

scenes.text: A complicated limit can be split into simpler limits — like splitting a big bill among friends.
The algebra of limits says how to split sums, products and quotients.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
If lim f = l and lim g = m (x → a):
- lim (f ± g) = l ± m; lim (fg) = lm; lim (kf) = kl
- lim (f/g) = l/m (m ≠ 0)

**Standard result:** **lim (x→a) (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n aⁿ⁻¹**.

For rational functions, if substitution gives 0/0, factorise or rationalise.

steps.title: Solved example 2: standard result
steps.body:
lim (x→1) (x¹⁵ − 1)/(x¹⁰ − 1).

- Divide top and bottom by (x − 1): (15·1¹⁴)/(10·1⁹) = **3/2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Splitting a quotient when the denominator's limit is 0.
- Cancelling (x − a) and then forgetting to substitute.
- Writing n aⁿ instead of n aⁿ⁻¹.

activity.prompt: Evaluate lim (x→2) (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2).

quiz.q: lim (x→−1) (x¹⁰ + x⁵ + 1)/(x − 1) is
quiz.why: The denominator x − 1 is −2 at x = −1, not zero, so substitute directly: (1 − 1 + 1)/(−2) = −1/2, since (−1)¹⁰ = 1 and (−1)⁵ = −1.

quiz.q: lim (x→a) (x⁴ − a⁴)/(x − a) equals
quiz.why: Using the standard limit lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n aⁿ⁻¹ with n = 4 gives 4a³.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) [(x + 1)⁵ − 1]/x is
quiz.why: Let y = x + 1, so y → 1. The limit becomes (y⁵ − 1)/(y − 1) → 5 · 1⁴ = 5. (It is also the derivative of (1 + x)⁵ at 0.)

quiz.q: lim (x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3) is
quiz.why: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), so after cancelling the limit is x + 3 = 6 at x = 3.
The denominator is 4 − 2 = 2, not zero, so direct substitution works: (4 × 4 + 3)/2 = 19/2.

scenes.text: Astronomers and engineers often replace sin x by x when the angle is tiny (in radians).
The reason is the famous limit sin x / x → 1.

steps.title: Two key limits (x in radians)
steps.body:
- **lim (x→0) sin x / x = 1** (proved with the sandwich theorem using areas in a unit circle: cos x < sin x/x < 1).
- **lim (x→0) (1 − cos x)/x = 0**.
- Consequences: lim sin(ax)/(bx) = a/b; lim tan x / x = 1.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
lim (x→0) (1 − cos 2x)/x².

- 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin²x.
- 2 (sin x/x)² → **2**.

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body: lim (x→0) tan x / x = lim (sin x/x)·(1/cos x) = 1 · 1 = **1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using degrees: sin x/x → 1 only for radians.
- Writing lim sin 5x/x = 1 (it is 5).
- Forgetting that (1 − cos x)/x² → 1/2, not 0.

activity.prompt: Match each limit (x → 0) with its value.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) sin ax / sin bx is
quiz.why: Write sin ax/sin bx = (sin ax/ax)·(bx/sin bx)·(a/b). Both standard limits tend to 1, leaving a/b.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) x / tan x is
quiz.why: x/tan x is the reciprocal of tan x/x. Since tan x/x → 1 as x → 0, the limit is 1.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) (cos x − 1)/x is
quiz.why: (cos x − 1)/x = −(1 − cos x)/x, and (1 − cos x)/x → 0 as x → 0 (it behaves like x/2). So the limit is 0, not −1.

quiz.q: lim (x→π) sin(π − x)/(π(π − x)) is
quiz.why: Let h = π − x, so h → 0. The expression becomes sin h/(πh), and sin h/h → 1, giving 1/π.

quiz.q: lim (x→0) (cosec x − cot x) is
quiz.why: cosec x − cot x = (1 − cos x)/sin x = tan(x/2). As x → 0, tan(x/2) → 0.

scenes.text: A stone falls s(t) = 4.9t² metres in t seconds. How fast is it moving at t = 2 s?
Average speed over [2, 2 + h] approaches 19.6 m/s as h → 0 — the derivative.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
The **derivative** of f at a:
**f′(a) = lim (h→0) [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h**, if the limit exists.

The derivative function: f′(x) = lim (h→0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h; also written dy/dx or d/dx f(x). Geometrically it is the **slope of the tangent**; physically, an instantaneous rate of change.

steps.title: Solved example 1: f(x) = x² at x = 2
Solved example 3: sin x
steps.body: d/dx sin x = lim [sin(x + h) − sin x]/h = lim 2cos(x + h/2) sin(h/2)/h = cos x · 1 = **cos x**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expanding f(x + h) wrongly, e.g. (x + h)² = x² + h².
- Putting h = 0 before cancelling h (gives 0/0).
- Confusing f′(a) (a number) with f′(x) (a function).

activity.prompt: Using first principles, find the instantaneous speed (m/s) at t = 2 for s(t) = 4.9t².

quiz.q: Derivative of f(x) = 3x at any x is
quiz.why: From first principles [3(x + h) − 3x]/h = 3h/h = 3, so the derivative is the constant 3, the slope of the line y = 3x.

quiz.q: Derivative of a constant is
quiz.why: For a constant function f(x + h) − f(x) = 0, so the difference quotient is 0 and the derivative is 0 (a horizontal line has zero slope).

quiz.q: Geometrically, f′(a) is
options: slope of the tangent at x = a
quiz.why: The derivative f′(a) is the limit of slopes of secant lines as the second point approaches a, which is the slope of the tangent at x = a.

quiz.q: From first principles, d/dx (x³) is
quiz.why: (x + h)³ − x³ = 3x²h + 3xh² + h³. Dividing by h gives 3x² + 3xh + h², and as h → 0 this is 3x².

quiz.q: d/dx cos x from first principles is
quiz.why: Using cos(x + h) − cos x = −2 sin(x + h/2) sin(h/2), dividing by h and letting h → 0 gives −sin x.

scenes.text: A factory's cost is C(x) = 0.005x³ − 0.02x² + 30x + 5000. The manager wants the cost of one more unit at x = 3.
The derivative C′(x) — the marginal cost — answers it without first principles every time.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- d/dx xⁿ = n xⁿ⁻¹ (any integer n; also rational n)
- (u ± v)′ = u′ ± v′; (ku)′ = ku′
- **Product:** (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
- **Quotient:** (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v² (v ≠ 0)
- d/dx sin x = cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x; sec x → sec x tan x; cosec x → −cosec x cot x; cot x → −cosec²x.

steps.title: Solved example 1: product
steps.body: d/dx (x² sin x) = 2x sin x + x² cos x.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- (uv)′ ≠ u′v′.
- Swapping the order in the quotient rule numerator (u′v − uv′, not uv′ − u′v).
- d/dx cos x is −sin x (sign!).

steps.title: Polynomial shortcut
steps.body: d/dx (aₙxⁿ + … + a₁x + a₀) = naₙxⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁.

activity.prompt: If f(x) = x³ − 4x + 7, find f′(2).

quiz.q: d/dx (5x⁴ − 3x + 2) is
quiz.why: Differentiate term by term: 5·4x³ = 20x³, −3x gives −3, and the constant 2 gives 0. So the derivative is 20x³ − 3.

quiz.q: d/dx (x sin x) is
quiz.why: By the product rule, (x)′ sin x + x (sin x)′ = sin x + x cos x.

quiz.q: d/dx tan x is
quiz.why: The standard result is d/dx (tan x) = sec²x. The expression −cosec²x is the derivative of cot x.

quiz.q: d/dx (1/x²) is
quiz.why: Write 1/x² as x⁻². The power rule gives −2x⁻³ = −2/x³.

quiz.q: d/dx (sin x / x) is
quiz.why: By the quotient rule, (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v² with u = sin x and v = x: (x cos x − sin x)/x².

questions.q: lim (x→2) (3x + 1) is
questions.why: 3x + 1 is continuous, so substitute x = 2: 3(2) + 1 = 7.

questions.q: lim (x→0) sin 5x / x is
questions.why: Write sin 5x/x = 5 · (sin 5x/5x). As x → 0, sin 5x/5x → 1, so the limit is 5.

questions.q: d/dx (x⁷) is
questions.why: By the power rule, d/dx (xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹. So d/dx (x⁷) = 7x⁶.

questions.q: lim (x→1) (x² − 1)/(x − 1) is
questions.why: x² − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1), so the quotient simplifies to x + 1, which is 2 at x = 1.

questions.q: d/dx (sin x + cos x) is
questions.why: Differentiate each term: (sin x)′ = cos x and (cos x)′ = −sin x. So the derivative is cos x − sin x.

questions.q: lim (x→0) (1 − cos 4x)/x² is
questions.why: 1 − cos 4x = 2 sin²2x, so (1 − cos 4x)/x² = 2 (sin 2x/x)² → 2 × 2² = 8.

questions.q: Assertion: lim (x→0) |x|/x does not exist. Reason: the left- and right-hand limits are unequal.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
Both true and R explains A
questions.why: Both are true. For x > 0, |x|/x = 1 and for x < 0 it is −1, so the left and right limits (−1 and 1) differ and the limit does not exist. The reason is exactly why the limit fails.

questions.q: lim (x→a) (√x − √a)/(x − a) for a > 0 is
questions.why: Using lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n aⁿ⁻¹ with n = 1/2 gives (1/2)a⁻¹ᐟ² = 1/(2√a). Alternatively multiply by (√x + √a)/(√x + √a).

questions.q: d/dx [(x² + 1)(x − 3)] is
questions.why: Expand: (x² + 1)(x − 3) = x³ − 3x² + x − 3. Differentiating gives 3x² − 6x + 1.

questions.q: d/dx (x/(1 + x)) is
questions.why: By the quotient rule: [1·(1 + x) − x·1]/(1 + x)² = 1/(1 + x)².

questions.q: If f(x) = x¹⁰⁰ + x⁹⁹ + … + x + 1, then f′(1) is
Case: A balloon's volume is V = (4/3)πr³. The rate of change of V with respect to r at r = 3 cm is
questions.why: The rate of change of V with respect to r is dV/dr = 4πr². At r = 3 this is 4π × 9 = 36π cm³ per cm.

questions.q: lim (x→0) (sin ax + bx)/(ax + sin bx) for a, b, a + b ≠ 0 is
questions.why: Divide numerator and denominator by x: (sin ax/x + b)/(a + sin bx/x). As x → 0, sin ax/x → a and sin bx/x → b, giving (a + b)/(a + b) = 1.

questions.q: For f(x) = 5x − 4 for 0 < x ≤ 1 and 4x³ − 3x for 1 < x < 2, lim (x→1) f(x) is
questions.why: Left limit: 5(1) − 4 = 1. Right limit: 4(1)³ − 3(1) = 1. Both equal 1, so the limit is 1.

questions.q: d/dx (sec x) from rules: (1/cos x)′ =
questions.why: Using the chain/quotient rule, (1/cos x)′ = −(−sin x)/cos²x = sin x/cos²x = sec x tan x.

questions.q: If lim (x→1) (x⁴ − 1)/(x − 1) = lim (x→k) (x³ − k³)/(x² − k²), then k =
questions.why: The left side is 4 (derivative of x⁴ at 1). The right side is 3k²/(2k) = 3k/2. Setting 3k/2 = 4 gives k = 8/3.

questions.q: Derivative of (x + cos x)/tan x is
options: [(1 − sin x) tan x − (x + cos x) sec²x]/tan²x
[(1 + sin x) tan x − (x + cos x) sec²x]/tan²x
questions.why: By the quotient rule with u = x + cos x (u′ = 1 − sin x) and v = tan x (v′ = sec²x): (u′v − uv′)/v² = [(1 − sin x) tan x − (x + cos x) sec²x]/tan²x.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Statistics
courses.summary: Measures of dispersion: range, mean deviation about mean and median for ungrouped and grouped data, variance and standard deviation including the shortcut method, and comparing variability.
outcomes: Learners can explain why central tendency alone is not enough
Learners can compute range and mean deviation for ungrouped and grouped data
Learners can compute variance and standard deviation by direct and shortcut methods
Learners can compare two distributions using the coefficient of variation

scenes.text: Batsmen A and B both average 50. A scores 48, 50, 52; B scores 0, 50, 100.
Same mean, very different consistency. Measures of dispersion capture the spread.

steps.title: Measures of dispersion
steps.body:
- **Range** = maximum − minimum (simple but uses only two values).
- **Mean deviation about a**: M.D.(a) = Σ|xᵢ − a| / n. Usually a = mean x̄ or median M.
- Mean deviation is least when taken about the median.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the absolute value (Σ(xᵢ − x̄) is always 0).
- Finding the median without sorting.
- Dividing by n − 1 (Class 11 uses n).

activity.prompt: Find the mean deviation about the mean for 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.

quiz.q: Range of 12, 5, 19, 7, 3 is
quiz.why: Range = largest value − smallest value = 19 − 3 = 16.

quiz.q: Σ(xᵢ − x̄) for any data equals
quiz.why: The deviations from the mean add up to zero, since values above the mean cancel those below it. So Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = 0.

quiz.q: Mean deviation is smallest about the
quiz.why: The mean deviation is smallest when it is taken about the median. This is a known property of the median.

quiz.q: M.D. about the mean of 1, 1, 1, 1 is
quiz.why: All the values are equal, so every deviation from the mean is zero and the mean deviation is 0 (no spread).

quiz.q: Batsman with scores 0, 50, 100 is ___ than one with 48, 50, 52.
quiz.why: Scores 0, 50, 100 are widely spread while 48, 50, 52 are close together, though both average 50. A bigger spread means less consistency.

scenes.text: A survey records daily wages of 50 workers in class intervals.
We cannot see each value, so we use class marks to estimate the spread.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Discrete frequency distribution: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ/N, **M.D.(x̄) = Σfᵢ|xᵢ − x̄|/N** (N = Σfᵢ).
- About the median: find the median from cumulative frequencies, then Σfᵢ|xᵢ − M|/N.
- Continuous classes: use class marks xᵢ (midpoints). Median = l + [(N/2 − c.f.)/f] × h.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying |xᵢ − x̄| by fᵢ is required — not optional.
- Using class limits instead of class marks.
- Locating the median class with N instead of N/2.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for mean deviation about the median (continuous data).
items: Find class marks and cumulative frequencies
Locate the median class using N/2
Compute the median with l + [(N/2 − c.f.)/f] × h
Find |xᵢ − M| for each class mark

quiz.q: For grouped data the deviations are measured from
quiz.why: For grouped data, each class is represented by its class mark (midpoint), so deviations are measured from the class marks.

quiz.q: N in the formula is
quiz.why: In these formulas, N is the total frequency, N = Σfᵢ, i.e. the number of observations.

quiz.q: Class mark of 20–30 is

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Variance** σ² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/n; for frequencies σ² = Σfᵢ(xᵢ − x̄)²/N.
- **Standard deviation** σ = √variance (same units as the data).
- Computing form: σ² = Σxᵢ²/n − x̄².
- **Shortcut (step deviation):** yᵢ = (xᵢ − A)/h, then σₓ = h·σᵧ, with σᵧ² = Σfy²/N − (Σfy/N)².
- Adding a constant to all data does not change σ; multiplying by k multiplies σ by |k|.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking σ as the variance (forgetting the square root).
- In the shortcut, forgetting to multiply by h² for variance (or h for σ).
- Using (Σx)² instead of Σx².

steps.title: Coefficient of variation
steps.body:
**C.V. = (σ / x̄) × 100**, a unitless percentage.
- The series with the **greater C.V.** is more variable; the smaller C.V. is more **consistent/stable**.
- With equal means, compare σ directly.

- Firm B has greater variability in individual wages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Using the variance in the C.V. formula instead of σ.
- Saying the larger C.V. is 'more consistent' (it is the opposite).

scenes.text: Before every cricket match, the captains toss a coin. Nobody can predict the outcome, but everyone knows the possibilities.
Listing all possible outcomes is the first step in probability.

steps.title: Definitions
Solved example 1
steps.body:
A coin is tossed; if it shows head a die is thrown, otherwise the coin is tossed again.

- S = {H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, TH, TT} → **8 outcomes**.

Two balls are drawn one after another (without replacement) from a bag of 2 red (R₁, R₂) and 1 blue (B).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating HT and TH as the same when order matters.
- Forgetting outcomes in multi-stage experiments.

quiz.q: Sample space for one die has
quiz.why: A die has six faces, so the sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, i.e. 6 points.

quiz.q: Number of outcomes when 2 dice are thrown is
quiz.why: Each of the 6 outcomes on the first die pairs with 6 on the second, so there are 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes.

quiz.q: Which is a random experiment?
options: Drawing a card from a well-shuffled deck
quiz.why: A random experiment has outcomes that cannot be predicted in advance. Drawing a card from a shuffled deck qualifies, while the others have fixed results.

lessons.title: Events and the algebra of events

scenes.text: In a board game, you move if you roll an even number, and get a bonus if you roll more than 4.
'Even' and 'more than 4' are events — subsets of the sample space — and we can combine them.

steps.title: Events
steps.body:
An **event** is a subset of S. It *occurs* if the outcome is in it.
- **Impossible event** φ; **sure event** S; **simple event** (one point); **compound event** (more than one).
- **Not A** = A′ = S − A; **A or B** = A ∪ B; **A and B** = A ∩ B; **A but not B** = A − B = A ∩ B′.
- **Mutually exclusive:** A ∩ B = φ.
- **Exhaustive:** E₁ ∪ E₂ ∪ … ∪ Eₙ = S. If also pairwise disjoint, they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Die thrown: A = even = {2, 4, 6}, B = more than 4 = {5, 6}.

- A ∪ B = {2, 4, 5, 6}; A ∩ B = {6}; A − B = {2, 4}; A′ = {1, 3, 5}.
- A and B are **not** mutually exclusive (6 is common).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Die: E₁ = {1, 2}, E₂ = {3, 4}, E₃ = {5, 6}.

- Pairwise disjoint and union is S → **mutually exclusive and exhaustive**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an event and its complement can both occur — they are mutually exclusive.
- Confusing 'mutually exclusive' with 'exhaustive'.
- Writing 'A but not B' as B − A.

activity.prompt: Match the description with the set.

quiz.q: Events A and A′ are
quiz.why: An event A and its complement A′ share no outcomes (mutually exclusive) and together cover the whole sample space (exhaustive).

quiz.q: When two coins are tossed, 'at least one head' is
quiz.why: 'At least one head' includes HH, HT and TH. Only TT has no head, so it is left out.

quiz.q: On a die, 'a number greater than 6' is
quiz.why: A die has only faces 1 to 6, so 'a number greater than 6' can never happen. It is an impossible event, with probability 0.
A ∩ B is the set of elements common to both. Only 3 is in both {1, 3, 5} and {2, 3}.
A and B share no element (mutually exclusive), and A ∪ B = {1, …, 6} is the whole sample space (exhaustive).

scenes.text: An app says 70% chance of rain. Could it say 120%? Could rain and no rain add to 90%?
No — probability obeys three simple axioms that keep it sensible.

steps.title: The axioms
steps.body:
A probability function P on events of S satisfies:
- (i) P(E) ≥ 0 for every event E
- (ii) P(S) = 1
- (iii) If E and F are mutually exclusive, P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F)

Consequences: P(φ) = 0; 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1; P(E) = sum of probabilities of its sample points.

**Equally likely outcomes:** if S has n equally likely points, **P(E) = n(E)/n(S)**.

steps.title: Solved example 1: valid assignment?
steps.body: S = {ω₁, ω₂, ω₃} with P = 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. Valid: each ≥ 0 and sum 1. With P = 0.6, 0.6, −0.2 it is **not valid** (negative value).

steps.title: Solved example 2: dice
steps.body:
Two dice: probability that the sum is 8.

- Favourable: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) → 5.
- P = **5/36**.

steps.title: Solved example 3: cards
steps.body:
A card is drawn from a 52-card deck. P(a king or a heart)?

- Kings 4, hearts 13, king of hearts counted twice: 4 + 13 − 1 = 16.
- P = 16/52 = **4/13**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not (e.g. sums of two dice).
- Probabilities outside [0, 1] — always a sign of an error.
- Counting the overlap twice.

activity.prompt: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability (as a decimal to 3 places) that the sum is 7?

quiz.q: P(S) equals
quiz.why: The probability of the whole sample space is 1, since some outcome in S is certain to occur.

quiz.q: Probability of a head on a fair coin is
quiz.why: A fair coin has 2 equally likely outcomes and one is a head, so P(head) = 1/2.

quiz.q: Probability of drawing an ace from a deck is
quiz.why: A deck has 4 aces out of 52 cards, so P = 4/52 = 1/13.

quiz.q: Which can be a probability?
quiz.why: A probability must lie between 0 and 1. Only 0.75 does; 3/2, 1.2 and −0.1 fall outside that range.

quiz.q: Probability of getting a prime on a die is
quiz.why: The prime numbers on a die are 2, 3 and 5, i.e. 3 favourable outcomes of 6, so P = 3/6 = 1/2. (1 is not prime.)

scenes.text: A school lottery picks 4 winners from 20 tickets. Aman holds 2 tickets.
Combining combinations with probability rules tells him his real chances.

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body:
- **P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)**
- If A, B mutually exclusive: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B)
- **P(A′) = 1 − P(A)**
- P(A − B) = P(A) − P(A ∩ B)
- 'At least one' = 1 − P(none)
- With counting: P = (favourable selections)/(total selections), often using ⁿCᵣ.

steps.title: Solved example 2: committee
steps.body:
A committee of 2 is chosen from 2 men and 2 women. P(at least one woman)?

- Total ⁴C₂ = 6; no woman = 1 (both men).
- P = 1 − 1/6 = **5/6**.

steps.title: Solved example 3: cards
steps.body: 4 cards from a deck: P(all four are diamonds) = ¹³C₄/⁵²C₄ = 715/270725 ≈ **0.0026**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding probabilities of events that overlap without subtracting the intersection.
- Using permutations in numerator and combinations in denominator (mixing).
- For 'at least one', counting cases one by one and double-counting.

activity.prompt: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3 and A, B are mutually exclusive. Find P(neither A nor B).

quiz.q: If P(A) = 0.35, then P(not A) is

quiz.why: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.8. The overlap must be subtracted so it is not counted twice.

quiz.q: P(at least one head in 3 tosses) is
quiz.why: The only outcome with no heads is TTT, with probability 1/8. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

quiz.q: A letter is chosen from 'ASSASSINATION'. P(vowel) is
quiz.why: ASSASSINATION has 13 letters, and the vowels are A (3 times), I (2 times) and O (1 time), 6 in all. So P(vowel) = 6/13.

quiz.q: For mutually exclusive A, B with P(A) = 1/2, P(B) = 1/3, P(A ∪ B) =
quiz.why: For mutually exclusive events there is no overlap, so P(A ∪ B) = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6.

questions.q: Number of sample points when a die is rolled twice is
questions.why: Each roll has 6 outcomes, and two rolls give 6 × 6 = 36 sample points.

questions.q: Probability of an impossible event is
questions.why: An impossible event contains no outcomes, so its probability is 0.

questions.q: If P(E) = 0.05, P(not E) is
questions.why: The probability of the complement is 1 − P(E) = 1 − 0.05 = 0.95.

questions.q: Probability of a sum of 12 with two dice is
questions.why: The sum 12 needs a 6 on both dice, which is only (6, 6). So the probability is 1/36.

questions.q: A card is drawn. P(red face card) is
questions.why: Red face cards are the J, Q, K of hearts and of diamonds: 6 cards. So P = 6/52 = 3/26.

questions.q: Events A, B with P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∪ B) = 0.7 are
questions.why: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.7 = 0.2, which is not zero. So the events can happen together and are not mutually exclusive.

questions.q: Assertion: P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.7 cannot be mutually exclusive. Reason: then P(A ∪ B) would be 1.3 > 1.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Both are true. If A and B were mutually exclusive, P(A ∪ B) = 0.6 + 0.7 = 1.3, which exceeds 1 and is impossible. So that is why they cannot be mutually exclusive.

questions.q: Three coins are tossed. P(exactly two heads) is
questions.why: Of the 8 equally likely outcomes, exactly two heads occur in HHT, HTH and THH. So P = 3/8.

questions.q: If A and B are events with P(A ∪ B) = 0.6 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2, then P(A′) + P(B′) =
Case: In a class, 40% study Maths, 30% Biology and 10% both. P(a random student studies Maths or Biology) is
questions.why: P(Maths or Biology) = 0.4 + 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.6. The 0.1 who take both would otherwise be counted twice.

questions.q: Case: For the same class, P(neither subject) is
questions.why: P(neither subject) = 1 − P(Maths or Biology) = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4.

questions.q: A bag has 9 discs: 4 red, 3 blue, 2 yellow. P(not blue) for one random disc is
questions.why: There are 9 − 3 = 6 discs that are not blue, so P(not blue) = 6/9 = 2/3. (Equivalently 1 − 3/9.)

questions.q: From 6 employees, 2 are chosen at random. If 2 of the 6 are a married couple, P(the chosen pair is that couple) is
questions.why: Choosing 2 of 6 employees gives ⁶C₂ = 15 equally likely pairs. Only one of them is the couple, so P = 1/15.

questions.q: 5 cards are drawn from a deck. P(all are spades) is
questions.why: The number of favourable 5-card hands is ¹³C₅ (all from the 13 spades), out of ⁵²C₅ total hands. So P = ¹³C₅/⁵²C₅.

questions.q: A 4-digit number is formed with the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition. P(it is divisible by 5) is
questions.why: A number divisible by 5 must end in 5. The other 3 places use the remaining 4 digits in ⁴P₃ = 24 ways, out of ⁵P₄ = 120 total. So P = 24/120 = 1/5.

questions.q: In a lottery, a person chooses 6 different numbers from 1 to 20. P(winning, i.e. matching the 6 drawn numbers) is
questions.why: There are ²⁰C₆ = 38760 equally likely sets of 6 numbers, and only one wins, so P = 1/38760.

questions.q: If P(A) = 3/5 and P(B) = 1/5 with A, B mutually exclusive, P(A′ ∩ B′) is
questions.why: A and B are mutually exclusive, so P(A ∪ B) = 3/5 + 1/5 = 4/5. A′ ∩ B′ is 'neither', whose probability is 1 − 4/5 = 1/5.

steps.title: Sets, relations, functions
steps.body:

- π rad = 180°, l = rθ

- sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x; cos 3x = 4cos³x − 3cos x

steps.body:
- i² = −1, iⁿ cycles every 4; |z| = √(a² + b²), z z̄ = |z|², z⁻¹ = z̄/|z|²
- Polar: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ)
- D < 0: x = (−b ± i√(4ac − b²))/2a

- ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!; ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!); ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ; ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ; identical objects n!/(p!q!…)

- Sign of trigonometric functions by quadrant
- Forgetting n + 1 terms in a binomial expansion

steps.title: Straight lines and conics
steps.body:
- m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); ∥: m₁ = m₂; ⟂: m₁m₂ = −1; tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|

steps.body:

lessons.title: Exam strategy and mixed practice

scenes.text: Kunal always ran out of time in maths papers — he got stuck on question 5 for 25 minutes.
This time he reads the whole paper first, does sure-shot questions, marks the hard ones and comes back. He finishes with 15 minutes to check.

steps.title: Before the exam
steps.body:
- Revise from your formula sheet and one solved example per topic.
- Re-solve your past mistakes — they repeat.
- Sleep well; tired brains make sign errors.

steps.title: In the exam
steps.body:
- First 10 minutes: read everything, tick easy questions.
- Show steps — marks are given for method.
- Box final answers with units.
- If stuck for 3–4 minutes, move on and return later.
- Keep 10–15 minutes to check signs, brackets and arithmetic.

steps.title: Mixed problem 1
steps.body:
If tan x = −4/3 with x in QII, find sin(x/2).

- cos x = −3/5. sin²(x/2) = (1 − cos x)/2 = (1 + 3/5)/2 = 4/5.
- x/2 lies in QI (π/4 < x/2 < π/2), so sin(x/2) = **2/√5**.

steps.title: Mixed problem 2
steps.body:
How many terms of the A.P. −6, −11/2, −5, … sum to −25?

- a = −6, d = 1/2: (n/2)[−12 + (n − 1)/2] = −25 → n² − 25n + 100 = 0 → n = 5 or 20.
- Both are valid (the terms from 6th to 20th sum to 0).

steps.title: Self-check list
steps.body:
- Did I answer what was asked (term vs coefficient, P vs C)?
- Did I include the domain restrictions?
- Is a probability between 0 and 1? Is a length positive?

quiz.why: If you are stuck, move on and come back later, so you do not lose time for questions you can solve. Guessing and never returning, or leaving, wastes marks.

quiz.q: Marks in board exams are often given for
quiz.why: Board examiners award marks for each correct step of the method, so showing working earns marks even if the final answer slips.

quiz.q: A probability answer of 1.2 indicates
quiz.why: A probability must be between 0 and 1, so a value of 1.2 means a mistake has been made somewhere in the working.

quiz.q: If tan x = −4/3 in QII, cos x is
quiz.why: tan x = −4/3 with x in the second quadrant gives a 3-4-5 triangle. There cosine is negative, so cos x = −3/5.

quiz.q: The best revision of formulas is to
options: write them yourself and test yourself
quiz.why: Writing formulas yourself and testing yourself is active recall, which builds memory better than just reading or memorising without practice.
