school-c11-physics-a.title: Class 11 Physics · Part A (Ch 1–4)
school-c11-physics-a.description: Class 11 Physics chapter by chapter: Units and Measurement, Motion in a Straight Line, Motion in a Plane and Laws of Motion — derivations, solved numericals and JEE/NEET bridge practice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Units and Measurement
courses.summary: SI units, significant figures, errors and their propagation, and dimensional analysis — the toolkit every later chapter uses.
outcomes: Learners can name the seven SI base quantities and units and build derived units
Learners can apply significant-figure and rounding rules in calculations
Learners can compute absolute, relative and percentage errors and combine them
Learners can use dimensions to check equations and derive simple relations

lessons.title: SI units, base and derived quantities

scenes.text: Riya's father drives at 72 km/h. Her physics sheet asks for speed in m/s.
She realises every formula in physics expects SI units — so she learns to convert before calculating.

steps.title: Base quantities and units
steps.body:
The SI system has **seven base quantities**:
- length — metre (m)
- mass — kilogram (kg)
- time — second (s)
- electric current — ampere (A)
- thermodynamic temperature — kelvin (K)
- amount of substance — mole (mol)
- luminous intensity — candela (cd)

Two supplementary units are used for angles: radian (rad) for plane angle and steradian (sr) for solid angle. Every other unit is **derived** from base units, e.g. force: kg m s⁻² = newton (N); energy: kg m² s⁻² = joule (J).

steps.title: Prefixes you must know
steps.body:
- kilo (k) 10³, mega (M) 10⁶, giga (G) 10⁹
- centi (c) 10⁻², milli (m) 10⁻³, micro (µ) 10⁻⁶, nano (n) 10⁻⁹, pico (p) 10⁻¹², femto (f) 10⁻¹⁵

Useful non-SI length units: 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, 1 fermi = 10⁻¹⁵ m, 1 light year ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m, 1 AU ≈ 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, 1 parsec ≈ 3.08 × 10¹⁶ m.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Convert 72 km/h to m/s.
- 1 km = 1000 m, 1 h = 3600 s
- 72 × 1000 / 3600 = 20 m/s
- Shortcut: multiply km/h by 5/18.

**Example 2:** Density of water is 1 g/cm³. Express in kg/m³.
- 1 g = 10⁻³ kg; 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³
- 1 × 10⁻³ / 10⁻⁶ = 10³ kg/m³ = 1000 kg/m³

**Example 3:** Express 1 N in CGS (dyne).
- 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻² = 10³ g × 10² cm s⁻² = 10⁵ dyne

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing units as plurals or with full stops: write 5 kg, not 5 kgs or 5 kg.
- Mixing CGS and SI inside one formula.
- Converting area or volume with the linear factor: 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², not 10² cm².
- Confusing mass (kg) with weight (N).

activity.prompt: Match each quantity to its SI unit

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an SI base unit?
quiz.why: The newton is a derived unit (kg·m·s⁻²). The candela, kelvin and mole are SI base units.

quiz.q: 36 km/h equals
quiz.why: To convert km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18: 36 × 5/18 = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: 1 light year is a unit of
quiz.why: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, so despite 'year' it measures distance, not time.

quiz.q: How many cm³ are there in 1 m³?
quiz.why: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m³ = (100 cm)³ = 10⁶ cm³. Cubing the length factor gives the volume factor.

quiz.q: The SI unit of solid angle is
quiz.why: The steradian (sr) is the SI unit of solid angle. The radian is for plane angle.

scenes.text: Arjun writes the length as 2.5 cm and the width as 3.42 cm, then reports area as 8.55 cm².
His teacher asks: can a product be more precise than the least precise measurement? Arjun corrects it to 8.6 cm².

steps.title: Rules for counting significant figures
steps.body:
- All non-zero digits are significant.
- Zeros between non-zero digits are significant (2005 has 4).
- Leading zeros are NOT significant (0.0045 has 2).
- Trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant (4.500 has 4).
- Trailing zeros in a whole number without a decimal point are ambiguous — use scientific notation: 4.50 × 10³ has 3.
- Exact numbers (counted items, defined constants like 2 in 2πr) have infinite significant figures.

steps.title: Arithmetic rules
steps.body:
**Multiplication/division:** the result keeps as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest significant figures.

**Addition/subtraction:** the result keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places.

**Rounding:** if the dropped digit is more than 5, round up; less than 5, leave; exactly 5 (followed by nothing), make the preceding digit even (2.745 → 2.74, 2.735 → 2.74).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** How many significant figures in 0.007020?
- Leading zeros 0.00 are not significant.
- 7, 0, 2 and the trailing 0 after the decimal are significant → **4**.

**Example 2:** 2.5 cm × 3.42 cm = ?
- Raw product 8.55; least s.f. = 2 (in 2.5)
- Answer **8.6 cm²**

**Example 3:** 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.013 = ?
- Raw sum 31.123; fewest decimal places = 1 (18.0)
- Answer **31.1**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding at every intermediate step — keep one extra digit and round only at the end.
- Counting leading zeros as significant.
- Applying the decimal-place rule to multiplication.
- Changing units changes s.f.? No: 2.30 m = 230 cm keeps 3 s.f. — write 2.30 × 10² cm to show it.

activity.prompt: Sort each number by its count of significant figures

quiz.q: Number of significant figures in 6.320 × 10⁴ is
quiz.why: In 6.320 × 10⁴, the digits 6, 3, 2 and the trailing 0 after the decimal point are all significant, giving 4 significant figures.

quiz.q: 4.0 × 2.123 should be reported as
quiz.why: In multiplication the answer has as many significant figures as the least precise number. 4.0 has 2, so 4.0 × 2.123 = 8.492 is rounded to 8.5.
In addition the result keeps the fewest decimal places of the numbers added. 3.5 has one decimal, so 4.861 is rounded to 4.9.

quiz.q: Rounded to 3 s.f., 2.745 becomes
quiz.why: When the digit to be dropped is exactly 5, the usual rule is to keep the preceding digit if it is even. Since the preceding digit 4 is even, 2.745 becomes 2.74.

quiz.q: The 2 in the formula C = 2πr has how many significant figures?
quiz.why: The 2 in C = 2πr is an exact number from the definition, so it has unlimited significant figures and does not limit the precision of the answer.

scenes.text: Five students time one pendulum swing and get slightly different values.
Instead of arguing, they compute the mean and the mean absolute error — and report the period as a value ± error.

steps.title: Types of error
steps.body:
- **Systematic errors** push results in one direction: instrumental (zero error), imperfect technique, personal bias. Reduced by better method and calibration.
- **Random errors** vary unpredictably; reduced by taking many readings and averaging.
- **Least count error** is the resolution of the instrument (e.g. vernier 0.01 cm, screw gauge 0.001 cm).

steps.title: Absolute, relative and percentage error
steps.body:
For readings a₁, a₂ … aₙ:
- Mean a = (Σaᵢ)/n
- Absolute error Δaᵢ = aᵢ − a
- Mean absolute error Δa = (Σ|Δaᵢ|)/n
- Relative error = Δa / a; Percentage error = (Δa / a) × 100%

**Combination rules:**
- Z = A ± B → ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB (absolute errors add)
- Z = AB or A/B → ΔZ/Z = ΔA/A + ΔB/B (relative errors add)
- Z = Aᵖ Bᑫ / Cʳ → ΔZ/Z = pΔA/A + qΔB/B + rΔC/C

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting errors when quantities are subtracted — errors always ADD.
- Forgetting to multiply by the power (a squared term doubles its relative error).
- Reporting more decimals in the error than the measurement supports.
- Ignoring zero error of the instrument.

activity.prompt: Length l = (20.0 ± 0.1) cm and breadth b = (10.0 ± 0.1) cm. What is the percentage error in the area l × b?

quiz.q: If x = a³/b² and errors in a and b are 1% and 2%, the % error in x is
quiz.why: For x = a³/b², the percentage errors multiply by the powers and add: 3 × 1% + 2 × 2% = 7%. Errors add, even for division.

quiz.q: Random errors are reduced by
quiz.why: Random errors vary unpredictably, so taking many readings and averaging reduces their effect. Calibration fixes systematic errors instead.

quiz.q: For Z = A − B, ΔZ equals
quiz.why: For both addition and subtraction the maximum absolute errors add: ΔZ = ΔA + ΔB. The errors never cancel in the worst case.

quiz.q: A zero error in a screw gauge is a
options: gross error that cannot be corrected
quiz.why: A zero error shifts every reading in the same direction by the same amount, so it is a systematic error, and it can be corrected by subtracting it.

quiz.q: Mean of 1.2, 1.4, 1.3 is 1.3. Mean absolute error is
quiz.why: The deviations from the mean 1.3 are 0.1, 0.1 and 0. The mean absolute error is (0.1 + 0.1 + 0)/3 ≈ 0.067.

story.title: Checking a formula without a textbook

scenes.text: Kabir half-remembers that a pendulum's period is T = 2π√(g/l). Something feels wrong.
He checks dimensions: √(g/l) has unit s⁻¹, not s. So it must be √(l/g). Dimensions caught the slip.

steps.title: Dimensions
steps.body:
The dimensions of a quantity show how it depends on base quantities, written with [M], [L], [T], [A], [K], [mol], [cd].
- Velocity [L T⁻¹]; acceleration [L T⁻²]
- Force [M L T⁻²]; work/energy [M L² T⁻²]
- Power [M L² T⁻³]; pressure [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]
- Gravitational constant G: [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]
- Angle, strain, refractive index: dimensionless [M⁰ L⁰ T⁰]

steps.title: Principle of homogeneity and uses
steps.body:
Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, subtracted or equated. Uses:
- **Checking** correctness of an equation (necessary, not sufficient).
- **Converting** units between systems.
- **Deducing** relations among quantities (when the dependence is a product of powers).

**Limitations:** cannot find dimensionless constants (like 2π), cannot handle sums of terms or trigonometric/exponential functions, cannot tell scalars from vectors.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Check v² = u² + 2as.
- LHS [L² T⁻²]; u² [L² T⁻²]; as = [L T⁻²][L] = [L² T⁻²] → consistent.

**Example 2:** Derive T for a pendulum depending on l, m, g: T = k lᵃ mᵇ gᶜ.
- [T] = [L]ᵃ [M]ᵇ [L T⁻²]ᶜ
- M: b = 0; T: −2c = 1 → c = −½; L: a + c = 0 → a = ½
- T = k√(l/g) (experiment gives k = 2π)

**Example 3:** Is ½mv² = mgh dimensionally correct? Both sides [M L² T⁻²] → yes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a dimensionally correct equation must be physically correct (E = mv² is dimensionally fine but wrong by ½).
- Forgetting that arguments of sin, log and exp must be dimensionless.
- Mixing up dimensions of work and torque — both [M L² T⁻²] but different physical meaning.
- Treating radian as having dimensions.

activity.prompt: Match each quantity to its dimensional formula

quiz.q: Dimensions of impulse are the same as those of
quiz.why: Impulse = force × time = change in momentum, so its dimensions are [M L T⁻¹], same as momentum.

quiz.q: Which pair has identical dimensions?
quiz.why: Both work and torque have dimensions [M L² T⁻²], even though they are different physical quantities.

quiz.q: Dimensional analysis cannot determine
options: the value of a dimensionless constant
quiz.why: Dimensional analysis cannot find pure numbers such as ½ or 2π, because they have no dimensions. It can still check consistency and unit conversions.

quiz.q: In x = A sin(ωt), the dimension of ω is
quiz.why: The argument of a sine must be dimensionless, so ωt has no dimensions. Since t is [T], ω is [T⁻¹].

quiz.q: Dimensional formula of surface tension (force per length) is
quiz.why: Surface tension is force per unit length: [M L T⁻²]/[L] = [M T⁻²].

questions.q: The SI unit of luminous intensity is
questions.why: The candela (cd) is the SI base unit of luminous intensity. The lumen and lux are derived units.

questions.q: 1 fermi equals
questions.why: The fermi, used for nuclear sizes, equals 10⁻¹⁵ m (also called a femtometre).

questions.q: Number of significant figures in 0.06900 is
questions.why: Leading zeros are not significant, but the trailing zeros after the decimal point are. So 0.06900 has 4 significant figures: 6, 9, 0, 0.

questions.q: 108 km/h in m/s is
questions.why: Multiply km/h by 5/18 to get m/s: 108 × 5/18 = 30 m/s.

questions.q: Dimensions of power are
questions.why: Power is energy per unit time: [M L² T⁻²]/[T] = [M L² T⁻³].

questions.q: Assertion: A dimensionally correct equation may be wrong. Reason: Dimensional analysis cannot find numerical constants.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. An equation can have matching dimensions but still be wrong, for example if a numerical constant like ½ is missing, which dimensions cannot detect.

questions.q: 5.74 g occupies 1.2 cm³. Density with correct significant figures is
questions.why: Density = 5.74/1.2 = 4.783 g/cm³. The volume 1.2 has only 2 significant figures, so the answer is rounded to 4.8 g/cm³.

questions.q: If P = a³b²/(cd) with % errors 1, 2, 3, 4 in a, b, c, d, the % error in P is
questions.why: For P = a³b²/(cd), percentage error = 3(1) + 2(2) + 3 + 4 = 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14%. All the errors add up.

questions.q: Which has the same dimensions as pressure?
questions.why: Energy per unit volume is J/m³ = N·m/m³ = N/m², which is the same as pressure.

questions.q: Case: A student measures a sphere's radius as (2.0 ± 0.1) cm. What is the percentage error in its volume?
questions.why: Since V ∝ r³, the percentage error in V is 3 times that in r. The error in r is 0.1/2.0 × 100 = 5%, so V has 3 × 5 = 15%.

questions.q: Using dimensions, the speed v of a wave on a string depending on tension F and mass per length µ is
questions.why: Tension has [M L T⁻²] and mass per length has [M L⁻¹], so F/μ has [L² T⁻²]. Taking the square root gives [L T⁻¹], which is speed: v = √(F/μ).

questions.q: Value of G is 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². In CGS (dyne cm² g⁻²) it is
questions.why: 1 N = 10⁵ dyne, 1 m² = 10⁴ cm², and 1 kg⁻² = (10³ g)⁻² = 10⁻⁶ g⁻². The net factor is 10⁵ × 10⁴ × 10⁻⁶ = 10³, so G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 10³ = 6.67 × 10⁻⁸.

questions.q: Readings of a length: 1.22, 1.24, 1.20, 1.26 cm. Mean absolute error is
questions.why: The mean is 1.23 cm. The deviations are 0.01, 0.01, 0.03, 0.03, and their average is 0.08/4 = 0.02 cm.

questions.q: In the relation y = a sin(bt − cx), dimensions of b/c are those of
questions.why: In sin(bt − cx), bt and cx are dimensionless, so b is [T⁻¹] and c is [L⁻¹]. Then b/c has dimensions [L T⁻¹], that of velocity.

questions.q: Which measurement is most precise?
questions.why: The last digit of 5.00 mm is the hundredths of a millimetre, so its uncertainty (about 0.01 mm) is the smallest of the options. The other values have larger absolute uncertainty.

questions.q: A physical quantity X = M L² T⁻² could be
questions.why: [M L² T⁻²] is the dimension of work and energy. Force is [M L T⁻²], momentum [M L T⁻¹] and pressure [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].

courses.title: Ch 2 · Motion in a Straight Line
courses.summary: Position, displacement, velocity and acceleration in one dimension; motion graphs; derivations of the kinematic equations; free fall and relative velocity.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish distance from displacement and speed from velocity
Learners can read and draw x–t and v–t graphs and use slopes and areas
Learners can derive and apply the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion
Learners can solve free-fall and relative-velocity problems

scenes.text: An auto goes 360 m east to drop a parcel, then comes back 120 m to pick up Meena.
Meena notices the meter charged for 480 m, but she is only 240 m from the start. Distance and displacement are different!

steps.title: Key definitions
steps.body:
- **Position** x: location relative to a chosen origin on a line, with sign showing direction.
- **Displacement** Δx = x₂ − x₁ (vector; can be negative or zero).
- **Path length (distance)**: total length travelled (scalar, never negative).
- **Average velocity** = Δx / Δt (vector).
- **Average speed** = path length / time (scalar). Average speed ≥ |average velocity|.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A car goes 360 m east in 18 s, then 120 m west in 6 s.
- Displacement = 360 − 120 = 240 m east; distance = 480 m; time = 24 s
- Average velocity = 240/24 = **10 m/s east**; average speed = 480/24 = **20 m/s**

**Example 2:** A runner completes one full lap of a 400 m track in 50 s.
- Displacement = 0 → average velocity = 0
- Average speed = 400/50 = **8 m/s**

steps.title: Sign convention
steps.body: Choose one direction as positive and stick to it for position, velocity and acceleration. A negative velocity just means motion in the negative direction — not 'slowing down'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Averaging speeds directly: going 30 km/h one way and 60 km/h back over the same distance gives average speed 40 km/h, not 45 (use total distance / total time).
- Treating distance and displacement as equal when the motion reverses.

activity.prompt: A cyclist rides 6 km at 12 km/h and returns the same 6 km at 6 km/h. What is the average speed for the round trip?

quiz.q: A body moves on a circle of radius r and completes half a revolution. Displacement is
quiz.why: After half a revolution, the body is at the opposite end of a diameter, so the displacement is the straight-line distance 2r. The path length would be πr.

quiz.q: Average speed is always
options: greater than or equal to |average velocity|
quiz.why: Average speed = total path length/time and |average velocity| = |displacement|/time. The path length is never less than the displacement, so average speed ≥ |average velocity|.

quiz.q: Displacement can be
quiz.why: Displacement is a vector along the line, so it can be positive, negative (opposite direction) or zero (returning to the start).

quiz.q: A man walks 4 m east then 3 m west in 7 s. Average velocity is
quiz.why: The net displacement is 4 − 3 = 1 m east. Average velocity = displacement/time = 1/7 m/s east, not distance/time.

quiz.q: Equal distances at speeds v₁ and v₂: average speed =
quiz.why: For equal distances d at speeds v₁ and v₂, total time = d/v₁ + d/v₂, so average speed = 2d/(d/v₁ + d/v₂) = 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂), the harmonic mean, not the simple average.

lessons.title: Instantaneous velocity, acceleration and motion graphs

scenes.text: A bike-taxi app plots position against time. The curve gets steeper.
Steeper slope means higher velocity. Sami learns to read speed straight off a graph.

steps.title: Instantaneous quantities
steps.body:
- **Instantaneous velocity** v = dx/dt = slope of the x–t graph at that instant.
- **Average acceleration** = Δv/Δt; **instantaneous acceleration** a = dv/dt = d²x/dt² = slope of the v–t graph.
- **Area under the v–t graph** between two times = displacement.
- Area under the a–t graph = change in velocity.

If v and a have the same sign the object speeds up; opposite signs → it slows down.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** x = 8.5 + 2.5t² (x in m, t in s). Find v and a at t = 2 s.
- v = dx/dt = 5t → v(2) = **10 m/s**
- a = dv/dt = **5 m/s²** (constant)

**Example 2:** v–t graph: velocity rises uniformly from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s, stays 20 m/s for 6 s, then falls to 0 in 5 s. Total displacement?
- Triangle ½ × 4 × 20 = 40 m; rectangle 6 × 20 = 120 m; triangle ½ × 5 × 20 = 50 m
- Total = **210 m**

steps.title: Graph shapes
steps.body:
- Uniform velocity: straight sloping x–t line; horizontal v–t line.
- Uniform acceleration: parabola on x–t; straight sloping v–t line.
- At rest: horizontal x–t line.
- An x–t graph can never be vertical (infinite speed) or double-valued in time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading displacement from the HEIGHT of a v–t graph instead of the AREA.
- Assuming zero velocity means zero acceleration — at the top of a vertical throw v = 0 but a = g.
- Counting area below the time axis as positive displacement (it is negative).

statements.s: The slope of an x–t graph gives acceleration.
statements.why: It gives velocity; the slope of v–t gives acceleration.

statements.s: Area under a v–t graph gives displacement.
A body can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration.
statements.why: Top point of a vertical throw.

statements.s: An x–t graph can be a vertical line.
If v and a are opposite in sign, the object slows down.
statements.why: Acceleration reduces the magnitude of velocity.

quiz.q: For x = 3t³ m, acceleration at t = 1 s is
quiz.why: Differentiate x = 3t³: v = 9t², a = 18t. At t = 1 s, a = 18 m/s².

quiz.q: A straight v–t line with positive slope indicates
quiz.why: The slope of a v–t graph is acceleration. A straight line has a constant slope, so the acceleration is uniform (and positive here).

quiz.q: Area under an acceleration–time graph is
quiz.why: The area under an acceleration–time graph is ∫a dt, which equals the change in velocity. The area under a v–t graph gives displacement.

quiz.q: A ball thrown up: at the top,
quiz.why: At the highest point the velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g downward.

quiz.q: x–t graph of uniformly accelerated motion from rest is a
quiz.why: Starting from rest with constant acceleration x = ½at², which is quadratic in t, so the x–t graph is a parabola.

scenes.text: A car at 126 km/h sees a stalled truck. The driver brakes hard and stops in 200 m.
Using v² = u² + 2as, the class finds the deceleration and stopping time — and why speed limits matter.

steps.title: The three equations (constant a)
steps.body:
- v = u + at
- s = ut + ½at²
- v² = u² + 2as

Also: displacement in the nth second sₙ = u + a(2n − 1)/2, and s = (u + v)t/2.

**Graphical derivation:** on a v–t straight line from u to v over time t, slope = a gives v = u + at; area (rectangle ut + triangle ½(v − u)t) gives s = ut + ½at². Eliminating t gives v² = u² + 2as.

**Calculus derivation:** a = dv/dt → ∫dv = ∫a dt → v = u + at; v = dx/dt → x = ut + ½at²; a = v dv/dx → v² − u² = 2as.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** u = 126 km/h = 35 m/s, stops in 200 m.
- 0 = 35² + 2a(200) → a = −1225/400 = **−3.06 m/s²**
- t = (0 − 35)/(−3.06) ≈ **11.4 s**

**Example 2:** A ball is thrown up at 20 m/s from the top of a 25 m building (g = 10 m/s²). When does it hit the ground?
- Take up as positive, origin at roof: −25 = 20t − 5t²
- t² − 4t − 5 = 0 → (t − 5)(t + 1) = 0 → **t = 5 s**
- Max height above roof = u²/2g = 400/20 = 20 m

steps.title: Free fall
steps.body:
Neglecting air resistance, all bodies near Earth fall with a = g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward. From rest: v = gt, h = ½gt², v² = 2gh.

**Galileo's law of odd numbers:** distances fallen in successive equal intervals from rest are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7 …

**Stopping distance** ∝ u²: doubling speed makes braking distance four times.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using kinematic equations when acceleration is NOT constant.
- Mixing sign conventions (taking g positive while upward velocity is also positive).
- Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s.
- Rejecting the negative root without thinking — check which root is physical.

activity.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest from a height of 80 m (g = 10 m/s²). How many seconds does it take to reach the ground?

quiz.q: A body starts from rest with a = 2 m/s². Distance in the 5th second is
quiz.why: Distance in the nth second = u + a(2n − 1)/2. With u = 0, a = 2 and n = 5, that is 2 × 9/2 = 9 m. (25 m is the distance in 5 seconds.)

quiz.q: If initial speed doubles, braking distance (same deceleration) becomes
quiz.why: With v = 0, stopping distance s = u²/(2a). Doubling u makes u² four times larger, so the distance becomes four times.

quiz.q: Ratio of distances fallen in 1st, 2nd and 3rd seconds of free fall is
quiz.why: From rest, distances in successive seconds are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5 (odd numbers), which is Galileo's law for free fall.

quiz.q: A ball thrown up at 30 m/s (g = 10) reaches maximum height
quiz.why: Maximum height H = u²/2g = 900/20 = 45 m.

quiz.q: Kinematic equations apply when
quiz.why: The kinematic equations of motion are derived assuming constant acceleration, so they apply only in that case.

scenes.text: A bus at 60 km/h is overtaken by a car at 80 km/h. To the bus passengers the car seems to crawl past.
On a parallel track, a train coming the other way at 40 km/h seems to rush past at 100 km/h.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
Velocity of A relative to B: **v_AB = v_A − v_B**. Similarly v_BA = v_B − v_A = −v_AB.

Relative position x_BA = x_B − x_A changes at rate v_BA. If v_A = v_B, the separation stays constant (x–t lines parallel). Same direction: relative speed = difference; opposite directions: relative speed = sum.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Car 80 km/h and bus 60 km/h, same direction.
- v_car,bus = 80 − 60 = **20 km/h** forward

**Example 2:** Two trains 100 m and 150 m long move in opposite directions at 15 m/s and 10 m/s. Time to cross each other?
- Relative speed = 25 m/s; distance = 100 + 150 = 250 m
- t = 250/25 = **10 s**

**Example 3:** Two cars 1 km apart move toward each other at 54 km/h (15 m/s) and 36 km/h (10 m/s). They meet after 1000/25 = **40 s**.

steps.title: Trick
steps.body: Freeze one body: give both bodies a velocity equal and opposite to the one you freeze. Then only one body moves, with the relative velocity, and the problem becomes simple.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Getting the order wrong: v_AB is A as seen from B (A minus B).
- Forgetting to add both train lengths when trains cross.
- Mixing km/h and m/s.

activity.prompt: Complete the statement
activity.text: Two bodies moving in opposite directions at 20 m/s and 30 m/s have relative speed ___ m/s; in the same direction it is ___ m/s.

quiz.q: A at +10 m/s, B at −5 m/s. v_AB =
quiz.why: The relative velocity of A with respect to B is v_A − v_B = 10 − (−5) = 15 m/s.

quiz.q: Two cars with equal velocity: x–t graphs are
quiz.why: Equal velocity means equal slope on x–t graphs, so the lines are parallel and the separation stays constant.

quiz.q: A 200 m train at 20 m/s crosses a 300 m bridge in
quiz.why: The train must cover its own length plus the bridge: 200 + 300 = 500 m. At 20 m/s the time is 500/20 = 25 s.

quiz.q: v_BA equals
quiz.why: v_BA = v_B − v_A = −(v_A − v_B) = −v_AB. Swapping the observer reverses the sign.

quiz.q: Two trains 120 m each at 36 km/h and 54 km/h in the same direction. Time for the faster to pass the slower:
quiz.why: 36 km/h = 10 m/s and 54 km/h = 15 m/s, so the relative speed is 5 m/s. To pass, the faster train must gain 120 + 120 = 240 m, so t = 240/5 = 48 s.

questions.q: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives
questions.why: The slope of a velocity–time graph is dv/dt, which is the acceleration.

questions.q: Odometer measures
questions.why: An odometer records the total path length travelled, i.e. distance, and not displacement.

questions.q: A body moving with uniform velocity has acceleration
questions.why: Uniform velocity means the velocity does not change with time, so the acceleration is zero.

questions.q: x = 2t² − 4t. Velocity is zero at
questions.why: v = dx/dt = 4t − 4. Setting v = 0 gives t = 1 s.

questions.q: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. Distance covered:
questions.why: With uniform acceleration, s = (u + v)t/2 = (10 + 30)/2 × 5 = 20 × 5 = 100 m.

questions.q: Assertion: A body can have constant speed but varying velocity. Reason: Velocity includes direction.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Velocity is a vector with direction, so even at constant speed the velocity changes if the direction changes, as in motion on a circle.

questions.q: A ball dropped from 45 m (g = 10) hits the ground with speed
questions.why: Using v² = 2gh = 2 × 10 × 45 = 900, so v = 30 m/s.

questions.q: Distance travelled in the 3rd second by a body starting from rest with a = 4 m/s²:
questions.why: Distance in the nth second = a(2n − 1)/2 for a start from rest. With a = 4 and n = 3: 4 × 5/2 = 10 m.

questions.q: Case: A cricket ball is thrown up with 20 m/s and caught at the same height (g = 10). Total time in air?
questions.why: The ball returns to the same height after T = 2u/g = 2 × 20/10 = 4 s (2 s up and 2 s down).

questions.q: A train starting from rest accelerates at 1 m/s² for 10 s, moves uniformly for 30 s, then decelerates to rest in 5 s. Total distance:
questions.why: After 10 s the speed is 10 m/s. Distances: ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 m, then 10 × 30 = 300 m, then ½ × 10 × 5 = 25 m. Total = 375 m.

questions.q: A stone is thrown up from a 40 m tower at 10 m/s (g = 10). Time to reach the ground:
questions.why: Taking up as positive, displacement = −40 m: −40 = 10t − 5t², so t² − 2t − 8 = 0 and (t − 4)(t + 2) = 0. The valid time is t = 4 s.

questions.q: Two balls are dropped from heights h and 4h. Ratio of their times of fall:
questions.why: From h = ½gt², time of fall t ∝ √h. For heights h and 4h the ratio of times is √1 : √4 = 1 : 2.

questions.q: A body covers 20 m in the 2nd second and 40 m in the 4th second (uniform a). Its acceleration is
questions.why: The distance in the nth second is u + a(2n − 1)/2. So s₄ − s₂ = a(7 − 3)/2 = 2a. Here 40 − 20 = 20 = 2a, so a = 10 m/s².

questions.q: Velocity v of a particle varies with position as v = α√x. Its acceleration is
questions.why: a = v dv/dx. With v = α√x, dv/dx = α/(2√x), so a = α√x × α/(2√x) = α²/2, a constant.

questions.q: Car A (25 m/s) is 100 m behind car B (15 m/s), same lane and direction. Time for A to catch B:
questions.why: A gains on B at the relative speed 25 − 15 = 10 m/s. To close a gap of 100 m takes 100/10 = 10 s.

questions.q: An x–t graph is a straight line parallel to the time axis. The body is
questions.why: A horizontal line on an x–t graph means the position does not change with time, so the body is at rest.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Motion in a Plane
courses.summary: Vectors and their algebra, motion in two dimensions with constant acceleration, projectile motion with full derivations, and uniform circular motion.
outcomes: Learners can add, subtract and resolve vectors graphically and analytically
Learners can describe 2D motion with position, velocity and acceleration vectors
Learners can derive time of flight, maximum height, range and trajectory of a projectile
Learners can compute centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion

scenes.text: Two friends pull a cart with ropes at an angle. Each pulls with 10 N.
The cart does not feel 20 N — it feels about 17 N. Direction matters, so forces add as vectors.

steps.title: Vectors and their properties
steps.body:
- **Scalar**: magnitude only (mass, time, energy). **Vector**: magnitude and direction, obeys triangle/parallelogram law (displacement, force, velocity).
- Equal vectors: same magnitude and direction. Negative vector −A: same magnitude, opposite direction.
- Multiplying by a scalar λ scales magnitude by |λ| (and reverses direction if λ < 0).
- Addition is commutative and associative. A − B = A + (−B).
- **Null vector** 0: zero magnitude, e.g. A + (−A).

steps.title: Analytical addition and resolution
steps.body:
Resultant of A and B with angle θ between them:
- R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)
- tan α = B sin θ / (A + B cos θ), α measured from A

**Resolution:** A = Aₓ î + A_y ĵ with Aₓ = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ; |A| = √(Aₓ² + A_y²), tan θ = A_y/Aₓ.

Add components: R = (Aₓ + Bₓ) î + (A_y + B_y) ĵ. Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ have magnitude 1 along x, y, z.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 3 N and 4 N at 90°.
- R = √(9 + 16) = **5 N**; tan α = 4/3 → α ≈ 53° from the 3 N force

**Example 2:** Two 10 N forces at 60°.
- R = √(100 + 100 + 200 × 0.5) = √300 = **17.3 N**, along the bisector (30° from each)

**Example 3:** A = 3î + 4ĵ, B = î − 2ĵ. Find A + B and |A − B|.
- A + B = 4î + 2ĵ; A − B = 2î + 6ĵ → |A − B| = √40 ≈ **6.32**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding magnitudes directly when vectors are not parallel.
- Using the angle between head and tail instead of between the vectors drawn tail to tail.
- Thinking the resultant must exceed each vector — range is |A − B| ≤ R ≤ A + B.
- Treating current as a vector (it has direction but does not add by vector law).

bands.text: 120°: R = 10 N — equal to each force.

quiz.q: Resultant of two equal forces F at 120° is
quiz.why: For two equal forces F at angle θ, R = √(F² + F² + 2F² cos θ). With θ = 120°, cos θ = −1/2, so R = √(2F² − F²) = F.

quiz.q: Which is a vector?
quiz.why: Impulse is force × time and has a direction (that of the change in momentum), so it is a vector. Work, current and temperature are scalars.
The magnitude is √(3² + (−4)²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

quiz.q: Two forces 5 N and 8 N can NOT have a resultant of
quiz.why: The resultant of 5 N and 8 N lies between their difference (3 N) and their sum (13 N). So 2 N is impossible.

quiz.q: Component of a 20 N force at 30° to the x-axis along x:
quiz.why: The component along x is F cos θ = 20 cos 30° = 20 × 0.866 ≈ 17.3 N. The component along y would be 10 N.

lessons.title: Motion in a plane and relative velocity in 2D

scenes.text: Rain falls straight down, but as Neha cycles fast, the rain seems to hit her face.
She tilts her umbrella forward — along the relative velocity of rain with respect to her.

steps.title: Position, velocity and acceleration vectors
steps.body:
- Position r = x î + y ĵ; velocity v = dr/dt = vₓ î + v_y ĵ (always tangent to the path).
- Acceleration a = dv/dt.
- With constant a: **v = u + at** and **r = r₀ + ut + ½at²** — these split into independent x and y equations. This is the key idea: motion in a plane = two independent 1D motions.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** r = 3t î + 2t² ĵ (m). Find v and a at t = 1 s.
- v = 3 î + 4t ĵ → at t = 1: 3î + 4ĵ, |v| = **5 m/s**
- a = 4 ĵ m/s² (constant, along y)

**Example 2:** Rain falls vertically at 35 m/s; wind blows east at 12 m/s.
- Resultant speed = √(35² + 12²) = √1369 = **37 m/s**
- Angle with vertical: tan θ = 12/35 → θ ≈ **19°** towards east — hold umbrella tilted that way.

**Example 3:** A boat at 4 km/h (relative to water) heads straight across a river flowing at 3 km/h. Resultant speed 5 km/h; it drifts downstream.

steps.title: River-boat ideas
steps.body:
- To cross in **minimum time**, head perpendicular to the flow: t = width / v_boat.
- To cross along the **shortest path** (straight across), head upstream at angle θ with sin θ = v_river / v_boat (possible only if v_boat > v_river).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking acceleration must be along the velocity — in a projectile it is downward while v is slanted.
- Subtracting speeds instead of vectors in 2D relative motion.
- Mixing up 'angle with vertical' and 'angle with horizontal'.

activity.prompt: A swimmer swims at 5 m/s relative to water, straight across a river 100 m wide that flows at 3 m/s. How long (in s) does she take to cross?

quiz.q: r = 2t² î + 3t ĵ. Acceleration is
quiz.why: Differentiate r = 2t² î + 3t ĵ once: v = 4t î + 3 ĵ. Again: a = 4 î (the ĵ term is constant, so it vanishes).

quiz.q: Velocity of a particle is always
quiz.why: Velocity v = dr/dt is always tangent to the particle's path. Acceleration need not be along it.

quiz.q: A man walks at 4 km/h; rain falls vertically at 3 km/h. Relative speed of rain to man:
quiz.why: Rain relative to the man = rain velocity − man velocity. The speed is √(4² + 3²) = √25 = 5 km/h.

quiz.q: To cross a river in minimum time, a boat should head
quiz.why: The component of the boat's velocity across the river decides the crossing time, and it is largest when the boat heads perpendicular to the flow, so the time is least.

quiz.q: Motion in a plane with constant acceleration can be treated as
quiz.why: With constant acceleration, the x and y components of motion are independent, so each can be treated as a separate one-dimensional motion.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: motion in a plane)

scenes.text: A fielder throws the ball at 20 m/s. At what angle should he throw to reach the keeper farthest away?
Physics says 45° for maximum range on level ground — and 30° and 60° give the same range!

steps.title: Derivations
steps.body:
Launch speed u at angle θ; take aₓ = 0, a_y = −g.
- x = (u cos θ) t; y = (u sin θ) t − ½gt²
- **Trajectory:** eliminate t → y = x tan θ − g x² / (2u² cos² θ), a parabola.
- **Time of flight:** y = 0 → T = 2u sin θ / g
- **Maximum height:** v_y = 0 → H = u² sin² θ / (2g)
- **Horizontal range:** R = (u cos θ)T = u² sin 2θ / g; maximum R = u²/g at θ = 45°.
- θ and (90° − θ) give the same range.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s².
- T = 2 × 20 × 0.5/10 = **2 s**
- H = 400 × 0.25/20 = **5 m**
- R = 400 × sin 60°/10 = 40 × 0.866 = **34.6 m**

**Example 2:** A ball is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a cliff 45 m high (g = 10).
- Time: 45 = ½ × 10 × t² → t = **3 s**
- Horizontal distance = 10 × 3 = **30 m**
- Speed on impact = √(10² + 30²) ≈ 31.6 m/s

steps.title: Handy relations
steps.body:
- At the top, speed = u cos θ (only horizontal) and acceleration = g downward.
- tan θ = 4H/R.
- When R is maximum (θ = 45°), H = R/4.
- Air resistance reduces range and height and makes the path non-symmetric.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using u instead of u cos θ for horizontal distance.
- Saying velocity is zero at the top — only the vertical component is zero.
- Applying R = u² sin 2θ / g when launch and landing heights differ.
- Using degrees vs radians inconsistently on the calculator.

activity.prompt: A projectile is launched at 40 m/s at 45° (g = 10 m/s²). What is its horizontal range?

quiz.q: Maximum range on level ground occurs at
quiz.why: Range R = u² sin 2θ/g is largest when sin 2θ = 1, i.e. 2θ = 90°, so θ = 45°.

quiz.q: Angles giving equal range for the same speed:
quiz.why: Since R ∝ sin 2θ, angles θ and 90° − θ give the same range. 30° and 60° are complementary angles.

quiz.q: At the highest point the acceleration of a projectile is
quiz.why: The only acceleration of a projectile (without air resistance) is gravity, g downward, at every point including the top.

quiz.q: u = 10 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10. Maximum height is
For θ = 45°, H/R equals
quiz.why: H = u² sin²θ/2g and R = u² sin 2θ/g, so H/R = tan θ/4. At θ = 45°, tan θ = 1, giving H/R = 1/4.

scenes.text: Dev whirls a stone tied to a string in a horizontal circle at steady speed.
If the string snaps, the stone flies off along the tangent — proof that it was being pulled toward the centre all along.

steps.title: Centripetal acceleration
steps.body:
In uniform circular motion speed is constant but direction changes, so there is acceleration directed toward the centre:
- **a_c = v²/R = ω²R**
- v = ωR; ω = 2π/T = 2πν (T = period, ν = frequency)

**Derivation idea:** velocity vectors at two nearby points have the same magnitude v and differ in angle Δθ. |Δv| ≈ vΔθ and Δθ = vΔt/R, so |Δv|/Δt = v²/R, pointing toward the centre.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A stone on a 12 cm string makes 7 revolutions in 25 s.
- ν = 7/25 = 0.28 Hz; ω = 2π × 0.28 = **1.76 rad/s**
- v = ωR = 1.76 × 0.12 = **0.21 m/s**
- a = ω²R = 3.10 × 0.12 ≈ **0.37 m/s²** toward the centre

**Example 2:** A car moves on a circular track of radius 50 m at 10 m/s.
- a_c = 100/50 = **2 m/s²**

steps.title: Where you see it
steps.body: A satellite in circular orbit, a ceiling fan blade tip, a merry-go-round, electrons in simple atomic models, and clothes in a washing-machine drum all show circular motion. The force providing centripetal acceleration differs: gravity, tension, friction, normal force.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying uniform circular motion has zero acceleration because speed is constant.
- Calling centripetal force a new kind of force — it is the net inward force supplied by tension, friction, gravity etc.
- Forgetting to convert rpm to rad/s (ω = 2π × rpm/60).

cards.back: a = v²/R = ω²R, directed toward the centre
Yes — direction of velocity changes continuously

quiz.q: In uniform circular motion, which is constant?
quiz.why: In uniform circular motion the speed (magnitude of velocity) stays constant, but the direction of velocity, and hence the velocity and acceleration vectors, keep changing.

quiz.q: If speed doubles on the same circle, centripetal acceleration becomes
quiz.why: Centripetal acceleration a = v²/R, so doubling v on the same circle makes a four times larger.

quiz.q: A body on a 2 m circle with ω = 3 rad/s has a_c =
quiz.why: a_c = ω²R = 3² × 2 = 18 m/s².

quiz.q: Direction of centripetal acceleration is
quiz.why: The centripetal acceleration always points toward the centre of the circle, along the radius.

quiz.q: The angle between velocity and centripetal acceleration in UCM is
quiz.why: In uniform circular motion velocity is along the tangent and centripetal acceleration along the radius, and these are perpendicular, at 90°.

questions.q: Which quantity is a scalar?
questions.why: Speed has only magnitude, so it is a scalar. Displacement, force and velocity have direction as well, making them vectors.

questions.q: The trajectory of a projectile (no air resistance) is a
questions.why: Without air resistance, x = u cos θ · t and y = u sin θ · t − ½gt², so y is a quadratic function of x. This is a parabola.

questions.q: Magnitude of î + ĵ + k̂ is
questions.why: The magnitude is √(1² + 1² + 1²) = √3.

questions.q: Two vectors of 6 and 8 units are perpendicular. Resultant is
questions.why: Perpendicular vectors combine by Pythagoras: √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10.

questions.q: Horizontal component of velocity in projectile motion
questions.why: There is no horizontal acceleration (aₓ = 0), so the horizontal component of velocity stays constant throughout the motion.

questions.q: A wheel turning at 120 rpm has angular speed
questions.why: 120 rpm is 2 revolutions per second, and each revolution is 2π rad, so ω = 2 × 2π = 4π rad/s.

questions.q: Assertion: Uniform circular motion is accelerated motion. Reason: Direction of velocity changes continuously.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. In uniform circular motion the direction of velocity keeps changing, so the velocity changes and the motion has acceleration (centripetal), even though the speed is constant.

questions.q: A projectile has range 100 m at 15°. Range at 45° with the same speed is
questions.why: R ∝ sin 2θ. At 15°, sin 30° = 0.5; at 45°, sin 90° = 1. So the range doubles to 200 m.

questions.q: Case: A ball rolls off a 1.25 m high table at 2 m/s (g = 10). How far from the table edge does it land?
questions.why: The time to fall 1.25 m is t = √(2h/g) = √(2.5/10) = 0.5 s. In that time the ball moves horizontally 2 × 0.5 = 1 m.

questions.q: Angle between A = î + ĵ and B = î − ĵ is
questions.why: The dot product A·B = (1)(1) + (1)(−1) = 0, so the vectors are perpendicular, and the angle is 90°.

questions.q: A particle on a 0.5 m circle completes 2 revolutions per second. Its centripetal acceleration is about
questions.why: 2 revolutions per second means ω = 2 × 2π = 4π rad/s. Centripetal acceleration = ω²R = 16π² × 0.5 = 8π² ≈ 79 m/s².

questions.q: For a projectile, R = 4H. The launch angle is
questions.why: For a projectile tan θ = 4H/R. If R = 4H, then 4H/R = 1, so tan θ = 1 and θ = 45°.

questions.q: A boat with speed 5 km/h in still water crosses a 1 km river flowing at 3 km/h along the shortest path. Time taken:
questions.why: To go straight across (shortest path) the boat points upstream so that its component against the current cancels 3 km/h. Its speed across is √(5² − 3²) = 4 km/h, so t = 1/4 h = 15 min.

questions.q: y = x − x²/40 (SI, g = 10) is a projectile's trajectory. Launch speed is
questions.why: Compare with y = x tan θ − gx²/(2u² cos²θ): tan θ = 1 so θ = 45°, cos²θ = 1/2. Then g/(2u² · ½) = 10/u² = 1/40, so u² = 400 and u = 20 m/s.

questions.q: Speed of a projectile at the top is half its launch speed. Launch angle:
questions.why: At the top only the horizontal component u cos θ remains. If that equals u/2, then cos θ = 1/2 and θ = 60°.

questions.q: Which statement about vector addition is false?
questions.why: The triangle inequality says |A + B| ≤ |A| + |B|, so the magnitude of the sum can never exceed the sum of magnitudes. Vector addition is commutative and associative.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Laws of Motion
courses.summary: Inertia and Newton's three laws, momentum and impulse, conservation of momentum, equilibrium, friction, circular motion on level and banked roads, and solving problems with free-body diagrams.
outcomes: Learners can state and apply Newton's laws with correct free-body diagrams
Learners can use impulse and momentum conservation in collisions and recoil
Learners can solve friction problems on horizontal and inclined surfaces
Learners can analyse circular motion on level and banked roads
Learners can solve connected-body and lift problems

lessons.title: Inertia, first and second laws, impulse

scenes.text: The bus brakes suddenly and standing passengers lurch forward.
Their bodies tend to keep moving — inertia. The bus floor stops their feet; their upper bodies carry on.

steps.title: First and second laws
steps.body:
**Galileo's idea:** a body moving on a frictionless surface keeps moving — rest and uniform motion are equally natural.

**First law:** every body continues in its state of rest or uniform straight-line motion unless an external net force acts. Inertia = resistance to change of motion; mass measures it.

**Momentum** p = mv. **Second law:** F = dp/dt; for constant mass **F = ma**. SI unit of force: newton (1 N = 1 kg m s⁻²). The law is a vector law and applies to each component: Fₓ = maₓ etc.

steps.title: Impulse
steps.body:
**Impulse** J = FΔt = Δp (for a large force acting briefly, use the change in momentum).

Why a cricketer draws hands back while catching: the same Δp spread over a longer Δt means a smaller force on the hands. Same idea: airbags, sand pits for long jump, packaging foam.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A 0.15 kg ball at 12 m/s is hit straight back at 12 m/s.
- Δp = 0.15 × (12 − (−12)) = **3.6 N s** (impulse, toward the bowler)

**Example 2:** A 2 kg body is acted on by a 6 N force for 4 s from rest.
- a = 6/2 = 3 m/s²; v = 12 m/s; Δp = 24 kg m/s = F × t ✓

**Example 3:** A 0.5 kg ball falling at 10 m/s stops in 0.05 s on sand. Average force = 0.5 × 10/0.05 = **100 N** (plus its weight while stopping).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing motion needs a force — force causes CHANGE of motion.
- Ignoring direction when computing Δp in rebounds (use signs).
- Using F = ma when mass changes (rockets, conveyor belts) — use F = dp/dt.
- Confusing mass (inertia) with weight (force).

statements.s: A body moving at constant velocity needs no net force.
Impulse has the same unit as momentum.
A heavier body has less inertia.
statements.why: Mass measures inertia; heavier = more inertia.

statements.s: Pulling the hands back while catching reduces the impulse.
statements.why: Impulse (Δp) is the same; force reduces because time increases.

statements.s: F = ma is valid in every component direction separately.

quiz.q: Unit of impulse is
quiz.why: Impulse = force × time, so its unit is newton-second (N s), the same as kg m/s. Joule is the unit of energy.

quiz.q: A 5 kg body accelerates at 2 m/s². Net force is
quiz.why: By Newton's second law, F = ma = 5 kg × 2 m/s² = 10 N.

quiz.q: A 1 kg ball hits a wall at 5 m/s and rebounds at 5 m/s. Impulse magnitude:
quiz.why: Impulse equals the change in momentum. The momentum goes from +5 to −5 kg m/s, so the change is 1 × (5 + 5) = 10 N s. The direction reversal means the speeds add.

quiz.q: Seat belts protect passengers mainly by
quiz.why: A seat belt stretches and increases the time over which the body stops. Since F = Δp/Δt, the same change in momentum over a longer time means a smaller force.

quiz.q: A force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg mass for 3 s from rest. Final speed:
quiz.why: Acceleration a = F/m = 10/2 = 5 m/s². Starting from rest, v = at = 5 × 3 = 15 m/s.

lessons.title: Third law, momentum conservation and equilibrium

scenes.text: A rocket shoots up as hot gases rush down.
At an NCC range, a cadet feels the rifle kick back. Both are action and reaction — momentum is conserved.

steps.title: Third law and conservation of momentum
steps.body:
**Third law:** to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Forces always occur in pairs, act on DIFFERENT bodies, and act simultaneously — so they never cancel each other.

**Conservation of linear momentum:** if net external force on a system is zero, total momentum stays constant. It follows from the second and third laws: internal forces F₁₂ = −F₂₁ change p₁ and p₂ by equal and opposite amounts.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A 4 kg rifle fires a 50 g bullet at 350 m/s.
- Initial p = 0 → 0.05 × 350 + 4V = 0
- V = −17.5/4 = **−4.375 m/s** (recoil)

**Example 2:** A 60 kg skater at rest throws a 3 kg ball forward at 10 m/s. Skater's speed: 30/60 = **0.5 m/s** backward.

**Example 3 (equilibrium):** A 6 kg mass hangs from a rope; it is pulled sideways by a horizontal force so the rope makes 30° with the vertical. Horizontal force F = mg tan 30° = 58.8 × 0.577 ≈ **34 N**; tension T = mg/cos 30° ≈ **68 N** (g = 9.8).

steps.title: Equilibrium of a particle
steps.body: A particle is in equilibrium when the net force is zero: ΣFₓ = 0, ΣF_y = 0, ΣF_z = 0. Three concurrent forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle when drawn head to tail.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cancelling an action–reaction pair (they act on different bodies).
- Calling weight and normal force an action–reaction pair — they act on the same body; the reaction to weight is the body's pull on the Earth.
- Forgetting that momentum is a vector — use signs.

activity.prompt: A 2 kg gun fires a 10 g bullet at 400 m/s. What is the recoil speed of the gun?

quiz.q: Action and reaction forces
quiz.why: Action and reaction forces act on two different bodies, which is why they do not cancel one another. They are equal in size and opposite in direction.

quiz.q: Momentum of an isolated system
quiz.why: With no external force on the system, its total momentum stays constant (conservation of momentum).

quiz.q: A bomb at rest explodes into two equal pieces. If one moves east at 10 m/s, the other moves
quiz.why: The bomb starts with zero momentum, and so the total must remain zero. For two equal pieces, the other piece must move west at the same speed, 10 m/s.

quiz.q: The reaction to the weight of a book on a table is
quiz.why: The weight is the Earth's pull on the book. By Newton's third law the reaction is the book's equal and opposite pull on the Earth, upward. The normal force acts on the book, so it is not its reaction.

quiz.q: For equilibrium of a particle,
quiz.why: A particle is in equilibrium when the net force on it is zero. It may still move at constant velocity, so equilibrium does not require zero velocity.

scenes.text: Rohan pushes a steel almirah. Nothing moves until he pushes harder — then it suddenly slides and gets easier to keep moving.
His father slips small rollers underneath and it rolls easily. Static, kinetic and rolling friction in one evening.

steps.title: Laws of friction
steps.body:
- **Static friction** fₛ adjusts to oppose impending motion, up to a maximum fₛ(max) = µₛN.
- **Kinetic friction** f_k = µ_k N, opposing relative motion; usually µ_k < µₛ.
- Friction is nearly independent of apparent contact area and (for kinetic) of speed.
- **Rolling friction** is much smaller — hence wheels, ball bearings.
- **Angle of repose / limiting angle** θ: block on an incline is about to slip when tan θ = µₛ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A box starts slipping on a plank when the plank is tilted to 15°.
- µₛ = tan 15° ≈ **0.27**

**Example 2:** A 10 kg block on a floor (µ_k = 0.2, g = 9.8) is pulled by a horizontal 50 N force.
- f_k = 0.2 × 10 × 9.8 = 19.6 N
- a = (50 − 19.6)/10 = **3.04 m/s²**

**Example 3:** A block slides down a 30° incline with µ_k = 0.2 (g = 9.8).
- a = g(sin θ − µ_k cos θ) = 9.8(0.5 − 0.173) ≈ **3.2 m/s²**

steps.title: Pushing vs pulling
steps.body: Pulling a lawn roller at an angle above horizontal reduces the normal force (N = mg − F sin θ), so friction is smaller. Pushing at an angle downward increases N and friction. That is why pulling is easier.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing static friction as always µₛN — it equals the applied force until the limit is reached.
- Taking N = mg on an incline (it is mg cos θ) or when an angled force acts.
- Assuming friction always opposes motion of the body — it opposes RELATIVE motion (friction pushes a walking person forward).

activity.prompt: A 5 kg block rests on a floor with µₛ = 0.4 (g = 10 m/s²). A horizontal force of 15 N is applied. What is the friction force (in N) acting on it?

quiz.q: Coefficient of friction is
quiz.why: The coefficient of friction is the ratio of two forces (friction/normal force), so the units cancel and it has no dimensions.

quiz.q: Angle of repose is 30°. µₛ =
quiz.why: At the angle of repose, tan θ = μₛ. So μₛ = tan 30° = 1/√3 ≈ 0.577.

quiz.q: Generally
quiz.why: Generally static friction is larger than kinetic friction, which is why it takes more force to start an object moving than to keep it moving. Friction does not depend on the contact area.

quiz.q: When we walk, friction on our feet acts
quiz.why: When we walk, the foot pushes back on the ground and the ground's static friction pushes the foot forward. This forward friction is what lets us move ahead.

quiz.q: A 2 kg block on a µ_k = 0.5 surface moving at 10 m/s (g = 10) stops after
quiz.why: Friction gives deceleration a = μg = 0.5 × 10 = 5 m/s². Using v² = u² − 2as: 0 = 100 − 10s, so s = 10 m. The mass cancels out.

lessons.title: Circular motion: level and banked roads

scenes.text: On a hill road, Priya's bus slows before each sharp curve. The road surface tilts inward.
Engineers bank the road so the normal force helps provide centripetal force — less reliance on friction.

steps.title: Level road
steps.body: On a flat curve, static friction alone provides centripetal force: mv²/R ≤ µₛmg → **v_max = √(µₛ R g)**, independent of mass.

steps.title: Banked road (angle θ)
steps.body:
Forces: weight mg, normal N, friction f along the incline.
- With no friction, ideal speed: N cos θ = mg and N sin θ = mv²/R → **v₀ = √(R g tan θ)** — at this speed no friction is needed, so tyre wear is least.
- With friction (acting down the slope at maximum speed):
**v_max = √[R g (µₛ + tan θ)/(1 − µₛ tan θ)]**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating centripetal force as an extra force in the free-body diagram.
- Putting friction up the slope at maximum speed (it acts down the slope then; up the slope at minimum speed).
- Thinking heavier vehicles can take curves faster — v_max is independent of mass.

a.text: You design a curve of radius 100 m for vehicles at 20 m/s on a wet road (low friction). What do you do?

choices.label: Bank the road at about tan θ = v²/(Rg) ≈ 0.41 (≈ 22°)
choices.feedback: Right: the normal force then supplies the centripetal force even with almost no friction.

choices.label: Keep it flat and rely on friction
choices.feedback: Wet roads may have µₛ well below 0.41, so cars would skid.

good.text: Correct design: v₀ = √(Rg tan θ) matches the design speed. Add signs for a speed limit.

bad.text: Needed µₛ = v²/(Rg) ≈ 0.41 — risky in rain. Banking is the safer choice.

quiz.q: Maximum safe speed on a level curve depends on
quiz.why: On a level curve friction supplies the centripetal force, so μₛmg = mv²/R and v_max = √(μₛRg). Mass cancels, so the car's mass does not matter.

quiz.q: Ideal banking speed is given by
quiz.why: On a banked road with no friction, N sin θ = mv²/R and N cos θ = mg. Dividing gives tan θ = v²/(Rg), so v = √(Rg tan θ).

quiz.q: At speeds above v₀ on a banked road, friction acts
quiz.why: Above the ideal speed v₀, the car tends to slide up and outward, so friction acts down the slope to help supply the extra centripetal force needed.

quiz.q: R = 40 m, µₛ = 0.4, g = 10. v_max on a level road is about
Banking a road reduces
quiz.why: On a banked road the horizontal part of the normal force supplies some or all of the centripetal force, so less friction is needed.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: circular motion dynamics)

lessons.title: Solving problems: free-body diagrams, lifts and pulleys

scenes.text: Aditya stands on a bathroom scale in a lift. As the lift starts up, the reading jumps above his weight.
When it starts down, the reading drops. The scale reads the normal force, not his weight.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Isolate each body and draw a **free-body diagram** (only forces ON that body).
2. Choose axes (along and perpendicular to acceleration).
3. Write ΣF = ma for each body and each axis.
4. Add constraint relations (same string → same tension for a light string over a smooth pulley; connected bodies → same |a|).
5. Solve and check units and limiting cases.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (lift):** A 50 kg person in a lift (g = 9.8).
- Accelerating up at 2 m/s²: N = m(g + a) = 50 × 11.8 = **590 N**
- Accelerating down at 2 m/s²: N = 50 × 7.8 = **390 N**
- Free fall: N = 0 (weightlessness)

**Example 2 (Atwood machine):** 5 kg and 3 kg hang over a smooth pulley.
- a = (5 − 3)g/(5 + 3) = 2 × 9.8/8 = **2.45 m/s²**
- T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 2 × 15 × 9.8/8 = **36.75 N**

**Example 3 (blocks in contact):** 2 kg and 3 kg on a smooth floor pushed by 10 N on the 2 kg block. a = 2 m/s²; contact force on 3 kg = 3 × 2 = **6 N**.

steps.title: Checks that save marks
steps.body:
- If m₁ = m₂ in an Atwood machine, a = 0 — your formula should show that.
- Tension in an Atwood machine lies between m₂g and m₁g.
- Apparent weight = m(g ± a); in free fall, apparent weight is zero.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including forces the body exerts on others in its own FBD.
- Assuming tension equals weight when the system accelerates.
- Forgetting that a lift moving up while slowing down has downward acceleration.

activity.prompt: Put the problem-solving steps in order
items: Write ΣF = ma along each axis

quiz.q: A 60 kg man in a lift moving up at constant speed. Scale reads (g = 10)
quiz.why: At constant speed, acceleration is zero, so the scale's normal force equals the weight: N = mg = 60 × 10 = 600 N.

quiz.q: In free fall, apparent weight is
quiz.why: In free fall the body and the scale accelerate together at g, so N = m(g − g) = 0. The apparent weight is zero.

quiz.q: Atwood machine with 4 kg and 6 kg (g = 10): acceleration
quiz.why: For an Atwood machine a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂) = (6 − 4) × 10/10 = 2 m/s².

quiz.q: A free-body diagram shows
options: all forces acting on the chosen body
forces by the body on others
quiz.why: A free-body diagram isolates one body and shows all the forces that act on it. Forces the body exerts on others are not drawn.

quiz.q: A lift moving up but slowing down has acceleration
quiz.why: The lift moves up but its speed is decreasing, so the velocity change is downward. Acceleration is therefore directed downward.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: solving problems in mechanics)

questions.q: Newton's first law defines
questions.why: Newton's first law says a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a net force acts, which defines inertia.

questions.q: SI unit of force
questions.why: The newton (N) is the SI unit of force, 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻². The dyne is the CGS unit.

questions.q: A 3 kg body moving at 4 m/s has momentum
questions.why: Momentum p = mv = 3 kg × 4 m/s = 12 kg m/s.

questions.q: Action–reaction forces never cancel because they
questions.why: Action and reaction act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel. Cancelling needs forces acting on the same body.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s is stopped in 5 s. Average braking force:
questions.why: The change in momentum is 1000 × 20 = 20000 kg m/s. The average force is Δp/Δt = 20000/5 = 4000 N.

questions.q: Assertion: It is easier to pull a roller than to push it. Reason: Pulling at an angle reduces the normal force.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. A pull at an angle has an upward component that lowers the normal force on the roller, so friction is less, which makes pulling easier than pushing (the push adds a downward component).

questions.q: A man of 70 kg stands in a lift accelerating down at 3 m/s² (g = 10). Normal force:
questions.why: In a lift accelerating down, N = m(g − a) = 70 × (10 − 3) = 490 N, which is less than his weight of 700 N.

questions.q: A block slips on an incline when tilted to 37° (tan 37° = 0.75). µₛ is
questions.why: A block just begins to slip when tan θ = μₛ. With tan 37° = 0.75, μₛ = 0.75.

questions.q: Case: A 20 g bullet at 300 m/s embeds in a 980 g wooden block at rest on ice. Common velocity afterwards:
questions.why: Momentum is conserved: 0.02 × 300 = 6 kg m/s = (0.02 + 0.98) × v = 1 × v, so v = 6 m/s.

questions.q: Two blocks 4 kg and 6 kg tied by a string on a smooth floor are pulled by 20 N on the 6 kg block. Tension in the string:
questions.why: The system accelerates at a = 20/(4 + 6) = 2 m/s². The tension alone pulls the 4 kg block, so T = 4 × 2 = 8 N.

questions.q: A car takes a level curve of radius 50 m. With µₛ = 0.5 and g = 10, maximum speed is about
A body of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m/s is acted on by a force of 4 N opposite to motion. Distance before it stops:
questions.why: The deceleration is a = F/m = 4/2 = 2 m/s². Using v² = 2as: 9 = 2 × 2 × s, so s = 9/4 = 2.25 m.

questions.q: Ideal banking angle for v = 20 m/s on R = 40 m (g = 10):
questions.why: For ideal banking tan θ = v²/(Rg) = 400/(40 × 10) = 1, so the angle is tan⁻¹(1) = 45°.

questions.q: A 5 kg block on a 30° smooth incline is held by a string parallel to the incline. Tension (g = 10):
questions.why: On a smooth incline the string must balance the component of weight along the slope: T = mg sin 30° = 5 × 10 × 0.5 = 25 N.

questions.q: A ball of 0.2 kg hits a wall at 10 m/s at 60° to the normal and rebounds with the same speed and angle. Impulse magnitude:
questions.why: Only the component normal to the wall reverses; the component along the wall is unchanged. So the impulse is 2mv cos 60° = 2 × 0.2 × 10 × 0.5 = 2 N s.

questions.q: Atwood machine: masses m and 3m. Tension in the string is
questions.why: In an Atwood machine, T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 2 × m × 3m × g/(4m) = 1.5 mg.

school-c11-physics-b.title: Class 11 Physics · Part B (Ch 5–8)
school-c11-physics-b.description: Class 11 Physics chapter by chapter: Work, Energy and Power; System of Particles and Rotational Motion; Gravitation; Mechanical Properties of Solids — with derivations and solved numericals.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Work, Energy and Power
courses.summary: Scalar product, work by constant and variable forces, the work–energy theorem, potential energy and springs, conservation of mechanical energy, power, and collisions in one dimension.
outcomes: Learners can compute work using the scalar product and area under F–x graphs
Learners can apply the work–energy theorem
Learners can use conservation of mechanical energy including springs
Learners can compute power and solve elastic and inelastic collision problems

scenes.text: At the railway station, Anu pulls her wheeled suitcase with the handle tilted at 60°.
Only the part of her pull along the platform does work. The upward part just lightens the load on the wheels.

steps.title: Scalar (dot) product
steps.body:
A · B = AB cos θ = AₓBₓ + A_yB_y + A_zB_z.
- Commutative; distributive.
- î·î = 1, î·ĵ = 0.
- A · B = 0 when vectors are perpendicular.
- cos θ = A·B / (AB) gives the angle between vectors.

steps.title: Work
steps.body:
Work by a constant force: **W = F · d = Fd cos θ** (unit joule, 1 J = 1 N m; scalar).
- θ < 90°: positive work (force helps motion)
- θ = 90°: zero work (normal force on a horizontal floor, tension in uniform circular motion)
- θ > 90°: negative work (friction, braking)

**Variable force:** W = ∫F dx = area under the F–x graph.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** F = 10 N at 60° to the floor moves a box 5 m.
- W = 10 × 5 × cos 60° = **25 J**

**Example 2:** F = (3î + 4ĵ) N, d = (2î − ĵ) m.
- W = 6 − 4 = **2 J**

**Example 3:** A force rises linearly from 0 to 20 N over 4 m, then stays at 20 N for 2 m.
- Area = ½ × 4 × 20 + 2 × 20 = 40 + 40 = **80 J**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a person holding a heavy bag still does work on it — displacement is zero, so W = 0 (muscles use chemical energy though).
- Forgetting the sign: friction does negative work.
- Using sin θ instead of cos θ (θ is between F and d).

activity.prompt: Is the work done by the named force positive, negative or zero?

items.text: Normal force on a car on a level road
Tension in a string for a stone in uniform circular motion
Gravity on a ball thrown upward (while rising)
Engine force on an accelerating car

quiz.q: Work done by a 5 N force moving a body 4 m along the force:
quiz.why: Work = force × displacement along the force = 5 N × 4 m = 20 J.
The dot product multiplies matching components and adds: (2)(4) + (3)(−2) = 8 − 6 = 2.

quiz.q: Work done by centripetal force in uniform circular motion is
quiz.why: The centripetal force is always perpendicular to the displacement in circular motion, so W = Fd cos 90° = 0.

quiz.q: Area under a force–displacement graph gives
quiz.why: The area under a force–displacement graph is ∫F dx, which is the work done by the force.

quiz.q: If A·B = 0 (both non-zero), the angle between them is
quiz.why: A·B = AB cos θ = 0 with A and B non-zero requires cos θ = 0, so θ = 90°.

lessons.title: Kinetic energy, work–energy theorem, potential energy

scenes.text: In a safety test, a bullet passes through a wooden plank and comes out slower.
The kinetic energy it lost equals the work done by the plank's resisting force — the work–energy theorem in action.

steps.title: Work–energy theorem
steps.body:
Kinetic energy K = ½mv² = p²/2m.

**Theorem:** the work done by the NET force on a body equals its change in kinetic energy: W_net = K_f − K_i.

**Derivation (constant force):** v² − u² = 2as → multiply by m/2: ½mv² − ½mu² = mas = Fs = W.

steps.title: Potential energy and conservative forces
steps.body:
A force is **conservative** if the work it does depends only on the initial and final positions (zero over a closed path): gravity, spring force, electrostatic force. Friction is non-conservative.

For a conservative force F(x) = −dV/dx.
- Gravitational PE near Earth: V = mgh.
- **Spring:** Hooke's law F = −kx; PE stored V = ½kx² (k = spring constant, N/m). Work by the spring from x₁ to x₂ = −½k(x₂² − x₁²).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A 50 g bullet at 200 m/s passes through a 2 cm plank and exits at 100 m/s.
- ΔK = ½ × 0.05 × (100² − 200²) = −750 J
- Average resistive force = 750/0.02 = **3.75 × 10⁴ N**

**Example 2:** A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s brakes to rest. Work by brakes = 0 − ½ × 1000 × 400 = **−2 × 10⁵ J**.

**Example 3:** A spring (k = 200 N/m) is compressed 10 cm. Stored energy = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = **1 J**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using only the applied force in the theorem — it is the NET work (all forces).
- Writing spring PE as kx (that is the force).
- Forgetting that K can never be negative, while PE depends on the chosen zero level.

activity.prompt: A 2 kg block moving at 3 m/s compresses a spring of k = 200 N/m on a smooth floor. Maximum compression (in m)?

quiz.q: If momentum doubles, kinetic energy becomes
quiz.why: Kinetic energy K = p²/2m. If p doubles for the same mass, K becomes 2² = 4 times.

quiz.q: Which force is non-conservative?
quiz.why: Kinetic friction is non-conservative: the work it does depends on the path taken, and energy is lost as heat. Gravity, spring and electrostatic forces are conservative.

quiz.q: Spring constant 100 N/m stretched by 0.2 m stores
quiz.why: The energy stored in a spring is ½kx² = ½ × 100 × (0.2)² = 50 × 0.04 = 2 J.

quiz.q: Net work on a body moving at constant velocity is
quiz.why: At constant velocity the kinetic energy does not change, so by the work–energy theorem the net work is zero.

quiz.q: A 4 kg body speeds up from 2 m/s to 4 m/s. Net work done:
quiz.why: By the work–energy theorem, W = ½m(v² − u²) = ½ × 4 × (16 − 4) = 2 × 12 = 24 J.

lessons.title: Conservation of mechanical energy and power

scenes.text: A hill-temple lift carries pilgrims up steadily. The motor must beat gravity and friction every second.
Engineers rate the motor by power — work done per second — in watts and horsepower.

steps.title: Conservation of mechanical energy
steps.body:
If only conservative forces do work, **K + V = constant**.

**Freely falling body:** at height H, E = mgH; at height h, E = mgh + ½mv² with v² = 2g(H − h) → E = mgH. Energy changes form but the total stays the same.

With friction, mechanical energy decreases; the 'lost' energy appears as heat and sound (total energy is still conserved).

steps.title: Power
steps.body:
- Average power P = W/t; instantaneous power **P = dW/dt = F · v**.
- SI unit watt (1 W = 1 J/s); 1 horsepower (hp) = 746 W.
- Electrical energy unit: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A ball is dropped from 20 m (g = 10). Speed just before hitting the ground:
- mgh = ½mv² → v = √(2 × 10 × 20) = **20 m/s**

**Example 2:** A lift of total mass 1800 kg moves up at a steady 2 m/s against friction of 4000 N (g = 10).
- Force needed = 18000 + 4000 = 22000 N
- P = Fv = 22000 × 2 = **44 kW ≈ 59 hp**

**Example 3:** A pendulum bob released from 0.2 m above its lowest point: speed at bottom = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.2) ≈ **1.98 m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying energy conservation when friction or air drag is significant.
- Confusing kWh (energy) with kW (power).
- Using P = Fv when F and v are not parallel (use F · v).

activity.prompt: A 60 kg student climbs 5 m of stairs in 10 s (g = 10 m/s²). What is her average power?

quiz.q: 1 kWh equals
For a freely falling body, the sum of KE and PE
quiz.why: In free fall only gravity, a conservative force, does work. So kinetic energy gained equals potential energy lost and the total stays constant.

quiz.q: A force of 50 N moves a body at 4 m/s along the force. Power:
quiz.why: Power = force × velocity (along the force) = 50 × 4 = 200 W.

quiz.q: 1 hp is about
quiz.why: One horsepower is about 746 W.

quiz.q: A 2 kg stone dropped from 5 m (g = 10) has KE just before impact of
quiz.why: By energy conservation, KE just before impact = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: energy conservation, power)

scenes.text: Sara's striker hits a coin head-on. The striker nearly stops and the coin shoots off.
For equal masses in an elastic head-on collision, velocities simply exchange.

steps.title: Types of collision
steps.body:
In all collisions (no external impulse) **momentum is conserved**.
- **Elastic:** kinetic energy also conserved.
- **Inelastic:** some KE lost (heat, sound, deformation).
- **Perfectly inelastic:** bodies stick together; maximum KE loss.

Coefficient of restitution e = (relative speed of separation)/(relative speed of approach): e = 1 elastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic.

steps.title: 1D elastic collision results
steps.body:
Mass m₁ with speed u₁ hits m₂ at rest:
- v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u₁/(m₁ + m₂)
- v₂ = 2m₁u₁/(m₁ + m₂)

Special cases: m₁ = m₂ → velocities exchange; m₁ ≪ m₂ → m₁ bounces back with nearly −u₁; m₁ ≫ m₂ → m₂ moves off at about 2u₁.

Perfectly inelastic: v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (perfectly inelastic):** 2 kg at 3 m/s sticks to 1 kg at rest.
- v = 6/3 = **2 m/s**; KE before 9 J, after ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 J → loss **3 J**

**Example 2 (elastic):** 2 kg at 4 m/s hits 1 kg at rest.
- v₁ = (1/3) × 4 = **1.33 m/s**; v₂ = (4/3) × 4 = **5.33 m/s**
- Check KE: 16 J before; ½·2·1.78 + ½·1·28.4 ≈ 1.78 + 14.2 = 16 J ✓

**Example 3:** Neutron hitting a stationary deuteron (mass 2m) elastically keeps (1/3)² = 1/9 of its KE — this is why light nuclei moderate neutrons in reactors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming KE is conserved in every collision.
- Forgetting signs for velocities in opposite directions.
- Using elastic formulas when one body is not initially at rest without generalising them.

activity.prompt: Match the collision to its property
pairs: Equal masses, elastic, one at rest

quiz.q: In every collision of an isolated system, what is conserved?
quiz.why: For an isolated system with no external forces, the total momentum is conserved in every collision. Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.

quiz.q: For an elastic collision, e =
quiz.why: For an elastic collision, the coefficient of restitution e = 1, because the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach.

quiz.q: 3 kg at 4 m/s sticks to 1 kg at rest. Final speed:
quiz.why: Momentum conservation: 3 × 4 = (3 + 1)v, so v = 12/4 = 3 m/s.

quiz.q: A ping-pong ball elastically hits a heavy wall at 5 m/s. It rebounds at
quiz.why: The heavy wall barely moves, so in an elastic collision the light ball rebounds with nearly the same speed (5 m/s) in the opposite direction.

quiz.q: KE loss is maximum in a
quiz.why: The loss of kinetic energy is greatest in a perfectly inelastic collision, where the bodies stick together and lose the relative motion between them.

questions.q: SI unit of work
questions.why: The joule (J) is the SI unit of work; 1 J = 1 N m.

questions.q: Work done by gravity on a satellite in circular orbit over one revolution is
questions.why: Gravity is perpendicular to the velocity of a satellite in circular orbit, so no work is done. After a full revolution it is zero.

questions.q: KE of a 2 kg body at 5 m/s
questions.why: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 25 = 25 J.

questions.q: A force F = 6 N moves a body 3 m at 60° to the force. Work:
questions.why: Work = Fd cos θ = 6 × 3 × cos 60° = 18 × 0.5 = 9 J.

questions.q: Assertion: Friction is a non-conservative force. Reason: Work done by friction over a closed path is not zero.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. A force is non-conservative when its work around a closed path is not zero, which is the case for friction, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: A 1.5 kW motor runs for 2 hours. Energy consumed:
questions.why: Energy = power × time = 1.5 kW × 2 h = 3 kWh.

questions.q: A spring stretched by x stores energy E. Stretched by 2x it stores
questions.why: Spring energy is ½kx², so it is proportional to x². Doubling the stretch makes the energy 2² = 4 times, i.e. 4E.

questions.q: Case: A 0.5 kg ball dropped from 10 m rebounds to 5 m (g = 10). Energy lost in the bounce:
questions.why: The ball loses potential energy of mg × (10 − 5) = 0.5 × 10 × 5 = 25 J in the bounce.

questions.q: A pump lifts 600 kg of water to 10 m in 1 minute (g = 10). Power:
A body of mass m moving at v collides elastically head-on with an identical body at rest. After collision
options: first stops, second moves at v
questions.why: Equal masses in a head-on elastic collision exchange velocities, so the first body stops and the second moves off at v.

questions.q: A 10 g bullet at 500 m/s stops in 5 cm of wood. Average resistive force:
questions.why: KE = ½ × 0.01 × 500² = 1250 J. This is work done against the resistive force over 0.05 m, so F = 1250/0.05 = 2.5 × 10⁴ N.

questions.q: A force F = 2x N acts on a body as it moves from x = 1 m to x = 3 m. Work done:
questions.why: Work = ∫F dx = ∫2x dx = x² from 1 to 3 = 9 − 1 = 8 J.

questions.q: 4 kg at 6 m/s collides perfectly inelastically with 2 kg moving at 3 m/s in the opposite direction. Common velocity:
questions.why: Take the 4 kg body's direction as positive: momentum = 4 × 6 − 2 × 3 = 24 − 6 = 18. The common velocity = 18/(4 + 2) = 3 m/s.

questions.q: Potential energy V(x) = 3x² − 6x. The force is zero at
questions.why: F = −dV/dx = −(6x − 6). Setting F = 0 gives x = 1.

questions.q: A car's engine delivers constant power P. Starting from rest, its speed after time t is proportional to
questions.why: At constant power P, the work done in time t is Pt, which equals the KE ½mv². So v ∝ √t.

questions.q: A ball of mass m hits a stationary ball of mass 2m elastically head-on. Fraction of KE retained by the first ball:
questions.why: For a head-on elastic collision with m hitting 2m, the first ball's final velocity is −u/3. Its KE fraction is (1/3)² = 1/9.

courses.title: Ch 6 · System of Particles and Rotational Motion
courses.summary: Centre of mass, vector product, torque and angular momentum, equilibrium of rigid bodies, moment of inertia, rotational kinematics and dynamics, and conservation of angular momentum.
outcomes: Learners can locate the centre of mass of particle systems and describe its motion
Learners can compute torque and angular momentum using the vector product

lessons.title: Centre of mass and its motion

scenes.text: A rocket bursts mid-air into glowing fragments flying everywhere.
Remarkably, the centre of mass of all the pieces keeps following the same parabola the rocket was on — internal forces cannot change it.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
For particles mᵢ at positions rᵢ: **R_cm = Σmᵢrᵢ / M**, M = Σmᵢ.
- Two particles on the x-axis: X = (m₁x₁ + m₂x₂)/(m₁ + m₂).
- For continuous bodies: R = (1/M)∫r dm.
- For uniform symmetric bodies (rod, ring, disc, sphere), the CM is at the geometric centre. CM may lie outside the material (ring).

steps.title: Motion of the centre of mass
steps.body:
M A_cm = F_ext — the CM moves as if all mass were concentrated there and only external forces act on it. Internal forces cancel in pairs (third law).

Total momentum P = M V_cm. If F_ext = 0, V_cm is constant (e.g. the decay of a nucleus at rest: fragments fly apart but CM stays at rest).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 2 kg at x = 0 and 3 kg at x = 5 m.
- X = (0 + 15)/5 = **3 m**

**Example 2:** 1 kg at (0, 0), 1 kg at (2, 0), 2 kg at (0, 2) m.
- X = (0 + 2 + 0)/4 = **0.5 m**; Y = (0 + 0 + 4)/4 = **1 m**

**Example 3:** A 50 kg man stands at one end of a 100 kg boat 3 m long on still water and walks to the other end. With no external horizontal force, the CM stays fixed: boat shifts by 50 × 3/150 = **1 m** opposite to him.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the CM must lie inside the body.
- Including internal forces when finding the acceleration of the CM.
- Forgetting to use mass weighting (CM is not the simple average of positions unless masses are equal).

activity.prompt: Masses 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg lie on the x-axis at x = 0, 1 m and 2 m. Find the x-coordinate of the centre of mass.

quiz.q: CM of a uniform ring lies
quiz.why: By symmetry the centre of mass of a uniform ring is at its geometric centre, even though no material is there.

quiz.q: Two equal masses at x = 2 m and x = 6 m. CM at
quiz.why: For equal masses the centre of mass is the average of positions: (2 + 6)/2 = 4 m.

quiz.q: Internal forces in a system can change
quiz.why: Internal forces cancel in pairs for the system as a whole, so they cannot change total momentum or the CM motion. But they do change how individual particles move.

quiz.q: A shell explodes mid-flight. Its CM
