questions.q: 3 mol of ideal gas at 400 K expands isothermally from 10 L to 20 L. Work done (ln 2 = 0.693):
questions.why: For an isothermal expansion W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 3 × 8.314 × 400 × 0.693 ≈ 6914 J ≈ 6.9 kJ.

questions.q: A monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) is compressed adiabatically to 1/8 of its volume. Pressure increases by a factor
questions.why: For an adiabatic change P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^γ = 8^(5/3) = (2³)^(5/3) = 2⁵ = 32.

questions.q: For 1 mol monatomic gas heated at constant pressure by 20 K, heat supplied is about (R = 8.31)
questions.why: At constant pressure, Q = nCpΔT with Cp = 5R/2 for a monatomic gas: 2.5 × 8.31 × 20 ≈ 416 J.

questions.q: Efficiency of a Carnot engine is 1/6. On lowering the sink temperature by 62 K it becomes 1/3. Source temperature:
questions.why: Efficiency 1/6 means T₂/T₁ = 5/6. With the sink lowered by 62 K, (T₂ − 62)/T₁ = 2/3. Subtracting gives 62/T₁ = 5/6 − 2/3 = 1/6, so T₁ = 372 K.

questions.q: Ideal gas in a cycle absorbs 500 J and rejects 300 J. Net work and ΔU:
questions.why: In a cycle ΔU = 0. Net work = heat absorbed − heat rejected = 500 − 300 = 200 J.

questions.q: Air at 27 °C (γ = 1.4) is suddenly compressed to 1/32 of its volume. Final temperature (32^0.4 = 4):
questions.why: For an adiabatic change TV^(γ−1) is constant, so T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^0.4 = 300 × 32^0.4 = 300 × 4 = 1200 K (27 °C = 300 K).

questions.q: COP of an ideal refrigerator between −3 °C and 27 °C:
questions.why: For an ideal refrigerator COP = T_cold/(T_hot − T_cold) = 270/(300 − 270) = 270/30 = 9, with temperatures in kelvin.

questions.q: Internal energy of an ideal gas is a function of
questions.why: There are no intermolecular forces in an ideal gas, so there is no potential energy, and internal energy depends only on temperature.

lessons.title: Molecular nature of matter and the ideal gas law

scenes.text: A balloon left in a parked car on a hot day looks tighter in the afternoon.
At constant volume-ish, pressure rises with temperature — the gas laws in everyday life.

steps.title: Ideal gas equation
steps.body:
- **PV = nRT = Nk_BT**, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
- **Boyle's law** (T const): PV = const.
- **Charles' law** (P const): V ∝ T.
- **Dalton's law** of partial pressures: P = P₁ + P₂ + … for non-reacting ideal gases.
- 1 mol of an ideal gas at STP (273 K, 1 atm) occupies about 22.4 L.

Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A gas at 2 atm occupies 3 L. At constant T, its volume at 6 atm = 2 × 3/6 = **1 L**.

**Example 2:** An oxygen cylinder of 30 L at 27 °C has 15 atm pressure. Moles: n = PV/RT = 15 × 1.013 × 10⁵ × 0.03/(8.314 × 300) ≈ **18.3 mol**.

**Example 3:** Number of molecules in 1 m³ of gas at STP: n = P/(k_BT) = 1.013 × 10⁵/(1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 273) ≈ **2.7 × 10²⁵ m⁻³**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C instead of K in gas laws.
- Mixing litres and m³ with R = 8.314 (use SI or R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ consistently).
- Applying ideal gas law at very high pressure without caution.

activity.prompt: A gas at 300 K and constant pressure is heated until its volume doubles. What is its new temperature in K?

quiz.q: Boltzmann constant k_B equals
quiz.why: The Boltzmann constant is the gas constant per molecule: k_B = R/N_A.

quiz.q: Boyle's law holds at constant
quiz.why: Boyle's law says that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, PV is constant.

quiz.q: Molar volume at STP is about
quiz.why: One mole of any ideal gas at STP occupies about 22.4 litres.

quiz.q: Real gases behave most ideally at
quiz.why: Real gases behave most like ideal gases at low pressure and high temperature, when molecules are far apart and move fast so intermolecular forces matter little.

quiz.q: Total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of partial pressures — this is
quiz.why: Dalton's law of partial pressures says the total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of the partial pressures.

lessons.title: Pressure from kinetic theory and meaning of temperature

scenes.text: Steady rain on an umbrella feels like a constant push, though it is millions of tiny impacts.
Gas pressure on a wall is the same idea: countless molecular collisions averaged into a steady force.

steps.title: Assumptions and derivation
steps.body:
Assumptions: many identical molecules, negligible size, elastic collisions, no forces except during collisions, random motion.

A molecule with velocity component vₓ hitting a wall transfers 2mvₓ. Number hitting area A in time Δt with speed vₓ is ½ n A vₓ Δt (half move toward the wall). Pressure = n m ⟨vₓ²⟩. By isotropy ⟨vₓ²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩/3:
**P = (1/3) n m ⟨v²⟩ = (1/3) ρ ⟨v²⟩**

steps.title: Kinetic interpretation of temperature
steps.body:
PV = (2/3) N × (½m⟨v²⟩). Comparing with PV = Nk_BT:
- **Average translational KE per molecule = (3/2) k_BT**
- **v_rms = √(3k_BT/m) = √(3RT/M)** (M = molar mass in kg/mol)

Temperature is a measure of the average molecular kinetic energy. At the same T, lighter molecules move faster: v_rms ∝ 1/√M.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** v_rms of O₂ at 300 K: √(3 × 8.314 × 300/0.032) = √233,800 ≈ **484 m/s**.

**Example 2:** Ratio v_rms(H₂)/v_rms(O₂) at the same T = √(32/2) = **4**.

**Example 3:** Average KE of a gas molecule at 300 K = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300 ≈ **6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J**, independent of the gas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using M in g/mol in √(3RT/M) — convert to kg/mol.
- Saying heavier gases have more KE at the same T — average KE depends only on T.
- Confusing v_rms with average speed or most probable speed (v_mp < v_avg < v_rms).

activity.prompt: At what temperature (K) will v_rms of a gas be double its value at 300 K?

quiz.q: Pressure from kinetic theory P =
quiz.why: The kinetic theory result is P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩, where ρ is the gas density and ⟨v²⟩ is the mean square speed.

quiz.q: Average KE per molecule
quiz.why: The average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)k_BT.

quiz.q: v_rms ∝
quiz.why: v_rms = √(3RT/M), so it is proportional to √T.

quiz.q: At the same T, which has the highest v_rms?
quiz.why: v_rms ∝ 1/√M. At the same temperature the lightest molecule, hydrogen, moves fastest.

quiz.q: If T is fixed and M becomes 4 times, v_rms becomes
quiz.why: Since v_rms ∝ 1/√M, making M four times larger halves v_rms.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: kinetic theory of pressure)

lessons.title: Equipartition of energy and specific heats

scenes.text: Helium and nitrogen at the same temperature need different heat to warm by 1 K per mole.
Nitrogen molecules can rotate as well as move; their energy spreads over more 'degrees of freedom'.

steps.title: Degrees of freedom and equipartition
steps.body:
- **Degrees of freedom (f):** independent ways a molecule can store energy. Monatomic: 3 translational. Rigid diatomic: 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5. Vibrational modes add 2 each (KE + PE) at high temperature.
- **Law of equipartition:** in thermal equilibrium each quadratic energy term contributes ½k_BT per molecule.
- So U per mole = (f/2)RT → **C_v = (f/2)R, Cₚ = C_v + R, γ = 1 + 2/f**.

steps.title: Standard values
steps.body:
- Monatomic (He, Ar): C_v = 3R/2, Cₚ = 5R/2, γ = 5/3
- Rigid diatomic (O₂, N₂): C_v = 5R/2, Cₚ = 7R/2, γ = 7/5
- Diatomic with vibration: C_v = 7R/2, γ = 9/7
- Non-linear polyatomic (rigid): f = 6, C_v = 3R, γ = 4/3
- **Solids (Dulong–Petit):** C ≈ 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (each atom oscillates in 3D: 6 quadratic terms)
- Water: about 75 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (~9R).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A mixture of 1 mol He and 1 mol O₂ (rigid). C_v(mix) = (3R/2 + 5R/2)/2 = **2R**; Cₚ = 3R; γ = **1.5**.

**Example 2:** Internal energy of 2 mol N₂ at 300 K = 2 × (5/2) × 8.314 × 300 ≈ **12.5 kJ**.

**Example 3:** γ for a gas with f = 7: 1 + 2/7 = **9/7 ≈ 1.29**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting vibrational modes count twice (kinetic and potential).
- Averaging γ directly for mixtures — average C_v and Cₚ by moles first.
- Applying classical equipartition at very low temperatures (quantum effects freeze modes).

activity.prompt: Match the molecule type to γ

quiz.q: Degrees of freedom of a rigid diatomic molecule
quiz.why: A rigid diatomic molecule has 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom, giving 5.

quiz.q: Each degree of freedom contributes energy
quiz.why: By the law of equipartition, each degree of freedom contributes ½k_BT of energy per molecule.

quiz.q: Dulong–Petit value for molar heat of solids
quiz.why: The Dulong–Petit law says the molar heat capacity of solids is about 3R (≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), from 6 quadratic energy terms per atom.

quiz.q: C_v of a monatomic ideal gas
quiz.why: A monatomic gas has f = 3 degrees of freedom, so Cv = (f/2)R = 3R/2.

quiz.q: γ = 1 + 2/f. For f = 3, γ =

lessons.title: Mean free path

scenes.text: Molecules move at hundreds of m/s, yet perfume takes many seconds to cross a room.
Each molecule collides billions of times a second and zig-zags — its mean free path is tiny.

steps.title: Definition and formula
steps.body:
The **mean free path** λ is the average distance a molecule travels between collisions.
**λ = 1/(√2 π d² n)** where d = molecular diameter, n = number density.
- λ ∝ 1/n: larger at low pressure (λ ∝ T/P at fixed d).
- Collision frequency ≈ v̄/λ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Nitrogen at STP: n ≈ 2.7 × 10²⁵ m⁻³, d ≈ 3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.
- λ = 1/(1.414 × 3.14 × 9 × 10⁻²⁰ × 2.7 × 10²⁵) ≈ **9.3 × 10⁻⁸ m (about 0.1 µm)** — roughly 300 molecular diameters.

**Example 2:** If pressure is halved at constant T, λ **doubles**.

**Example 3:** With v̄ ≈ 500 m/s and λ ≈ 10⁻⁷ m, collision frequency ≈ **5 × 10⁹ s⁻¹**.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Vacuum tubes, electron microscopes and particle accelerators need very low pressure so the mean free path becomes longer than the apparatus. Slow diffusion of smells and gases in still air is also explained by short mean free paths.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using radius instead of diameter in λ.
- Thinking λ grows with molecular size (it falls as 1/d²).
- Forgetting the √2 factor from relative motion.

statements.s: Mean free path increases as pressure decreases (constant T).
Bigger molecules have longer mean free paths.
At STP the mean free path in air is about 0.1 µm.
Diffusion is slow because molecules move slowly.
statements.why: They move fast but collide very often.

quiz.q: Mean free path is inversely proportional to
quiz.why: The mean free path is λ = 1/(√2 π d² n), so it is inversely proportional to d², the square of the molecular diameter.

quiz.q: Doubling the number density makes λ
quiz.why: Since λ ∝ 1/n, doubling the number density halves the mean free path.

quiz.q: Order of λ for air at STP
quiz.why: For air at STP, the mean free path is about 10⁻⁷ m (roughly 0.1 µm), much larger than a molecular diameter.

quiz.q: Vacuum in an electron gun is needed to
quiz.why: A vacuum reduces the number of gas molecules, so the mean free path of electrons becomes longer and they have fewer collisions.

quiz.q: Collision frequency ≈
quiz.why: Collision frequency is the average speed divided by the mean free path (distance between collisions): v̄/λ.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: mean free path)

questions.q: Value of R
questions.why: The gas constant is R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The 1.38 × 10⁻²³ is k_B and 6.02 × 10²³ is Avogadro's number.

questions.q: Average KE of a gas molecule depends on
questions.why: The average kinetic energy per molecule, (3/2)k_BT, depends only on the temperature.

questions.q: γ for helium
questions.why: Helium is monatomic, so γ = 5/3 ≈ 1.67.

questions.q: A gas at 27 °C is heated to 327 °C at constant volume. Pressure becomes
questions.why: At constant volume P ∝ T (kelvin). 27 °C = 300 K and 327 °C = 600 K, so the pressure doubles.

questions.q: Assertion: At the same temperature, H₂ molecules move faster than O₂. Reason: v_rms ∝ 1/√M.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Since v_rms ∝ 1/√M and H₂ is far lighter than O₂, hydrogen molecules move faster at the same temperature.

questions.q: v_rms of a gas at 400 K is v. At 100 K it is
questions.why: v_rms ∝ √T. Going from 400 K to 100 K gives √(100/400) = 1/2, so the speed is v/2.

questions.q: C_v for a rigid diatomic gas
questions.why: A rigid diatomic gas has f = 5, so Cv = (5/2)R.

questions.q: Case: A 10 L vessel holds O₂ at 2 atm and 300 K. Moles present (R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹):
v_rms of N₂ at 300 K (M = 0.028 kg/mol) is about
Total KE of 1 mol of a monatomic gas at 300 K
questions.why: Total KE of 1 mol of a monatomic gas = (3/2)RT = 1.5 × 8.314 × 300 ≈ 3741 J = 3.74 kJ.

questions.q: Mixture: 2 mol He and 1 mol N₂ (rigid). C_v of mixture:
questions.why: Helium has Cv = 3R/2 and rigid N₂ has 5R/2. The mixture's Cv = (2 × 3/2 + 1 × 5/2)R/3 = (3 + 2.5)R/3 = 11R/6.

questions.q: Pressure of a gas is P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩. Gas density 1.25 kg/m³ at 10⁵ Pa. v_rms:
Mean free path at 1 atm is λ. At 0.01 atm and the same T it is
questions.why: At fixed temperature, λ ∝ 1/n ∝ 1/P. Lowering the pressure to 1/100 makes the mean free path 100 times longer.

questions.q: Temperature at which v_rms of O₂ equals that of H₂ at 300 K:
questions.why: v_rms ∝ √(T/M). For equal speeds, T/M must be equal: T/32 = 300/2, so T = 300 × 16 = 4800 K.

questions.q: For a gas γ = 1.4. Fraction of heat supplied at constant pressure that goes into internal energy:
questions.why: At constant pressure the heat supplied is nCpΔT and the part going into internal energy is nCvΔT. The fraction is Cv/Cp = 1/γ = 1/1.4 = 5/7.

questions.q: Which assumption is NOT part of kinetic theory?
options: Molecules attract strongly at all distances
questions.why: Kinetic theory assumes there are no intermolecular forces except during collisions. Strong attraction at all distances contradicts that assumption.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Oscillations
courses.summary: Periodic and oscillatory motion, simple harmonic motion and its equations, velocity and acceleration in SHM, the force law, energy in SHM, the spring–mass system and the simple pendulum.
outcomes: Learners can describe SHM with x = A cos(ωt + φ)
Learners can find velocity, acceleration and energy at any displacement
Learners can derive periods of spring–mass systems and the simple pendulum
Learners can combine springs and analyse simple SHM variations

scenes.text: A courtyard swing goes back and forth, each swing taking the same time.
Its position plotted against time looks like a cosine curve — the signature of simple harmonic motion.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body:
- **Periodic motion** repeats after a fixed time T (period). Frequency ν = 1/T (Hz).
- **Oscillatory motion:** periodic to-and-fro motion about a mean position.
- **SHM:** x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ)
  - A = amplitude, (ωt + φ) = phase, φ = phase constant
  - **ω = 2π/T = 2πν** (angular frequency)
- SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** x = 5 cos(2πt + π/4) cm.
- A = **5 cm**, ω = 2π rad/s → T = **1 s**, ν = 1 Hz, φ = π/4
- At t = 0: x = 5 cos 45° ≈ **3.54 cm**

**Example 2:** Is sin ωt + cos ωt SHM? = √2 sin(ωt + π/4) → **yes**, amplitude √2, period 2π/ω.

**Example 3:** Is e^(−ωt) periodic? **No** — it never repeats.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking every periodic motion is SHM (a bouncing ball is periodic but not SHM).
- Confusing ω (rad/s) with ν (Hz).
- Forgetting the calculator must be in radians for phase.

activity.prompt: Classify each motion

items.text: A ball bouncing elastically on the floor

quiz.q: Angular frequency of SHM with T = 0.5 s
quiz.why: Angular frequency ω = 2π/T = 2π/0.5 = 4π rad/s.

quiz.q: In x = A cos(ωt + φ), A is
quiz.why: In x = A cos(ωt + φ), A is the amplitude, the maximum displacement from the mean position.

quiz.q: SHM is the projection of
quiz.why: SHM can be seen as the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter of the reference circle.

quiz.q: Frequency of a motion with period 0.02 s
quiz.why: Frequency is the reciprocal of period: ν = 1/T = 1/0.02 = 50 Hz.

quiz.q: sin ωt − cos ωt represents
quiz.why: sin ωt − cos ωt = √2 sin(ωt − π/4), a sinusoid with amplitude √2. So it is SHM with amplitude √2.

lessons.title: Velocity, acceleration, force law and energy in SHM

scenes.text: When a bike goes over a bump, the spring compresses and bounces.
Energy keeps switching between spring PE and kinetic energy — total staying constant in ideal SHM.

steps.title: Kinematics of SHM
steps.body:
From x = A cos(ωt + φ):
- v = −Aω sin(ωt + φ); in terms of x: **v = ω√(A² − x²)**; v_max = Aω at the mean position
- **a = −ω²x**; a_max = Aω² at the extremes

**Force law:** F = ma = −mω²x = **−kx** with k = mω² → ω = √(k/m). A restoring force proportional to displacement always gives SHM.

steps.title: Energy
steps.body:
- KE = ½mω²(A² − x²) = ½k(A² − x²)
- PE = ½kx²
- **Total E = ½kA² = ½mω²A²** (constant)
- KE = PE when x = A/√2.
- Both KE and PE oscillate with frequency 2ν.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** For x = 5 cos(2πt) cm: v_max = 5 × 2π = **10π cm/s ≈ 31.4 cm/s**; a_max = 5 × 4π² ≈ **197 cm/s²**.

**Example 2:** k = 200 N/m, A = 0.1 m. Total energy = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = **1 J**. At x = 0.05 m: PE = 0.25 J, KE = **0.75 J**.

**Example 3:** A particle in SHM has v = 3 cm/s at x = 4 cm and v = 4 cm/s at x = 3 cm. Then 9 = ω²(A² − 16), 16 = ω²(A² − 9) → subtract: 7 = 7ω² → ω = 1 rad/s, A = **5 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking acceleration is maximum at the mean position (it is zero there).
- Forgetting the minus sign in a = −ω²x (it points toward the mean).
- Saying energy frequency equals oscillation frequency (it is double).

activity.label: Displacement as a fraction of amplitude (x/A)

bands.text: Mean position: all energy kinetic, speed maximum, acceleration zero.
Extreme: all energy potential, speed zero, acceleration maximum.

quiz.q: Speed in SHM is maximum at
quiz.why: In SHM v = ω√(A² − x²), which is greatest at x = 0, the mean position.

quiz.q: Acceleration in SHM is proportional to
quiz.why: In SHM, a = −ω²x: the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction.

quiz.q: Total energy of SHM is proportional to
quiz.why: The total energy in SHM is ½kA², so it is proportional to the square of the amplitude.

quiz.q: KE equals PE at
quiz.why: KE equals PE when ½k(A² − x²) = ½kx², so x² = A²/2 and x = A/√2.

quiz.q: If SHM frequency is ν, KE oscillates with frequency
quiz.why: KE is proportional to sin² (or cos²) of ωt, which repeats twice as often as the displacement. So KE oscillates at 2ν.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: energy in SHM)

lessons.title: Spring–mass system and simple pendulum

scenes.text: Grandfather's pendulum clock runs slow every summer.
Heat lengthens the pendulum rod; since T = 2π√(l/g), a longer pendulum ticks slower.

steps.title: Spring–mass system
steps.body:
F = −kx → ω = √(k/m), **T = 2π√(m/k)** (independent of amplitude and of g for a vertical spring — g only shifts the equilibrium).
- Springs in **parallel:** k = k₁ + k₂
- Springs in **series:** 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂
- Cutting a spring into n equal parts makes each part n times stiffer.

steps.title: Simple pendulum (derivation)
steps.body:
Bob of mass m on a light string of length L. Restoring torque about the support: τ = −mgL sin θ. With I = mL² and α = d²θ/dt²:
mL² α = −mgL sin θ → for small θ (sin θ ≈ θ): α = −(g/L)θ → SHM with ω = √(g/L).
**T = 2π√(L/g)** — independent of mass and (for small angles) of amplitude.

**Seconds pendulum:** T = 2 s → L = gT²/4π² ≈ 0.993 m (≈ 1 m).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** m = 1 kg, k = 100 N/m. T = 2π√(0.01) = 2π/10 ≈ **0.628 s**.

**Example 2:** Length of a seconds pendulum (g = 9.8): L = 9.8 × 4/(4π²) ≈ **0.993 m**.

**Example 3:** A pendulum is taken to the Moon (g/6). T becomes **√6 ≈ 2.45 times** longer.

**Example 4:** Two springs of 100 N/m each: parallel k = 200 N/m; series k = 50 N/m. With 2 kg: T_parallel = 2π√(0.01) ≈ 0.63 s; T_series = 2π√(0.04) ≈ 1.26 s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a heavier bob swings slower — T is independent of mass.
- Using T = 2π√(L/g) for large angles.
- Measuring L to the top of the bob instead of to its centre.

activity.prompt: A pendulum of length 2.45 m swings where g = 9.8 m/s². What is its period in seconds? (use π = 3.14)

quiz.q: Period of a simple pendulum depends on
quiz.why: For a simple pendulum T = 2π√(L/g), which depends on the length and g, not on the mass of the bob (for small amplitudes).

quiz.q: Length of a pendulum is made 4 times. Period becomes
quiz.why: T ∝ √L. Making L four times as long multiplies T by √4 = 2.

quiz.q: Two springs k₁ and k₂ in series give
quiz.why: For springs in series 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂, so k = k₁k₂/(k₁ + k₂).

quiz.q: Mass on a spring: mass made 4 times. Period
quiz.why: T = 2π√(m/k) ∝ √m. With four times the mass, the period doubles.

quiz.q: A pendulum clock in a lift accelerating upward will
quiz.why: In an upward-accelerating lift the effective gravity is g + a, which is larger, so T = 2π√(L/g_eff) decreases and the clock runs fast.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: spring and pendulum)

lessons.title: Problem practice: identifying SHM and JEE bridge

scenes.text: Sahil pushes a floating bottle down and lets go — it bobs up and down.
Extra buoyancy is proportional to extra depth: a restoring force ∝ displacement. It's SHM again!

steps.title: Recipe for proving SHM
steps.body:
1. Displace the system by small x from equilibrium.
2. Find the net restoring force (or torque) F.
3. Show F = −(constant) × x.
4. Then ω = √(constant/m) (or √(constant/I) for rotation) and T = 2π/ω.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (floating cylinder):** Cross-section A, mass m, liquid density ρ. Pushing down by x adds buoyancy ρAgx → F = −(ρAg)x → **T = 2π√(m/(ρAg))**.

**Example 2 (liquid in U-tube):** Column of total length L. Displacing one side by x makes a height difference 2x: F = −(2Aρg)x, mass = AρL → **T = 2π√(L/2g)**.

**Example 3 (tunnel through Earth):** Inside a uniform Earth, g(r) = g r/R → a = −(g/R)r → T = 2π√(R/g) ≈ **84 min** (same as a low-orbit satellite).

steps.title: Damping and resonance (JEE bridge)
steps.body: Real oscillators lose energy to friction: amplitude decays (damped oscillations). Driven by a periodic force, an oscillator responds most strongly when the driving frequency is near its natural frequency — **resonance** (soldiers break step on bridges; tuning a radio).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the small-displacement approximation.
- Using total length instead of displaced length in U-tube problems.
- Using g at the surface for points inside the Earth.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for proving a motion is SHM
items: Displace the body slightly from equilibrium
Write the net restoring force or torque
Show it is proportional to displacement with a minus sign

quiz.q: For a floating body bobbing vertically, the restoring force comes from
quiz.why: A body floating in a liquid gets a restoring force from the extra (or reduced) buoyant force when it is pushed down (or up), which is proportional to the displacement.

quiz.q: Period of liquid in a U-tube with column length L
quiz.why: If the liquid is displaced by y in one limb, the height difference is 2y, so the restoring force is 2ρAgy, giving T = 2π√(L/2g).

quiz.q: Resonance occurs when driving frequency
quiz.why: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the system's natural frequency, giving the maximum amplitude response.

quiz.q: A body dropped into a tunnel through Earth's centre would
quiz.why: Inside the Earth the gravitational force on a body is proportional to its distance from the centre and directed toward it, which is the condition for SHM.

quiz.q: Damping causes
quiz.why: Damping removes energy from the oscillator, so the amplitude decays over time.

questions.q: Unit of angular frequency
questions.why: Angular frequency ω = 2πν is measured in radians per second.

questions.q: In SHM, acceleration is zero at
questions.why: Since a = −ω²x, the acceleration in SHM is zero where the displacement is zero, at the mean position.

questions.q: Period of a seconds pendulum
questions.why: A seconds pendulum takes 1 second for each swing, so its full period is 2 s.

questions.q: x = 3 sin(4t) m. Maximum speed
questions.why: For x = A sin ωt with A = 3 m and ω = 4 rad/s, the maximum speed is Aω = 3 × 4 = 12 m/s.

questions.q: Assertion: Period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass of the bob. Reason: Both the restoring force and the inertia are proportional to mass.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. For a pendulum, the restoring force (mg sin θ) and the inertia (m) are both proportional to m, so m cancels in T = 2π√(L/g).

questions.q: Spring of k = 400 N/m with 1 kg. Frequency:
questions.why: ω = √(k/m) = √400 = 20 rad/s. The frequency is ν = ω/2π = 20/6.28 ≈ 3.18 Hz.

questions.q: A particle in SHM has amplitude 4 cm. Speed is half its maximum at x =
questions.why: v = ω√(A² − x²) = ωA/2 gives √(A² − x²) = A/2, so x² = 3A²/4 and x = (√3/2)A = (√3/2) × 4 = 2√3 cm.

questions.q: Case: A clock pendulum is 1% too long. Roughly how many seconds does the clock lose per day (86400 s)?
questions.why: T ∝ √L, so a 1% longer pendulum has a period 0.5% longer. The clock loses 0.005 × 86400 = 432 s per day.

questions.q: Energy of a 0.5 kg mass in SHM with A = 0.2 m and ω = 10 rad/s:
questions.why: Energy = ½mω²A² = ½ × 0.5 × 100 × 0.04 = 1 J.

questions.q: A spring is cut into two equal halves. Each half's spring constant is (original k)
questions.why: A spring's stiffness is inversely proportional to its length, so halving the length doubles the spring constant: 2k.

questions.q: A 1 kg block between two springs k₁ = 100 N/m and k₂ = 300 N/m fixed to walls on either side. Period (π ≈ 3.14):
questions.why: A block between two springs attached to walls on both sides feels both springs together, so k_eff = 100 + 300 = 400 N/m. T = 2π√(1/400) = 2π/20 ≈ 0.314 s.

questions.q: A particle's displacement is x = 2 sin²(ωt). Its motion is
options: SHM with amplitude 1 about x = 1, frequency 2ω/2π
questions.why: 2 sin²ωt = 1 − cos 2ωt, which is SHM about x = 1 with amplitude 1 and angular frequency 2ω (frequency 2ω/2π).

questions.q: A pendulum's period on Earth is 2 s. On a planet with g' = g/4 it is
questions.why: T = 2π√(L/g) ∝ 1/√g. With g/4, T becomes √4 = 2 times as long: 2 × 2 = 4 s.

questions.q: A cylinder of mass 0.8 kg and cross-section 10 cm² floats upright in water. Period of small vertical oscillation (g = 10, π² ≈ 10):
questions.why: The restoring force per unit displacement is ρAg, so T = 2π√(m/(ρAg)) = 2π√(0.8/(1000 × 10⁻³ × 10)) = 2π√0.08 ≈ 2π × 0.283 ≈ 1.78 s.

questions.q: In SHM, phase difference between displacement and acceleration
questions.why: Since a = −ω²x, the acceleration is opposite to the displacement, so they are π (180°) out of phase.

questions.q: Which graph is a straight line for SHM?
questions.why: In SHM, a = −ω²x, so a vs x is a straight line. The others, v vs x, KE vs x and x vs t, are curves.

courses.title: Ch 14 · Waves
courses.summary: Transverse and longitudinal waves, displacement relation of a progressive wave, wave speed on strings and in fluids, Newton's formula with Laplace's correction, superposition, reflection, standing waves in strings and pipes, and beats.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish transverse and longitudinal mechanical waves
Learners can read amplitude, wavelength, frequency and speed from y = a sin(kx − ωt + φ)
Learners can compute wave speeds in strings and gases
Learners can find harmonics of strings and pipes
Learners can calculate beat frequency

lessons.title: Types of waves and the displacement relation

scenes.text: At a cricket stadium the crowd does a 'Mexican wave' — the wave travels round, but each spectator just stands and sits.
A wave carries energy and pattern, not the medium itself.

steps.title: Types of waves
steps.body:
- **Mechanical** waves need a medium (sound, waves on strings); electromagnetic waves do not.
- **Transverse:** particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation (string waves). Need a medium with shear rigidity, so they do not travel through the bulk of fluids.
- **Longitudinal:** particles oscillate along the direction of propagation — compressions and rarefactions (sound in air).

steps.title: Displacement relation
steps.body:
A wave travelling in +x: **y(x, t) = a sin(kx − ωt + φ)**
- a = amplitude; k = 2π/λ (angular wave number, rad/m)
- ω = 2πν = 2π/T
- **Wave speed v = ω/k = λν**
- A wave in −x direction: y = a sin(kx + ωt + φ).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** y = 0.005 sin(80x − 3t) (SI).
- a = **5 mm**; k = 80 rad/m → λ = 2π/80 ≈ **7.85 cm**
- ω = 3 rad/s → T = 2π/3 ≈ **2.09 s**; v = ω/k = **0.0375 m/s**

**Example 2:** A sound wave of 500 Hz travels at 340 m/s. λ = 340/500 = **0.68 m**.

**Example 3:** Phase difference between two points 0.17 m apart on that wave: Δφ = 2πΔx/λ = 2π × 0.25 = **π/2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing particle velocity (∂y/∂t) with wave velocity (ω/k).
- Reading k as wavelength.
- Saying sound can be transverse in air.

activity.prompt: Transverse or longitudinal?

quiz.q: Sound waves in air are
quiz.why: Sound in air travels as compressions and rarefactions along the direction of travel, so it is a longitudinal wave.

quiz.q: Wave speed equals
quiz.why: For a travelling wave v = ω/k (the same as λν).

quiz.q: For y = 0.02 sin(2πx − 100πt), the frequency is
quiz.why: Comparing with sin(kx − ωt), ω = 100π rad/s, so ν = ω/2π = 50 Hz.

quiz.q: A wave carries
quiz.why: A wave transports energy; the particles of the medium only oscillate about their positions and are not carried along.

quiz.q: λ for a 680 Hz sound at 340 m/s

lessons.title: Speed of waves: strings and sound

scenes.text: A veena player tightens a peg and the note rises.
More tension means a faster wave on the string and a higher frequency for the same length.

steps.title: Transverse wave on a string
steps.body: **v = √(T/µ)**, T = tension, µ = mass per unit length. Depends only on the string's properties, not on frequency.

steps.title: Longitudinal (sound) waves
steps.body:
- In a fluid: **v = √(B/ρ)**; in a solid rod: v = √(Y/ρ).
- **Newton's formula** (assumed isothermal, B = P): v = √(P/ρ) ≈ 280 m/s for air at STP — too low.
- **Laplace's correction** (adiabatic, B = γP): **v = √(γP/ρ)** ≈ 331 m/s for air at 0 °C ✓.
- v ∝ √T (in kelvin); independent of pressure at constant T; increases with humidity (moist air is less dense).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A string with µ = 0.01 kg/m under 100 N tension: v = √(100/0.01) = **100 m/s**.

**Example 2:** Air at STP (P = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, ρ = 1.29 kg/m³, γ = 1.4).
- Newton: √(1.01 × 10⁵/1.29) ≈ **280 m/s**
- Laplace: √(1.4 × 1.01 × 10⁵/1.29) ≈ **331 m/s**

**Example 3:** Speed of sound at 0 °C is 331 m/s. At 27 °C: 331 × √(300/273) ≈ **347 m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the string's total mass instead of mass per length.
- Thinking sound speed depends on pressure at constant temperature.
- Using °C in v ∝ √T.

activity.prompt: A wire of mass per length 0.004 kg/m is under 64 N tension. Wave speed in m/s?

quiz.q: Wave speed on a string is
quiz.why: The speed of a transverse wave on a string is v = √(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is mass per unit length.

quiz.q: Laplace corrected Newton by assuming sound propagation is
quiz.why: Newton assumed isothermal compression and got a wrong speed. Laplace showed the compressions are too rapid for heat to flow, so the process is adiabatic.

quiz.q: Tension made 4 times; wave speed becomes
quiz.why: v = √(T/μ) ∝ √T. Four times the tension doubles the wave speed.

quiz.q: Sound travels fastest in
quiz.why: Sound travels fastest in solids such as steel, because of their high elasticity relative to their density.

quiz.q: At constant temperature, doubling air pressure makes sound speed
quiz.why: v = √(γP/ρ), and at constant temperature P/ρ stays the same when P doubles (ρ also doubles). So the speed does not change.

sources: NCERT Physics Class 11 (topic: speed of waves)

scenes.text: A bansuri player covers holes to change the length of the vibrating air column.
A guitarist presses frets to shorten the string. Both select standing-wave patterns of different frequencies.

steps.title: Superposition and reflection
steps.body:
- **Principle of superposition:** net displacement = algebraic sum of individual displacements.
- Reflection at a **rigid boundary:** phase change of π (inverted pulse). At an **open/free boundary:** no phase change.
- Two identical waves in opposite directions form a **standing wave**: y = 2a sin kx cos ωt. **Nodes** (zero amplitude) and **antinodes** (maximum) are λ/2 apart; node to adjacent antinode = λ/4.

steps.title: Normal modes
steps.body:
- **String fixed at both ends** (length L): λₙ = 2L/n, **νₙ = nv/2L**, n = 1, 2, 3… All harmonics.
- **Pipe closed at one end:** node at the closed end, antinode at the open end: **ν = (2n − 1)v/4L** — only odd harmonics.
- **Pipe open at both ends:** antinodes at both ends: **ν = nv/2L** — all harmonics.
- Fundamental = first harmonic; higher modes are overtones.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A 0.5 m open pipe, v = 340 m/s. Fundamental = 340/(2 × 0.5) = **340 Hz**; next harmonics 680, 1020 Hz.

**Example 2:** Same length closed at one end: fundamental = 340/(4 × 0.5) = **170 Hz**; next allowed 510, 850 Hz (odd multiples).

**Example 3:** A 1 m string with wave speed 200 m/s: ν₁ = 200/2 = **100 Hz**; third harmonic **300 Hz**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Allowing even harmonics in a closed pipe.
- Using λ = L for the fundamental of a string (it is 2L).
- Forgetting the inversion on reflection from a rigid end.

activity.prompt: Match the system to its fundamental frequency
pairs: String fixed at both ends, length L
Pipe open at both ends, length L
Pipe closed at one end, length L

quiz.q: Distance between adjacent nodes
quiz.why: In a standing wave, adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength, λ/2.

quiz.q: A closed pipe produces
quiz.why: A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so only odd harmonics are possible.

quiz.q: Reflection from a rigid end causes a phase change of
quiz.why: On reflection from a fixed or rigid end the wave is inverted, which is a phase change of π.

quiz.q: Fundamental of a 0.85 m closed pipe (v = 340 m/s)
quiz.why: The fundamental of a closed pipe is v/4L = 340/(4 × 0.85) = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz.

quiz.q: An open pipe and a closed pipe of the same length: ratio of fundamentals (open : closed)
quiz.why: An open pipe has fundamental v/2L and a closed pipe has v/4L. The ratio open : closed is 2 : 1.

scenes.text: A harmonium tuner plays a reed together with a tuning fork and hears 'wah-wah-wah'.
He adjusts until the wavering stops — beats vanish when frequencies match.

steps.title: Beats
steps.body:
Two waves of slightly different frequencies ν₁ and ν₂ superpose to give a loudness that rises and falls periodically.
- **Beat frequency = |ν₁ − ν₂|**
- Resultant: s = [2a cos(πΔν t)] cos(2π ν_avg t) — a tone at the average frequency with slowly varying amplitude.
- Ear distinguishes beats up to about 10 per second.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz → **4 beats/s**.

**Example 2:** A fork of unknown frequency gives 5 beats/s with a 400 Hz fork. On loading the unknown fork with wax (lowers its frequency), beats become 3/s. Unknown frequency?
- Possible: 405 or 395 Hz. Loading lowers it; if 405 → 403 → beats 3 ✓; if 395 → lower → beats increase ✗.
- Answer **405 Hz**.

**Example 3:** Filing a fork's prongs RAISES its frequency — use the same logic in reverse.

steps.title: JEE bridge: Doppler effect
steps.body: When source or listener moves, the observed frequency changes: ν' = ν (v + v_L)/(v − v_S) for approach (v = speed of sound, v_L listener speed toward source, v_S source speed toward listener). A passing ambulance siren drops in pitch as it goes by.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that beats give only the DIFFERENCE, so two answers are possible until extra information is used.
- Mixing up loading (frequency down) and filing (frequency up).
- Applying beats to frequencies that differ a lot (then you hear two separate notes).

a.text: Fork A is 512 Hz. Fork B gives 6 beats/s with A. You put a little wax on B and now hear 4 beats/s. What is B's original frequency?

choices.label: 518 Hz
506 Hz
choices.feedback: Wax would lower 506 further, increasing the beats above 6.

wrong.text: Think again: loading lowers frequency. Only 518 Hz is consistent with fewer beats.

quiz.q: Beat frequency of 300 Hz and 304 Hz
quiz.why: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies: 304 − 300 = 4 Hz.

quiz.q: Loading a tuning fork with wax
quiz.why: Wax adds mass to the prong, which lowers the frequency of the tuning fork.

quiz.q: Beats are a result of
quiz.why: Beats arise from the superposition of two waves of nearly equal frequency, which alternately reinforce and cancel.

quiz.q: Perceived pitch while beats occur corresponds to
quiz.why: While beating, the sound heard has the average of the two frequencies, with its loudness rising and falling at the beat frequency.

quiz.q: As an ambulance moves away from you, its siren pitch
quiz.why: By the Doppler effect, a source moving away makes the observer hear a lower frequency, so the pitch falls.

questions.q: Which needs a medium?
questions.why: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium. Light, X-rays and radio waves can travel through vacuum.

questions.q: k = 2π/λ is called
questions.why: The quantity k = 2π/λ is called the angular wave number (or propagation constant).

questions.q: Speed of sound at STP is about
questions.why: The speed of sound in air at STP (0 °C) is about 331 m/s, using Laplace's adiabatic correction.

questions.q: y = 0.1 sin(10πx − 400πt). Wave speed:
questions.why: Wave speed v = ω/k = 400π/10π = 40 m/s.

questions.q: Assertion: Transverse waves cannot travel through the interior of a gas. Reason: Gases have no shear rigidity.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Transverse waves need a restoring force against shear, and gases have no rigidity (no shear modulus), so they cannot support transverse waves.

questions.q: Distance between a node and the adjacent antinode
questions.why: In a standing wave, a node and the next antinode are λ/4 apart.

questions.q: A string's tension is increased by 44%. Its fundamental frequency rises by
questions.why: ν ∝ √T. If T becomes 1.44 times, the frequency becomes √1.44 = 1.2 times, a rise of 20%.

questions.q: Case: A 34 cm pipe closed at one end (v = 340 m/s). Its first two resonant frequencies are
questions.why: For a pipe closed at one end, ν₁ = v/4L = 340/(4 × 0.34) = 250 Hz. The next resonance is the third harmonic, 3 × 250 = 750 Hz.

questions.q: Ratio of speed of sound in hydrogen to oxygen at the same T (both diatomic):
questions.why: v = √(γRT/M), so at the same T and γ, v ∝ 1/√M. H₂ is 16 times lighter than O₂, so its speed of sound is √16 = 4 times larger: 4 : 1.

questions.q: An open pipe's 2nd harmonic equals a closed pipe's fundamental. Ratio of lengths (open : closed):
questions.why: The open pipe's 2nd harmonic is 2 × v/2L₀ = v/L₀, and the closed pipe's fundamental is v/4L_c. Equating gives L₀ = 4L_c, so the ratio is 4 : 1.

questions.q: Fork P (unknown) gives 4 beats/s with a 256 Hz fork. Filing P makes beats 6/s. P's frequency was
questions.why: 4 beats with 256 Hz means P was 252 or 260 Hz. Filing raises P's frequency. If P were 260, the beats would go up to 6 (as observed), whereas from 252 they would fall to 2 or fewer, so P was 260 Hz.

questions.q: A sonometer wire of length 1 m vibrates at 256 Hz. Length for 384 Hz (same tension):
questions.why: For a string at fixed tension ν ∝ 1/L, so L = 1 × 256/384 = 0.667 m.

questions.q: A steel wire 0.72 m long, mass 5 × 10⁻³ kg, under 72 N tension vibrates in its fundamental. Frequency:
Two waves y₁ = a sin(kx − ωt), y₂ = a sin(kx + ωt) superpose. Amplitude at x = λ/8:
questions.why: The sum is a standing wave 2a sin kx cos ωt. At x = λ/8, kx = 2π/λ × λ/8 = π/4, so the amplitude is 2a sin(π/4) = 2a/√2 = √2 a.

questions.q: Speed of sound at 0 °C is 332 m/s. Temperature at which it doubles:
questions.why: v ∝ √T (kelvin). For v to double, T must become four times: 4 × 273 = 1092 K = 819 °C.

questions.q: Which is a longitudinal wave?
questions.why: Sound in air is a longitudinal wave (compressions and rarefactions). Light, waves on a rope and surface ripples are mainly transverse.

She compresses each chapter to its five most-used formulas and checks units for each.

steps.title: Units, kinematics, vectors
steps.body:
- % error of Z = AᵖBᑫ/Cʳ: p%A + q%B + r%C
- v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; sₙ = u + a(2n − 1)/2
- R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ)
- Projectile: T = 2u sin θ/g, H = u² sin² θ/2g, R = u² sin 2θ/g
- Circular: a = v²/r = ω²r

steps.title: Laws of motion, work–energy
steps.body:
- F = dp/dt; impulse = Δp
- f_s ≤ µₛN; f_k = µ_kN; tan θ_repose = µₛ
- Level curve v_max = √(µRg); banked v₀ = √(Rg tan θ)
- W = F·d; K = p²/2m; spring U = ½kx²; P = F·v
- Elastic 1D (m₂ at rest): v₁ = (m₁ − m₂)u/(m₁ + m₂), v₂ = 2m₁u/(m₁ + m₂)

steps.title: Rotation and gravitation
steps.body:
- X_cm = Σmx/Σm; τ = r × F; L = Iω; τ = Iα; KE_rot = ½Iω²
- I: ring MR², disc ½MR², sphere (2/5)MR², rod ML²/12 (centre), ML²/3 (end)
- F = Gm₁m₂/r²; g = GM/R²; g_h ≈ g(1 − 2h/R); g_d = g(1 − d/R)
- vₑ = √(2gR); v₀ = √(GM/r); T² ∝ r³; E = −GMm/2r

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body:
- Draw a diagram for every mechanics question — FBD, vector triangle or v–t graph.
- Check dimensions of your final expression.
- Do limiting-case checks (m₁ = m₂, θ = 0, h → 0).

quiz.q: Dimensions of angular momentum
quiz.why: Angular momentum = r × p, so its dimensions are [L][M L T⁻¹] = [M L² T⁻¹].

quiz.q: A ball thrown up at 15 m/s (g = 10) returns after
quiz.why: A ball thrown up at u returns to the starting height after 2u/g = 2 × 15/10 = 3 s.

quiz.q: Momentum conservation follows from Newton's
quiz.why: Momentum conservation follows from Newton's second law (F = dp/dt) and third law (internal forces are equal and opposite and cancel).

quiz.q: KE of a body is increased by 300%. Its momentum increases by
quiz.why: KE rises by 300%, so the new KE is 4 times the old one. Since p = √(2mK), the momentum becomes √4 = 2 times, an increase of 100%.

quiz.q: g at depth R/2 vs height R/2 (ratio depth : height)
quiz.why: At depth R/2, g′ = g/2. At height R/2, g′ = g/(1.5)² = 4g/9. Ratio = (1/2)/(4/9) = 9/8.

quiz.q: I of a disc about its diameter (perpendicular-axis theorem)
quiz.why: By the perpendicular-axis theorem, I_z = I_x + I_y = 2I_d, and I_z = MR²/2 for a disc. So I_d = MR²/4.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: properties of matter, heat and thermodynamics (Ch 8–12)

scenes.text: Four friends split the thermal chapters and each teaches one to the others.
Teaching forces them to state each formula with its conditions — when it applies and when it doesn't.

steps.title: Solids and fluids
steps.body:
- Y = FL/(AΔL); B = −p/(ΔV/V); energy density ½ stress × strain
- P = Pₐ + ρgh; Pascal: F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁
- A₁v₁ = A₂v₂; P + ½ρv² + ρgh = const; Torricelli v = √(2gh)
- F = 6πηrv; v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η; Re = ρvd/η
- Drop 2S/r; soap bubble 4S/r; h = 2S cos θ/ρgr

steps.title: Heat and thermodynamics
steps.body:
- ΔL = αLΔT; β = 2α; γ = 3α
- Q = mcΔT; Q = mL
- H = KAΔT/L; P = eσAT⁴; λₘT = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K
- ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW; Cₚ − C_v = R
- Isothermal W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁); adiabatic PV^γ = const, W = nR(T₁ − T₂)/(γ − 1)
- η = 1 − T₂/T₁ (Carnot); COP = T₂/(T₁ − T₂)

steps.title: Kinetic theory
steps.body:
- PV = nRT = Nk_BT
- P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩; KE_avg = (3/2)k_BT
- v_rms = √(3RT/M)
- C_v = (f/2)R; γ = 1 + 2/f
- λ = 1/(√2πd²n)

steps.title: Top exam traps
steps.body:
- Kelvin vs Celsius in gas laws, Stefan's law and Carnot.
- Soap bubble has two surfaces.
- ΔU = nC_vΔT for every process of an ideal gas.

activity.prompt: Match the formula to its law

quiz.q: Water rises 4 cm in a capillary. In a tube of half the radius it rises
quiz.why: Capillary rise h ∝ 1/r. Halving the radius doubles the rise to 8 cm.

quiz.q: Efficiency of a Carnot engine between 400 K and 300 K
Two drops of water combine. Surface energy
quiz.why: When two drops merge, the total surface area decreases, so the surface energy decreases and the extra energy is released as heat.

quiz.q: v_rms at 27 °C is 500 m/s. At 927 °C it is
quiz.why: v_rms ∝ √T. Going from 27 °C (300 K) to 927 °C (1200 K) multiplies it by √4 = 2, so 1000 m/s.

quiz.q: For an adiabatic process
quiz.why: An adiabatic process is one with no heat exchange with the surroundings, so ΔQ = 0.

quiz.q: Thermal stress in a clamped rod
quiz.why: A clamped rod cannot expand, so the prevented strain is αΔT. Thermal stress = Y × strain = YαΔT.

scenes.text: In the mock, Imran wasted 40 minutes on one hard question and could not finish.
Next time he does a first pass of easy questions, marks hard ones, and returns — scoring 20 marks more.

steps.title: Oscillations
steps.body:
- x = A cos(ωt + φ); v = ω√(A² − x²); a = −ω²x
- E = ½kA²; KE = PE at x = A/√2
- Spring T = 2π√(m/k); pendulum T = 2π√(L/g)
- Series 1/k = Σ1/kᵢ; parallel k = Σkᵢ

steps.title: Waves
steps.body:
- y = a sin(kx − ωt); v = ω/k = λν
- String v = √(T/µ); gas v = √(γP/ρ) ∝ √T
- String/open pipe νₙ = nv/2L; closed pipe ν = (2n − 1)v/4L
- Beats = |ν₁ − ν₂|

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body:
- **First pass (≈ 40% of time):** all 1- and 2-mark questions and easy numericals.
- **Second pass:** long answers/derivations — write the statement, diagram, steps, final boxed result with units.
- **Third pass:** hardest numericals; partial working earns marks in boards.
- In MCQ entrance tests, eliminate options using dimensions and limiting cases; skip if unsure when negative marking applies.

steps.title: Last-minute checks
steps.body:
- Units in every final answer.
- Significant figures consistent with data.
- Vector directions stated (east, upward, toward centre).

activity.prompt: Exam-day checklist
items: Revise the three formula sheets once
Carry admit card, pens, pencil, scale, eraser
Read the whole paper in the first 10 minutes
Leave 10 minutes to recheck units and answers

quiz.q: Pendulum of length 1 m on Earth (g ≈ π²) has period
quiz.why: With g ≈ π², T = 2π√(L/g) = 2π√(1/π²) = 2 s (which is why a 1 m pendulum is nearly a seconds pendulum).

quiz.q: Fundamental of a string doubles when its length is
quiz.why: For a string, the fundamental frequency is ν ∝ 1/L, so it doubles when the length is halved.

quiz.q: The best first step in a mechanics problem is usually
quiz.why: Drawing a diagram or free-body diagram organises the information and forces, and is usually the best first step in a mechanics problem.

quiz.q: Total energy in SHM if amplitude triples
quiz.why: SHM energy E = ½kA² ∝ A². If the amplitude triples, the energy becomes 9 times.

quiz.q: Beats heard with 440 Hz and 437 Hz
quiz.why: The beat frequency equals the difference of the frequencies: 440 − 437 = 3 beats per second.

lessons.title: Mock paper 1 (mixed, timed)

scenes.text: Set a timer, keep the formula sheet away, and attempt these questions in one sitting.
Then read each explanation — the mistakes you make today are the marks you gain tomorrow.

steps.title: How to use this mock
steps.body:
- Time limit: about 1.5 minutes per question.
- No calculator for simple arithmetic — practise approximations (√2 ≈ 1.41, π² ≈ 10, g ≈ 10).
- Mark doubtful questions and come back.

steps.title: Approximation toolkit
steps.body:
- (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx for small x
- sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ (radians) for small angles
- ln 2 ≈ 0.693, log₁₀ 2 ≈ 0.301

steps.title: After the mock
steps.body: Make an error log with three columns: concept gap, careless slip, time pressure. Fix concept gaps by re-doing that chapter's lesson; fix slips by writing units and signs every time.

activity.prompt: After the mock paper: which two chapters cost you the most marks, and what is your plan for each?
activity.hint: Be specific: e.g. 'Rotation — revise moment of inertia table, do 10 problems on τ = Iα by Sunday.'

quiz.q: A car moving at 72 km/h stops in 4 s. Deceleration:
quiz.why: 72 km/h = 20 m/s. Deceleration = Δv/t = 20/4 = 5 m/s².

quiz.q: Two masses 2 kg and 8 kg have equal KE. Ratio of momenta (2 kg : 8 kg):
quiz.why: For equal KE, p = √(2mK) ∝ √m. The ratio of momenta is √2 : √8 = 1 : 2.

quiz.q: A satellite orbits at height R. Its period relative to a near-surface satellite (84 min):
quiz.why: By Kepler's third law, T ∝ r^(3/2). At height R the radius is 2R, so T = 2^(1.5) × 84 ≈ 2.83 × 84 ≈ 238 min.

quiz.q: Heat needed to raise 1 mol of a monatomic gas by 10 K at constant volume (R = 8.3):
quiz.why: At constant volume, Q = nCvΔT = 1 × (3/2)(8.3) × 10 = 124.5 J.

quiz.q: A closed pipe resonates at 300 Hz and 500 Hz consecutively. Its fundamental is
quiz.why: A closed pipe has only odd harmonics, so consecutive resonant frequencies differ by 2ν₁. Here 500 − 300 = 200, so ν₁ = 100 Hz.

quiz.q: A wire extends 1 mm under a load. The same load on a wire of the same material, double length and double radius, gives
quiz.why: The extension ΔL = FL/(πr²Y) ∝ L/r². Double length and double radius give 2/4 = 1/2, so the extension is 0.5 mm.

quiz.q: Torque on a body is zero. Which must be constant?
quiz.why: Since τ = dL/dt, zero torque means the angular momentum is constant. KE or linear momentum need not remain constant.

quiz.q: A body moves under F = −16x with m = 1 kg. Its period:
quiz.why: F = −16x with m = 1 kg gives ω² = 16, so ω = 4 rad/s. T = 2π/ω = 2π/4 = π/2 s.

sources: Original mock questions based on the NCERT Class 11 Physics syllabus

questions.q: Mock 2 · Number of significant figures in 3.0800
questions.why: In 3.0800, all digits are significant including the trailing zeros after the decimal point, giving 5 significant figures.

questions.q: Mock 2 · SI unit of coefficient of viscosity
questions.why: The coefficient of viscosity has unit Pa s (N s m⁻²), from Newton's law of viscosity F = ηA dv/dx.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A body is thrown horizontally. Its horizontal velocity
questions.why: There is no horizontal force on a projectile, so its horizontal velocity stays constant while the vertical velocity changes under gravity.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Unit of Stefan's constant
questions.why: From P = σAT⁴, σ = P/(AT⁴), so its unit is W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Momentum of a 10 g bullet at 300 m/s
questions.why: Momentum = mass × velocity = 0.01 kg × 300 m/s = 3 kg m/s (10 g converted to 0.01 kg).

questions.q: Mock 2 · Assertion: The surface of a liquid behaves like a stretched membrane. Reason: Surface molecules have extra energy and the surface tends to contract.
options: Both true, Reason does not explain
questions.why: Both are true. Surface molecules have extra energy and the surface tends to shrink to the smallest area, so it behaves like a stretched membrane, which is surface tension.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A projectile is fired at 60°. At the top its KE is what fraction of the initial KE?
questions.why: At the top only the horizontal velocity u cos 60° remains. KE ∝ v², so the fraction is cos²60° = (1/2)² = 1/4.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A man pushes a wall but it does not move. Work done by him on the wall:
questions.why: Work needs displacement. The wall does not move, so the man does zero work on it, however tired he gets.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Moment of inertia of a uniform rod (2 kg, 3 m) about its centre (⟂)
questions.why: For a rod about its centre, I = ML²/12 = 2 × 9/12 = 1.5 kg m².

questions.q: Mock 2 · An ideal gas is compressed isothermally. Heat is
questions.why: In isothermal compression ΔU = 0, so the work done on the gas is released as heat. The gas gives out heat.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Case: A lift of mass 500 kg accelerates upward at 2 m/s² (g = 10). Cable tension:
questions.why: For a lift accelerating upward, T − mg = ma, so T = m(g + a) = 500 × 12 = 6000 N.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Two wires of the same material, radii in ratio 1:2, lengths in ratio 2:1, carry the same load. Ratio of strains:
questions.why: Strain = F/(AY) ∝ 1/r² for the same load and material (length does not matter). Radii in ratio 1 : 2 give strains in ratio 4 : 1.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Ratio of escape speed to orbital speed for a satellite orbiting just above the surface
questions.why: Escape speed √(2gR) divided by orbital speed √(gR) just above the surface is √2.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A ball is dropped from 80 m. Distance covered in the last second (g = 10):
questions.why: From 80 m, fall time t = √(2h/g) = 4 s. Distance in the 4th second = g(2n − 1)/2 = 10 × 7/2 = 35 m.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Water flows through a horizontal pipe: at A (area 4 cm²) speed 1 m/s; at B (area 1 cm²). Pressure difference P_A − P_B (ρ = 1000):
questions.why: By continuity v_B = 4 × 1 = 4 m/s. By Bernoulli, P_A − P_B = ½ρ(v_B² − v_A²) = ½ × 1000 × (16 − 1) = 7500 Pa.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A Carnot engine of efficiency 40% has its sink at 300 K. To raise efficiency to 50%, the source temperature must rise by
questions.why: At 40% efficiency, 1 − 300/T₁ = 0.4, so T₁ = 500 K. At 50%, 1 − 300/T₁ = 0.5, so T₁ = 600 K. The source temperature must rise by 100 K.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A 2 kg block on a smooth floor is attached to a spring (k = 50 N/m) and pulled 0.2 m. Maximum speed:
questions.why: ω = √(k/m) = √(50/2) = 5 rad/s. The maximum speed is Aω = 0.2 × 5 = 1 m/s.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Two simple pendulums of lengths 1 m and 1.21 m start swinging together in phase. After how many oscillations of the shorter one will they be in phase again?
questions.why: T ∝ √L, so the periods are in the ratio 1 : 1.1. When the shorter one has made 11 oscillations the longer has made 10, so they are in phase again after 11 oscillations of the shorter pendulum.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A uniform chain of length L lies on a smooth table with length l hanging over the edge. Work needed to pull the hanging part back (mass M):
questions.why: The hanging part has mass Ml/L and its centre of mass is l/2 below the table. Raising it by l/2 needs W = (Ml/L) g (l/2) = Mgl²/2L.

questions.q: Mock 2 · A gas with γ = 1.5 expands adiabatically to 4 times its volume. Its absolute temperature becomes
questions.why: For an adiabatic process TV^(γ−1) is constant. With γ = 1.5 and V → 4V, T₂ = T₁(1/4)^0.5 = T₁/2.

school-c11-polsci.title: Class 11 Political Science · Indian Constitution at Work
school-c11-polsci.description: Chapter courses for Class 11 political science on the Indian Constitution: why and how it was made, fundamental rights, elections and representation, and the executive — with articles, timelines, case studies and source-based practice. General education, not legal advice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Constitution: Why and How?
courses.summary: What a constitution does, what makes it authoritative, how the Constituent Assembly was formed and worked, the Objectives Resolution, and the provisions India adapted from other constitutions.
outcomes: Learners can state the functions of a constitution
Learners can explain the composition and working of the Constituent Assembly
Learners can relate the Objectives Resolution to the Preamble
Learners can identify borrowed features and their sources
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Why do we need a constitution?

scenes.text: In a new housing society, residents fight over parking, water timings and who decides.
They agree on a written rulebook: who is the committee, how it is chosen, and what it cannot do.

steps.title: Functions of a constitution
steps.body:
1) **Coordination and assurance** — a set of basic rules allowing minimal coordination among members.
2) **Specification of decision-making powers** — who has power to make decisions and how governments are constituted.
3) **Limitations on the powers of government** — fundamental rights that government cannot violate.
4) **Aspirations and goals of society** — e.g. a just society (Directive Principles).
5) **Fundamental identity of a people** — the collective identity; a moral identity and political institutions.

steps.title: What makes it authoritative
steps.body:
- **Mode of promulgation**: who drafted it and how — the Indian Constitution was drafted by a Constituent Assembly of popular leaders with wide legitimacy.
- **Substantive provisions**: does it protect freedom and equality for all?
- **Balanced institutional design**: no single institution monopolises power — checks and balances; flexible yet not easily changed.

steps.title: Solved: case on limits
steps.body: **Case:** A government passes a law banning all criticism of ministers. **Q:** Which function of the Constitution is relevant? **A:** **Limiting government power** — freedom of speech (Art 19) is a fundamental right; courts can strike down laws that violate it, subject only to reasonable restrictions.

steps.title: Solved: Nepal and South Africa
steps.body: Constitutions can fail if designed by few or not accepted by people (e.g. Nepal's monarchy-era constitutions were replaced after people's movements; Nepal adopted a new constitution in 2015). South Africa's 1996 constitution emerged from negotiation after apartheid — wide legitimacy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: A constitution is not just 'a book of laws' — it is the **framework** that sets up and limits government.

activity.prompt: Match the function to the example
pairs: Agreed rules for everyone in society
Parliament makes laws; how it is elected

quiz.q: Fundamental Rights mainly serve to:
quiz.why: Limits.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a function of a constitution?
quiz.why: Not a function.

quiz.q: Authority of a constitution depends partly on:
quiz.why: Who made it.

quiz.q: Balanced institutional design means:
quiz.why: Checks.

quiz.q: Directive Principles express:
quiz.why: Goals.

scenes.text: Members gather in the Constitution Hall (now Central Hall of Parliament) in New Delhi.
About three years later, on 26 November 1949, they adopt the Constitution.

steps.title: Composition
steps.body: Formed under the **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946)**. Members were **elected indirectly** by members of the provincial legislative assemblies — roughly one seat per 10 lakh population; seats in each province divided among Muslims, Sikhs and General in proportion to population. Princely states nominated their representatives. After Partition, the Assembly for India had **299 members** (as of 31 December 1947). First meeting: **9 December 1946**; re-assembled as the Assembly of divided India on **14 August 1947**.

steps.title: How it worked
steps.body:
- **Dr Rajendra Prasad** — President of the Assembly.
- **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** — Chairman of the **Drafting Committee**.
- **Eight major committees**, e.g. headed by Nehru, Patel, Prasad, Ambedkar, Maulana Azad.
- Decisions by debate and consensus; inherited the **national movement's** consensus (e.g. Nehru Report **1928**; Karachi session of Congress **1931** resolution on rights).
- Adopted **26 November 1949** (now Constitution Day); came into force **26 January 1950**. Total time: **2 years, 11 months and 18 days**; 166 days of sittings.

steps.title: Solved: was the Assembly representative?
steps.body: 1) Not elected by universal franchise — but it included members of all religious communities, castes, women and diverse views. 2) Debates were open and principled. 3) Its legitimacy also came from the national movement's broad consensus. So it was broadly representative, though indirectly elected.

steps.title: Solved: date arithmetic
steps.body: From 9 Dec 1946 to 26 Nov 1949 = 2 years, 11 months, 17 days counted strictly; the commonly quoted figure is **2 years, 11 months and 18 days** (counting both ends).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adopted 26 Nov 1949 ≠ in force 26 Jan 1950. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, not the Assembly.

activity.prompt: Order these events

events.text: Nehru Report outlines a constitution for India
Karachi Congress resolution on fundamental rights
Cabinet Mission Plan; Assembly first meets on 9 December

quiz.q: President of the Constituent Assembly:
quiz.why: Prasad.

quiz.q: Members were elected by:
quiz.why: Indirect.

quiz.q: Constitution came into force on:
quiz.why: Republic Day.

quiz.q: Members after Partition (Dec 1947):
The Constituent Assembly was formed under the:

scenes.text: The framers studied constitutions of Britain, the USA, Ireland, France and Canada.
They borrowed tools but shaped them to India's needs.

steps.title: Objectives Resolution (13 Dec 1946, Nehru)
steps.body: Key points: India an **independent, sovereign republic**; a union of territories; autonomous units with residuary powers (later changed); all power derived from the people; **justice — social, economic, political; equality of status and opportunity; freedoms** of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship, vocation, association and action; safeguards for minorities, backward and tribal areas, depressed classes; integrity of territory; India to contribute to world peace. It inspired the **Preamble**.

steps.title: Borrowed features
steps.body:
- **British**: first-past-the-post; parliamentary government; rule of law; Speaker's office; law-making procedure.
- **USA**: charter of fundamental rights; **judicial review**; independence of judiciary.
- **Ireland**: **Directive Principles of State Policy**.
- **France**: liberty, equality, fraternity.
- **Canada**: quasi-federal government (strong centre); idea of residual powers with the centre.

steps.title: Solved: was borrowing 'blind'?
steps.body: No: 1) Framers adapted provisions to Indian conditions (e.g. fundamental rights with reasonable restrictions). 2) They added unique features (e.g. reservation, DPSP blended with rights). 3) They debated each clause. The Constitution is a **creative adaptation**.

steps.title: Solved: identify the source
steps.body: 'Courts can strike down unconstitutional laws' → judicial review → **USA**. 'Candidate with most votes wins' → FPTP → **UK**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: DPSP came from **Ireland**, not the USSR.

activity.prompt: Match the feature to its source

quiz.q: The Objectives Resolution was moved by:
quiz.why: Nehru.

quiz.q: Judicial review was borrowed from:
quiz.why: USA.

quiz.q: Liberty, equality, fraternity — source:
quiz.why: French Revolution.

quiz.q: The Objectives Resolution inspired the:
quiz.why: Preamble.

quiz.q: Parliamentary form came from:
quiz.why: UK.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — sit in the Constituent Assembly

scenes.text: You are a member in 1948. A clause on rights is being debated.
You must balance freedom, unity and social justice.

steps.title: How framers reasoned

courses.title: Ch 2 · Rights in the Indian Constitution
courses.summary: Bill of rights, the six Fundamental Rights with articles, writs and constitutional remedies, the NHRC, Directive Principles, Fundamental Duties, and the relationship between rights and directive principles.
outcomes: Learners can list the six Fundamental Rights with article numbers
Learners can match situations to the correct writ
Learners can distinguish Fundamental Rights from Directive Principles
Learners can analyse cases involving rights
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A girl is refused entry to a public well because of her caste.
Her family learns the Constitution forbids this — and that untouchability is abolished.

steps.title: Bill of rights
steps.body: Fundamental Rights (**Part III**) are a **bill of rights** — protected and guaranteed by the Constitution, enforceable in courts. They can be limited only by reasonable restrictions, and changed only by constitutional amendment.

steps.title: The six rights
steps.body:
1) **Right to Equality** (Arts **14–18**): equality before law/equal protection; no discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; equal opportunity in public employment; **abolition of untouchability (Art 17)**; abolition of titles.
2) **Right to Freedom** (Arts **19–22**): six freedoms in Art 19 (speech & expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession); protection in conviction; **Art 21 life and personal liberty**; **Art 21A** education for children 6–14 (added by the 86th Amendment, 2002); protection against arbitrary arrest (Art 22).
3) **Right against Exploitation** (Arts **23–24**): no trafficking or forced labour; no child below 14 in hazardous work.
4) **Freedom of Religion** (Arts **25–28**).
5) **Cultural and Educational Rights** (Arts **29–30**): minorities can set up and run educational institutions.
6) **Right to Constitutional Remedies** (Art **32**).

steps.title: Right to property
steps.body: Originally a Fundamental Right; removed by the **44th Amendment (1978)** and made a legal right under **Art 300A**.

steps.title: Solved: identify the right
steps.body: A factory employs 12-year-olds in fireworks → **Right against Exploitation (Art 24)**. A state law says only locals can sell vegetables in a market without reason → **Right to Equality / Freedom of profession**.

steps.title: Solved: Art 21 expanded
steps.body: Courts read Art 21 broadly to include right to livelihood, shelter, clean environment, privacy (privacy judgment 2017, Puttaswamy), and speedy trial.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: There are **six** Fundamental Rights now, not seven (property removed).

scenes.text: A young man is detained by police and not produced before a magistrate.
His sister's lawyer files a petition asking the court to order: 'produce the body'.

steps.title: Heart and soul
steps.body: Dr Ambedkar called the **Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art 32)** the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. Citizens can move the **Supreme Court** (Art 32) or **High Courts** (Art 226) directly when rights are violated.

steps.title: Five writs
steps.body:
- **Habeas corpus** ('have the body'): produce an arrested person before court; release if detention unlawful.
- **Mandamus**: order to a public official to perform a legal duty.
- **Prohibition**: higher court orders a lower court to stop proceeding beyond its jurisdiction.
- **Quo warranto**: 'by what authority' — challenges a person holding a public office without right.
- **Certiorari**: higher court transfers a case from a lower court/authority to itself (quash).

steps.title: National Human Rights Commission
steps.body: Established in **1993** by law. Composition: a former Chief Justice of India (chair), former judges, and experts. It inquires into complaints of human rights violations, visits jails, makes recommendations — it cannot punish but its role in raising awareness and recommending action is important.

steps.title: Solved: choose the writ
steps.body: Municipal officer refuses to issue a licence despite all conditions met → **mandamus**. A person appointed to a public post without required qualification → **quo warranto**.

steps.title: Solved: why Art 32 is 'heart and soul'
steps.body: Without a remedy, rights are mere words. Art 32 makes rights enforceable, and itself is a fundamental right.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Prohibition stops a case in progress; certiorari quashes/transfers an order already made.

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the writ

scenes.text: A state launches midday meals to improve nutrition and school attendance.
No court ordered it originally — but the Constitution's Directive Principles guide such policies.

steps.title: Directive Principles (Part IV)
steps.body: Guidelines for governments, **non-justiciable** (not enforceable in court) but 'fundamental in governance'. Goals: welfare of people; social, economic and political justice; raising standard of living; equitable distribution of resources; international peace. Policies: uniform civil code; prohibition of alcohol; promotion of cottage industries; prevention of cow slaughter; village panchayats. Non-justiciable rights: adequate livelihood; equal pay for equal work for men and women; right to work.

steps.title: Fundamental Duties
steps.body: Added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)** in **Article 51A** — e.g. respect the Constitution, national flag and anthem; defend the country; promote harmony; protect the environment; develop scientific temper; safeguard public property; (11th duty added in 2002) parents to provide opportunities for education to children 6–14. Duties do not make rights conditional.

steps.title: Solved: FR vs DPSP
steps.body:
| FR | DPSP |
- Justiciable vs non-justiciable.
- Protect individuals vs promote social welfare.
- Restrict state ('negative') vs direct state to act ('positive').
Conflicts (e.g. property rights vs land reform) were resolved through amendments and court judgments balancing both.

steps.title: Solved: case
steps.body: **Case:** A state bans liquor. **Q:** Which part supports it? **A:** DPSP (prohibition of intoxicating drinks injurious to health).

steps.title: Common mistakes

courses.title: Ch 3 · Election and Representation
courses.summary: Direct and indirect democracy, first-past-the-post vs proportional representation, why India chose FPTP, reserved constituencies, universal adult franchise, the Election Commission and electoral reforms.
outcomes: Learners can compare FPTP and PR with worked examples
Learners can explain why India adopted FPTP
Learners can describe reservation of constituencies and delimitation
Learners can describe the powers of the Election Commission
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: In a constituency, candidate A gets 38% votes, B 35%, C 27%.
A wins the seat — even though 62% voted for someone else.

steps.title: Democracy and elections
steps.body: In large societies, **indirect (representative) democracy** is the norm — citizens elect representatives. Elections are the mechanism; the Constitution sets the rules.

steps.title: First-past-the-post (FPTP)
steps.body: Country divided into small geographical constituencies; each elects **one** representative; the candidate with **most votes** wins (need not be majority) — 'plurality system'. Used for **Lok Sabha and state assemblies**. Voters vote for a **candidate**. Can give a party more seats than its vote share.

steps.title: Proportional representation (PR)
steps.body: Larger constituencies; several representatives; seats shared in **proportion to votes**. Voters often vote for a **party**; parties release lists. Example: **Israel** (whole country one constituency; threshold — currently 3.25%); **Netherlands** similar. India uses PR with **single transferable vote** for **Rajya Sabha, President and Vice-President**.

steps.title: Solved: PR seat allocation
steps.body: 100 seats; A 40%, B 35%, C 25% → A 40, B 35, C 25 seats. Under FPTP, if A narrowly leads in most constituencies, A could win, say, 60+ seats with 40% votes.

steps.title: Solved: STV quota (Rajya Sabha)
steps.body: Quota = (Total votes ÷ (seats + 1)) + 1. A state with 200 MLAs electing 4 members: 200/5 + 1 = **41** first-preference votes needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: FPTP winner needs **plurality**, not majority (50%+).

activity.prompt: A state assembly has 140 MLAs and must elect 6 Rajya Sabha members by STV. What is the quota of votes needed (formula: total/(seats+1) + 1, take the whole-number part of the division)?

lessons.title: Why FPTP in India, reservations and franchise

scenes.text: A constituency is reserved for Scheduled Castes.
Only SC candidates can contest — but every voter in the constituency, of any caste, votes.

steps.title: Why FPTP?
steps.body: 1) **Simple** — easy for voters, many of whom were not literate in 1950. 2) Clear choice of candidates, not just parties. 3) Representative **accountable to a locality**. 4) Tends to produce **stable governments**. 5) Encourages broad coalitions of social groups within parties rather than parties for single groups.

steps.title: Reserved constituencies
steps.body: Seats reserved for **SCs and STs** in Lok Sabha and assemblies in proportion to their population. All voters vote; only members of the group can contest. **Delimitation Commission**, appointed by the President, works with the Election Commission to draw boundaries and decide reserved seats. Women's reservation: the **106th Amendment (2023)** provides one-third reservation for women in Lok Sabha and assemblies, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.

steps.title: Universal adult franchise
steps.body: Every adult citizen can vote regardless of caste, religion, gender, education, property. Voting age reduced from **21 to 18** by the **61st Amendment (1988; in force 1989)**. Any citizen aged **25+** can contest Lok Sabha/assembly elections (30 for Rajya Sabha/Legislative Council).

steps.title: Solved: why reserved constituencies, not separate electorates?
steps.body: Separate electorates (only group members vote) could divide society, as seen under colonial rule. Reserved constituencies ensure representation while candidates still need support of all communities.

steps.title: Solved: eligibility
steps.body: A 23-year-old can vote but cannot contest Lok Sabha (needs 25).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: In a reserved seat, **all** voters vote; only candidates are restricted.

statements.why: All voters vote; only candidates must be SC.

scenes.text: Once elections are announced, a minister cannot inaugurate new schemes to win votes.
The Election Commission enforces the Model Code of Conduct.

steps.title: Constitution and composition
steps.body: **Article 324**: superintendence, direction and control of elections vested in an **Election Commission**. Headed by the **Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)**; a multi-member body (CEC + two Election Commissioners) since **1993**. CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge (special majority of both Houses). State Election Commissions conduct local body elections.

steps.title: Functions
steps.body:
- Prepare and update **voters' lists**.
- Decide **election schedule**.
- Enforce **Model Code of Conduct**.
- Order **re-poll**; cancel election if irregularities.
- Recognise political parties and allot **symbols**.
- Appoint observers; officers on poll duty work under EC control.

steps.title: Reforms and debates
steps.body: Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) with **VVPAT**; NOTA option (since 2013); candidates' affidavits on criminal record, assets, education; debates on state funding of elections, curbing money and muscle power, and FPTP vs PR.

steps.title: Solved: case
steps.body: **Case:** Booth capturing is reported. **Q:** What can the EC do? **A:** Countermand/stop the poll in that booth and order a **re-poll**.

steps.title: Solved: why multi-member?
steps.body: Collective decisions reduce concentration of power in one person and improve checks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The EC conducts Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, assembly, President and VP elections — **not** panchayat/municipal elections (State Election Commissions do).

courses.title: Ch 4 · Executive
courses.summary: Types of executive, the parliamentary executive in India, the President's election, powers and discretion, the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, and the permanent executive (bureaucracy).

lessons.title: Types of executive and the President

story.title: Rashtrapati Bhavan and the Cabinet room

scenes.text: The President signs a bill into law.
But the decision to propose it was taken by the Cabinet led by the Prime Minister.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Presidential** (USA, Brazil): President is head of state and government, directly elected, not accountable to legislature.
- **Parliamentary** (UK, India, Japan, Germany): PM head of government, accountable to legislature; head of state is a monarch (UK) or president (India, Germany).
- **Semi-presidential** (France, Russia, Sri Lanka): president and PM share powers.

steps.title: The President of India
steps.body: Nominal (formal) head; real power with the Council of Ministers. **Election**: indirect, by an **electoral college** of **elected MPs and elected MLAs** (and of Delhi and Puducherry), using PR with single transferable vote. Term **5 years**; removable by **impeachment** for violation of the Constitution (special majority in both Houses). **Article 74(1)**: President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers; may send advice back **once** for reconsideration (44th Amendment) — then must act on it.

steps.title: Discretionary powers
steps.body: 1) **Send back advice** for reconsideration once. 2) **Pocket veto** — the Constitution sets no time limit to act on ordinary bills; President Zail Singh held the **Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986** without action. 3) **Appointing the PM** when no party/coalition has a clear majority (hung parliament) — choosing who can prove majority.

steps.title: Solved: why indirect election?
steps.body: A directly elected president would have a popular mandate rivalling the PM; indirect election keeps the President a symbolic head and maintains parliamentary supremacy.

steps.title: Solved: case
steps.body: **Case:** After elections no party has majority; two leaders claim support. **A:** President uses discretion to invite the leader most likely to prove majority on the floor of the Lok Sabha.

steps.title: Common mistakes

lessons.title: Prime Minister and Council of Ministers

scenes.text: Several parties negotiate a common minimum programme to form a government.
The PM must keep allies happy to survive.

steps.title: Position of the PM
steps.body: The PM is the head of government and must have majority support in the **Lok Sabha**. Leader of the majority party/coalition; links Council of Ministers with President and Parliament; allocates portfolios; can recommend dissolution of Lok Sabha. PM must be or become an MP within **six months**.

steps.title: Council of Ministers
steps.body: Three ranks: **Cabinet ministers**, **Ministers of State**, **Deputy Ministers**. **Collective responsibility**: the whole ministry is responsible to the Lok Sabha; a no-confidence motion passed means the government must resign. **91st Amendment (2003)**: size of Council of Ministers limited to **15%** of the total strength of the Lok Sabha (or assembly; minimum 12 in states).

steps.title: Coalition era
steps.body: From **1989**, coalition governments became common; PMs had to consult allies, weakening single-party dominance; regional parties gained influence. Since 2014, single-party majorities returned, though in alliances.

steps.title: Solved: size limit
steps.body: Lok Sabha strength 543 → 15% = 81.45 → maximum **81** ministers.

steps.title: Solved: collective responsibility
steps.body: If the cabinet decides a policy, all ministers must defend it in public even if they disagreed privately; dissenting ministers resign.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Council of Ministers is responsible to the **Lok Sabha**, not the Rajya Sabha.
