steps.title: Political vs permanent executive
steps.body: **Political executive**: elected leaders (PM, ministers) who change with elections. **Permanent executive**: civil servants who implement policies, remain in office regardless of government, and must be **politically neutral** and professional.

steps.title: Recruitment
steps.body: **Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)** recruits for central services; **State PSCs** for state services. Members of UPSC/PSCs have fixed tenure and are removable only through an inquiry by a Supreme Court judge — ensuring independence. **All India Services** (IAS, IPS) are recruited by the centre but serve in states; state cannot take disciplinary action without consulting the centre. Reservations for SC, ST, OBC; open competitive exams ensure merit.

steps.title: Solved: why neutrality matters
steps.body: If officials favour one party, administration loses public trust; neutral civil servants give continuity and impartial service to all citizens.

steps.title: Solved: critique
steps.body: Common criticisms: red tape, insensitivity to ordinary citizens, political interference (transfers). Remedies: **RTI Act 2005**, citizen charters, e-governance.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Rules

school-c11-psychology.title: Class 11 Psychology (NCERT-based)
school-c11-psychology.description: Original, exam-ready chapter notes for Class 11 Psychology: what psychology is, methods of enquiry, learning and memory, with solved examples, common mistakes and chapter tests. General education, not clinical advice.

courses.title: Ch 1 · What is Psychology?
courses.summary: Definition, goals, evolution, branches and fields of psychology, and how it differs from other sciences.
outcomes: Define psychology as a science of mental processes, experiences and behaviour
State the goals: describe, explain, predict, control
Trace the schools: structuralism, functionalism, behaviourism, Gestalt, psychoanalysis, humanism, cognitivism
Name major branches and the role of a psychologist

story.title: Why did Aman freeze on stage?

scenes.text: Aman, a confident student, forgot his speech on stage and his hands shook.
A psychologist would observe what he did, ask how he felt and thought, and look for causes such as fear of evaluation.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
Psychology is the **scientific study of mental processes, experiences and behaviour in different contexts**. *Mental processes* = thinking, remembering, feeling. *Experiences* = subjective, internal (e.g. pain). *Behaviour* = observable responses (walking, speaking, blushing).

It is a **science** because it uses systematic, objective, empirical methods and its findings can be checked by others.

steps.title: Solved example · four goals
steps.body:
Case: A school notes that marks fall in Class 11 in the Physics unit test.
- **Describe:** record how many students and which topics lost marks.
- **Explain:** find why — e.g. weak maths base, exam anxiety.
- **Predict:** who is likely to struggle in the next test.
- **Control/influence:** introduce remedial classes and relaxation training; then re-measure.
NCERT also adds *enhancement of quality of life* as an application goal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying psychology only studies abnormal behaviour; it studies normal and abnormal.
- Equating behaviour only with observable acts; mental processes are inferred from behaviour.
- Confusing *explain* (find causes) with *predict* (forecast outcomes).

activity.prompt: Match goal to example
pairs: Counting how many students feel exam stress
Finding that sleep loss lowers attention

quiz.why: It covers mental processes, experiences and behaviour.

quiz.why: Explanation = identifying causes.

quiz.q: Why is psychology called a science?
quiz.why: Science = systematic, empirical, verifiable.

lessons.title: Evolution of psychology and its schools

scenes.text: In 1879 Wilhelm Wundt opened a laboratory in Leipzig to study conscious experience by introspection.
Later thinkers argued that only observable behaviour, or the unconscious, or the whole person should be studied.

steps.title: Schools in order
steps.body:
- **Structuralism** (Wundt, Titchener): break consciousness into elements using introspection.
- **Functionalism** (William James): what is the *purpose* of mental processes in adapting.
- **Behaviourism** (Watson, later Skinner): study only observable behaviour and learning.
- **Gestalt** (Wertheimer, Köhler, Koffka): the whole is more than the sum of parts.
- **Psychoanalysis** (Freud): unconscious motives and childhood.
- **Humanism** (Maslow, Rogers): free will, growth, self-actualisation.
- **Cognitivism**: mind as information processor; memory, thinking, language.

steps.title: Psychology in India
steps.body: Modern psychology began in India at the University of Calcutta, where the first department was set up in 1915 and the first practical laboratory in 1916 (Narendra Nath Sen Gupta, Girindrasekhar Bose in psychoanalysis). Indian traditions like yoga and the Gita also offer ideas on self and mind.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving Freud as founder of the first laboratory — it was Wundt (1879).
- Mixing structuralism (what elements) with functionalism (what for).
- Writing that behaviourists study the mind directly; they avoided it.

scenes.text: Meera works in a school helping children with learning difficulties.

steps.title: Major branches
steps.body:
- **Cognitive:** attention, memory, thinking.
- **Developmental:** change across the lifespan.
- **Social:** how people influence each other.
- **Clinical/Counselling:** diagnosis, therapy, guidance.
- **Educational:** learning and teaching.
- **Industrial/Organisational:** workplace behaviour.
- **Health, Sports, Environmental, Forensic** psychology are applied fields.

steps.body:
1. Studying why teenagers conform to peers → **Social**.
2. Designing a study plan for a child with dyslexia → **Educational**.
3. Treating panic attacks with CBT → **Clinical**.
Tip: first ask *who is studied* and *what problem*.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Methods of Enquiry in Psychology
courses.summary: Goals of enquiry, observation, experiment, survey, case study, tests, variables, and ethics.
outcomes: Identify independent, dependent and extraneous variables
Compare experimental, correlational and survey methods
Describe observation and interview types
Apply ethical guidelines in research

scenes.text: Nisha believes soft music improves recall, so she tests two groups of 20 students.
One group learns a word list with music and the other in silence; both are tested after 10 minutes.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body:
- **Independent variable (IV):** manipulated by the researcher (music vs silence).
- **Dependent variable (DV):** measured outcome (words recalled).
- **Extraneous variables:** other factors that may affect DV (noise, time of day) — must be controlled.
- **Experimental group** gets the treatment; **control group** does not.
- **Random assignment** spreads individual differences evenly.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Music group mean = 14 words, silence group mean = 11 words.
- Difference = 14 − 11 = **3 words**.
- IV = music; DV = number of words recalled.
- If the music group were all morning-batch students, time of day would be a **confounding extraneous variable**; random assignment fixes this.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the measured variable independent.
- Believing correlation proves cause; only a controlled experiment supports causation.
- Using different tests for the two groups.

quiz.why: IV is manipulated.

lessons.title: Observation, survey, interview, case study, tests

scenes.text: A principal wants to know why attendance drops in winter.
She could observe classes, survey students, interview teachers, study one failing class in depth, or use a test.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **Observation:** naturalistic (real setting) or controlled; participant vs non-participant.
- **Survey:** questionnaires/interviews on large samples; quick but self-report bias.
- **Interview:** structured, unstructured, focus-group.
- **Case study:** in-depth study of one person/group; rich detail but cannot generalise.
- **Psychological tests:** standardised, reliable and valid tools to measure traits.
- **Correlational research:** relation between variables, coefficient from −1 to +1.

steps.title: Solved example · reading r
steps.body:
- r = +0.82 between hours of study and marks: strong positive.
- r = −0.45 between screen time and sleep: moderate negative.
- r = 0.05: practically no relation.
Never say r = +0.82 means study *causes* 82% of marks.

steps.title: Reliability vs validity
steps.body: A test is **reliable** if it gives consistent results; **valid** if it measures what it claims. A faulty scale that always reads 2 kg more is reliable but not valid.

pairs: Behaviour of children in a playground

quiz.why: Consistency = reliability.

scenes.text: Before a stress study, volunteers read what will happen and sign if they agree.
One participant decides to leave halfway; the researcher thanks her and deletes her data.

steps.title: Ethical principles
steps.body:
- **Informed consent** (parent/guardian consent for minors).
- **Voluntary participation** and the right to withdraw.
- **Confidentiality / anonymity** of data.
- **No harm**, minimising stress.
- **Debriefing** after deception, which must be justified.
- Honest reporting; no fabrication.

steps.title: Solved example · spot the violation
steps.body: A teacher reads out students' counselling scores in class → breach of **confidentiality**. A researcher tells students their marks depend on joining the study → breach of **voluntariness**.

steps.title: Limitations
steps.body: Human behaviour varies with culture and context; people may give socially desirable answers; observer bias; findings are probabilistic, not certainties.

courses.title: Ch 6 · Learning
courses.summary: Classical and operant conditioning, observational learning, cognitive learning, and applications.
outcomes: Explain Pavlov's classical conditioning with UCS, UCR, CS, CR
Apply Skinner's reinforcement and punishment
Describe Bandura's observational learning
Distinguish insight and latent learning

scenes.text: A bell rings every time a dog is fed.
After many pairings the dog salivates to the bell alone.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body:
**Learning** = relatively permanent change in behaviour due to experience (not maturation, fatigue or drugs).
- **UCS** food → **UCR** salivation (natural).
- **Neutral stimulus** bell becomes **CS** after pairing; the learned response is **CR**.
- **Acquisition**, **extinction** (CS without UCS), **spontaneous recovery**, **generalisation**, **discrimination**.
- Timing: CS just *before* UCS works best (delayed conditioning).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
A child gets an injection (UCS → fear UCR) from a doctor in a white coat. Later white coats alone cause fear.
- UCS = injection; UCR = fear/pain.
- CS = white coat; CR = fear.
- Extinction: repeated visits with no injection reduce the fear.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the bell the UCS.
- Saying extinction erases learning permanently — spontaneous recovery can occur.
- Assuming CR and UCR are identical in strength; the CR is usually weaker.

activity.prompt: Sort the parts of Pavlov's experiment

quiz.why: Learned response.

quiz.why: Generalisation.

scenes.text: Riya's teacher praises her each time she submits homework on time.
Riya submits on time more often.

steps.title: Skinner's principles
steps.body:
Behaviour is shaped by its **consequences**.
- **Positive reinforcement:** add a pleasant stimulus → behaviour increases.
- **Negative reinforcement:** remove an unpleasant stimulus → behaviour increases (taking a pill to remove a headache).
- **Punishment:** reduces behaviour (positive: add unpleasant; negative: remove pleasant).
- Schedules: fixed/variable ratio and interval; **variable ratio** gives the most resistance to extinction (e.g. slot machines).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
1. A child gets a sticker for each 5 sums solved → **fixed ratio**, positive reinforcement.
2. A student studies to escape a parent's nagging → **negative reinforcement**.
3. Phone taken away for lying → **negative punishment**.
Test: does the behaviour go up (reinforcement) or down (punishment)?

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. It *strengthens* behaviour by removing something unpleasant.

scenes.text: Four-year-old Kabir copies how his sister brushes her teeth.
A monkey in a room stacks boxes to reach a banana after sitting still for a while.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Observational learning** (Bandura): learning by watching a model. Processes: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation; vicarious reinforcement matters. Bandura's Bobo doll study showed children copy aggression.
- **Insight learning** (Köhler): sudden grasp of the solution, as chimpanzee Sultan joined sticks.
- **Latent learning** (Tolman): learning without reinforcement shows up later when rewarded (cognitive maps in rats).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Rats given no food reward wander a maze; later food is placed and they quickly run to it, as fast as always-rewarded rats.
- Learning was hidden until motivation arrived → **latent learning**.
- Supports cognitive maps, a challenge to strict behaviourism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that observational learning needs the learner's own reinforcement; vicarious reinforcement is enough.
- Confusing insight (sudden) with trial and error (gradual).

courses.title: Ch 7 · Human Memory
courses.summary: Memory processes, stores, levels of processing, types of long-term memory, forgetting and improving memory.
outcomes: Explain encoding, storage and retrieval
Describe sensory, short-term and long-term memory with capacity and duration
Distinguish declarative and procedural memory
Apply mnemonics and spaced practice

scenes.text: Tara hears a number, repeats it silently, dials it, then forgets it by evening.
Her own home address, however, is never forgotten.

steps.title: Atkinson–Shiffrin model
steps.body:
- **Encoding** (put in), **storage** (retain), **retrieval** (get out).
- **Sensory memory:** very brief (about 0.25–0.5 s for iconic, 2–4 s for echoic).
- **Short-term memory (STM):** about 7 ± 2 items (Miller), roughly 20–30 seconds without rehearsal; **chunking** raises capacity.
- **Long-term memory (LTM):** very large capacity, potentially lifelong.
Maintenance rehearsal keeps items in STM; elaborative rehearsal moves them to LTM.

steps.title: Solved example · chunking
steps.body: The 10 digits 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 are 10 items. Grouped as 987 – 654 – 3210 they become 3 chunks, well within STM span.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying STM holds 7 ± 2 *letters*; it is 7 ± 2 *chunks*.
- Mixing retrieval with storage.

quiz.why: Miller's STM span.

quiz.why: Chunking.

lessons.title: Types of long-term memory and levels of processing

scenes.text: Dev hasn't ridden a cycle for years yet balances at once.
He also remembers that Jaipur is the capital of Rajasthan and his last birthday party.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- **Declarative (explicit):** knowing *what* — **episodic** (personal events) and **semantic** (facts).
- **Procedural (implicit):** knowing *how* (cycling, typing).
- **Levels of processing** (Craik & Lockhart): shallow (structural, phonetic) vs deep (semantic) — deeper processing gives better retention.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
- 'I ate dosa at my cousin's wedding' → episodic.
- 'Water boils at 100 °C at sea level' → semantic.
- Tying shoelaces → procedural.
A word judged for meaning ('is it a fruit?') is remembered better than one judged for font — depth effect.

steps.title: Study tip
steps.body: Ask yourself why and how for each fact; link it to something you know.

steps.title: Why we forget
steps.body:
- **Ebbinghaus forgetting curve:** fast loss early, then levelling.
- **Decay/trace theory**, **interference** (proactive: old blocks new; retroactive: new blocks old), **retrieval failure** (tip-of-the-tongue), **motivated forgetting** (repression).
- Cues and context help retrieval (encoding specificity).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: After learning a new mobile number, a student can no longer recall her old one → **retroactive interference** (new interferes with old). If the old number keeps coming to mind when typing the new one → **proactive interference**.

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body: Spaced practice, active recall, mnemonics (acronyms, method of loci), organisation, adequate sleep, and elaborative rehearsal.

school-c11-sociology.description: Original, exam-ready chapter notes for Class 11 Introducing Sociology: sociology and society, concepts, culture and socialisation, and research methods.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Sociology and Society
courses.summary: The sociological imagination, individual and society, pioneers, scope and relation to other social sciences.
outcomes: Explain the sociological imagination (C. Wright Mills)
Relate personal troubles and public issues
Describe the emergence of sociology
Compare sociology with economics, political science, history and anthropology

story.title: One job loss or a million?

scenes.text: When one man is unemployed in a town of 50,000 it may be a personal failing.
When a factory closes and 15 million are unemployed across a country, it is a public issue about the structure of society.

steps.title: Core idea
steps.body:
C. Wright Mills: the **sociological imagination** is the ability to link **personal troubles of milieu** to **public issues of social structure**, and individual biography to history.
- Example: divorce, unemployment, caste or gender disadvantage — each affects individuals but has social roots.
- Sociology studies society systematically, avoiding common-sense explanations that are often untested.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Question: Is a student's low attendance only a personal matter?
- Personal view: laziness.
- Sociological view: a village with no safe transport; girls' attendance falls when buses are unavailable; family pressure to work.
Both personal and structural levels matter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating common sense as sociology.
- Saying sociology only studies problems; it studies all social life.
- Writing that the term was coined by Durkheim (it was Auguste Comte).

activity.prompt: Personal trouble or public issue?

items.text: Rising divorce rate across a region

quiz.q: The sociological imagination was given by
quiz.why: Mills, 1959.

quiz.q: The term 'sociology' was coined by
quiz.why: Auguste Comte, 1830s.

quiz.q: Mass unemployment is best described as
quiz.why: Structural.

scenes.text: Between the 17th and 19th century Europe saw scientific, democratic and industrial changes.
Villagers moved to factory towns, creating new problems that demanded systematic study.

steps.title: Context
steps.body:
Sociology arose from the **Enlightenment**, the **French Revolution** and the **Industrial Revolution**: urbanisation, factory labour, poverty and shifting authority.
- Founders: Comte, Spencer, Durkheim, Marx, Weber.
- **Scope:** wide — it studies families, castes, markets, religion, state, media; can be studied at **micro** (small-scale interaction) and **macro** (large structures) levels.
- It is both a science (empirical methods) and a perspective.

steps.title: Solved example · micro or macro
steps.body: A study of how two friends talk in a canteen → micro. A study of rural–urban migration in India → macro.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Assuming sociology emerged only in India after independence; Indian sociology grew in the 20th century with Bombay (1919), Lucknow, and Delhi departments.

activity.prompt: Match

quiz.q: Macro-level study examines
quiz.why: Macro = large scale.

quiz.q: A cause of sociology's rise was
quiz.why: Industrial Revolution.

quiz.q: Sociology studies
quiz.why: Wide scope.

scenes.text: A famine in a village could be studied by an economist, a historian, a political scientist, an anthropologist and a sociologist.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Comparisons
steps.body:
- **Economics:** production, distribution and consumption of goods; sociology sees the social setting of markets (e.g. caste and trade).
- **Political science:** power, state, government; sociology studies power in all social relations.
- **History:** the past; sociology links past with present structures.
- **Anthropology:** traditionally small non-industrial societies; boundaries have blurred.
- **Psychology:** individual mind; sociology looks at groups and structures.
No discipline is isolated; they overlap and borrow methods.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Topic: 'Women's participation in the workforce.' Economist: wage rates. Political scientist: policy. Sociologist: family norms, gender roles and work opportunities. Psychologist: motivation.

steps.title: Answer-writing
steps.body: For a compare-question, use 'focus, level of study, method' in a table.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Terms, Concepts and their Use in Sociology
courses.summary: Social groups, status and role, stratification, social control, and the relation between values, norms and conflict.
outcomes: Distinguish primary and secondary groups, in-groups and out-groups
Explain status, role, role conflict and role set
Describe ascribed and achieved status
Explain social stratification and social control

scenes.text: Sunita's family is warm and personal.
Her office team meets for a specific task and relations are formal.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
A **social group** has regular interaction and a sense of belonging (unlike a mere *category* or *aggregate* such as people waiting at a bus stop).
- **Primary group** (Cooley): small, intimate, face-to-face — family, close friends.
- **Secondary group:** larger, impersonal, goal-oriented — school, company.
- **In-group / out-group** (Sumner): 'we' and 'they'.
- **Reference group** (Merton): the group whose standards we use to judge ourselves.
- **Quasi-groups** and **peer groups** also form.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Classify: (i) people at a railway platform → aggregate; (ii) a cricket club → secondary group; (iii) grandparents and grandchildren at home → primary group.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling every crowd a group; a group needs interaction and awareness.

activity.prompt: Primary or secondary group?

quiz.q: Primary groups are
quiz.why: Cooley.

quiz.q: Reference group is used for
quiz.why: Merton.

quiz.q: People waiting at a bus stop form
quiz.why: No lasting interaction.

scenes.text: Meena is a doctor, a mother and a daughter.
Her son's school event clashes with a surgery.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Status:** socially defined position with rights and duties. **Ascribed** (by birth: caste, sex, age) vs **achieved** (by effort: doctor, champion).
- **Role:** behaviour expected of a status. **Role set:** the roles attached to one status (a teacher relates to students, colleagues, parents).
- **Role conflict:** incompatible demands from different statuses. **Role strain:** tension inside one status.
- **Role stereotyping**, e.g. that nursing is only for women, and **role distance**.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Meena's surgery vs school event = **role conflict** (two statuses). A teacher expected to be both strict and friendly = **role strain** (within one status).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Mixing status and role: status is the position; role is the performance.

quiz.why: Definition.

story.title: Who sits where in the village?

scenes.text: In some villages, different castes eat, live and draw water separately.
Law and custom enforce these rules unevenly.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Social stratification:** hierarchical ranking of groups, with unequal access to resources, in systems such as caste, class, gender, race.
- Features: social, ancient, universal but variable, supported by ideology, and persistent across generations.
- **Social control:** mechanisms that secure conformity — **formal** (law, police, courts) and **informal** (family, custom, gossip, ostracism). **Sanctions** = rewards/punishments.
- **Conflict, competition, cooperation** are social processes; Indian caste inequality is challenged through constitutional provisions and movements.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: A student is fined by school for cheating (formal sanction); friends stop talking to him (informal sanction). Both enforce honesty norms.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Remember that stratification is a property of society, not an individual difference.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Culture and Socialisation
courses.summary: Meaning and dimensions of culture, cultural change, ethnocentrism, and agencies of socialisation.
outcomes: Define culture and its cognitive, normative and material dimensions
Explain cultural lag, diffusion and ethnocentrism
Describe primary and secondary socialisation and agencies
Explain how socialisation shapes the self

scenes.text: A visitor wonders why people eat with their hands while another finds forks odd.
Both are following learned, shared ways of life.

steps.title: Dimensions
steps.body:
**Culture** is the learned, shared way of life of a society (E.B. Tylor: complex whole of knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom).
- **Cognitive:** what we perceive and know — beliefs, ideas.
- **Normative:** rules of conduct — **folkways**, **mores**, laws.
- **Material:** tools, buildings, technology.
- Culture is learned, not inherited biologically, and varies across societies; **cultural relativism** vs **ethnocentrism** (judging others by one's own standards).
- **Cultural diversity** is a strength; India shows linguistic, religious and regional diversity.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Classify: 'Rain is caused by gods' → cognitive; 'Remove shoes before entering a home' → normative; 'A smartphone' → material.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating culture with only art or 'high culture'.
- Using ethnocentric judgments such as 'primitive culture'.

activity.prompt: Dimension of culture

quiz.q: Judging others by own standards is
quiz.why: Ethnocentrism.

quiz.q: Technology belongs to the
quiz.why: Physical objects.

quiz.q: Culture is
quiz.why: Acquired through learning.

scenes.text: Smartphones spread quickly but social rules about using them in meetings are still forming.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Cultural lag** (Ogburn): non-material culture changes slower than material culture.
- **Diffusion:** spread of cultural traits between societies.
- **Acculturation, assimilation, cultural diversity** and **multiculturalism**.
- **Sanskritisation** and **westernisation** (M.N. Srinivas) as processes of cultural change in India.
- **Subcultures** and **counter-cultures** exist within a culture.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Internet banking arrives faster than elderly users' trust and digital literacy → cultural lag between material tool and adjustment of attitudes.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Sanskritisation: lower castes adopting practices of higher castes for mobility; Westernisation: adopting western dress, technology, ideas.

scenes.text: A baby learns language, food habits and fear from those around her.
At school she learns rules, punctuality and peer norms.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
**Socialisation** is the lifelong process of learning culture and developing a self.
- **Primary socialisation:** early childhood in the family. **Secondary:** school, peers, media, workplace. **Anticipatory socialisation:** preparing for future roles.
- **Agencies:** family, peer group, school, mass media, religion, workplace.
- **Mead:** self develops through role-taking (play stage, game stage, 'generalised other'); **Cooley:** looking-glass self.
- **Hidden curriculum:** values learned implicitly at school.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: A child pretends to be a doctor in play → play stage (Mead). A cricketer who understands all teammates' positions → game stage.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying socialisation ends in childhood; adults learn new roles (resocialisation in migration, jail, new job).

courses.title: Ch 5 · Doing Sociology: Research Methods
courses.summary: Objectivity, subjectivity, survey, observation, interview, questionnaire and sampling.
outcomes: Explain objectivity and subjectivity in sociology
Describe survey, participant observation, interview and questionnaire
Apply simple random and stratified sampling
Recognise research problems and ethics

scenes.text: A student wants to study water use in her own locality, where she lives.
She must prevent personal bias from shaping findings.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Objectivity:** reporting facts as they are, free from personal bias; **subjectivity:** personal values and feelings that colour views. Sociologists use **reflexivity** and clear methods to reduce bias.
- Weber: understanding (*verstehen*) the meaning people attach to actions is needed in addition to observing.
- **Research steps:** choose topic → review literature → formulate hypothesis/question → decide method and sample → collect data → analyse → report.
- **Insider vs outsider** perspective: closeness gives insight but risks bias.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Hypothesis: 'Households with a tap supply use less time fetching water.' Variables: tap supply (independent) and time fetching water (dependent). Method: survey of 200 households.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Believing sociology can be 100% value-free; the aim is disciplined, transparent objectivity.

activity.prompt: Order the research steps

quiz.why: Definition.

quiz.q: Reflexivity means
options: Examining one's own role and bias
quiz.why: Self-awareness.

quiz.q: A hypothesis is
quiz.why: Proposed relationship.

scenes.text: A researcher can ask many people short questions, live among a community, or hold long conversations.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **Survey:** structured data from a large sample; strengths: breadth, quantification; weaknesses: shallow, non-response.
- **Participant observation:** researcher lives with the group; deep insight (e.g. fieldwork), time-consuming, ethical issues.
- **Non-participant observation.**
- **Interview:** structured, semi-structured, unstructured; flexible but costly.
- **Questionnaire:** written questions, open and closed; cheap but low response.
- **Secondary sources:** census, documents.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: To measure literacy across a district → survey with questionnaire. To understand rituals in a tribal village → participant observation. To study life stories of migrants → unstructured interviews.

steps.title: Triangulation
steps.body: Combining methods improves reliability.

scenes.text: A school has 500 students and the researcher can only interview 50.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Sampling
steps.body:
- **Population:** whole group; **sample:** part chosen; **sampling frame:** list from which chosen.
- **Simple random:** every unit has equal chance (lottery/random numbers).
- **Systematic:** every k-th unit with k = N ÷ n.
- **Stratified:** divide into strata (e.g. class, gender) and sample proportionally.
- **Quota, convenience, snowball:** non-probability methods.
- Good samples are representative; larger random samples reduce error.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · systematic
steps.body: N = 500, n = 50 → k = 500 ÷ 50 = **10**. Choose a random start between 1 and 10 (say 4) then 4, 14, 24 …

steps.title: Solved example 2 · stratified
steps.body: Strata: 300 girls and 200 boys; sample n = 50. Girls = 50 × 300/500 = **30**; boys = 50 × 200/500 = **20**.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling a convenient group of friends a random sample.
